### Sect. 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

...in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. For the *natural* <note>original: "animal"</note> man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God; unto him it is foolishness, and he cannot understand it. 

<margin>1 Corinthians 3:19</margin>Again, he says, "The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, for God knows that the thoughts of the wise are foolish" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia hujus mundi stultitia est apud Deum, Deus enim novit cogitationes sapientum quod stultæ sunt"</note>. By this, we may also discern that there is a wisdom falsely so called, which is entirely contrary in effect to true wisdom. Therefore, the Apostle terms it "foolishness." Consequently, the concepts of such wise men as the pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers and their followers—though they think very well of themselves—are indeed foolish and dull before God. 

Of this kind of philosophers, the prophet utters these words: 
<margin>Isaiah 5:20</margin>"Woe unto them that speak good of evil and evil of good; who put darkness for light and light for darkness; woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight." 

Does not St. James also, in open and plain terms, assign a most palpable difference between these two kinds of wisdom? 
<margin>James 3:15</margin>He says: "Wisdom that contradicts the truth does not descend from above from the Father of lights, but is earthly, natural, and diabolical; on the contrary, the wisdom which descends from above is of God" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia contradicens veritati non est de sursum descendens a patre luminum, sed terrena, animalis, diabolica: sapientia vero de sursum, est a Deo"</note>. 

By this, therefore, it is made evident that through the whole harmony of Holy Writ, "sapience" or "wisdom" is taken in a two-fold manner. Namely, there is a worldly and counterfeit wisdom which is earthly, mundane, and human—that is to say, it is of man’s invention, framed after the rudiments or elements of this world. So also, there is a true, essential, and perfect wisdom which has its root or beginning in Christ, who is God. 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:5</margin>This is according to the words of the wise man: "The word of God most high is the fountain of wisdom" <note>original Latin: "Verbum dei altissimi est sapientiæ fons"</note>. 

Since this is so, we ought not to embrace with such fervor that false and bastard philosophy which has its origin in pagan inventions, nor should we neglect that which is true and essential. I mean that which is from God, the main foundation of which is the cornerstone, Jesus Christ, who (as St. Paul tells us) fills and gives life to all things. In doing otherwise, we shall imitate the foolish Israelites, of whom the prophet Baruch says: 
<margin>Baruch 3:12</margin>"Israel has forsaken the fountain of wisdom" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia fontem Israel reliquit"</note>. He said this because they forsook or neglected the true wisdom and searched after arts, sciences, and understanding in foreign and Gentile nations—as did the Agarens <note>descendants of Hagar</note> and those who were in Teman <note>a region in Edom known for its wise men</note>, who never attained the knowledge or perfection of true wisdom because they did not acknowledge the fountain or giver of it, which is God alone. 

Shall we not, in doing so, transgress the precept of the wise prophet who says: 
<margin>Jeremiah 10:2</margin>"Do not learn the ways of the heathen, for their laws are vain" <note>original Latin: "Vias gentium nolite discere, quia leges populorum vana sunt"</note>? 

The Apostle, in another place, sufficiently and in few words signifies to us the variety and dissonance of these two several sorts of wisdom. At the same time, he seems to express a kind of bifurcation <note>original: "by-forkedness"</note> or two-fold difference in the worldly branch: 
<margin>1 Corinthians 1:22</margin>"The Greeks seek wisdom, the Jews desire signs, but we preach Christ crucified" <note>original Latin: "Sapientiam Græci quærebant, Judai signa, nos Christum crucifixum prædicamus"</note>. By this, he argues against the human, contemplative philosophy of the Greeks—such as that of the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, Stoics, and Epicureans—and the practical philosophy and visual demonstrations which the Jews preferred. Lastly, he seems to express the true and essential philosophy or study of wisdom which consists in Jesus Christ crucified. This philosophy is only of God because its essential wisdom issued from the mouth of the Almighty, the fountain of which is the word of God. 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 24:5</margin>"I came out of the mouth of the most High," says Wisdom <note>original Latin: "Ab ore Altissimi prodii"</note>. 

Therefore, the Apostle, showing the difference between the Greekish philosophy (which was spurious) and this which was truly essential, gives this warning to the chosen: 
<margin>Colossians 2:2, 8</margin>"That their hearts might be comforted, being instructed in charity and in all the riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgment of the mystery of God the Father and of Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. I say this so that no man may deceive you with enticing words. As you have therefore received Jesus Christ our Lord, so walk in him, being rooted and abounding in thanksgiving. See to it that no man deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. And you are complete in him, who is the head of all principality and power" <note>This is a modernization of a long Latin passage from Colossians 2:2–10</note>. # Mosaical Philosophy. Book 2.

*...charity, into all the riches of the fullness of understanding, in the acknowledgment of the mystery of God the Father and of Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and science <note>original: "science" here refers to systematic knowledge or the Latin "scientia."</note>. This I speak unto you, so that no one may deceive you by subtlety or persuasive speeches. As therefore you have received our Lord Jesus Christ, so walk in him, deeply rooted <note>original: "radicatedly"</note>, abounding in thanksgiving. See that no man deceives you by philosophy and vain fallacies or sophistries, framed through the tradition of men, according to the elements of this world and not by Christ, forasmuch as in him dwells the plenitude or fullness of the Godhead bodily. And you are full in him, who is the head of all principalities and powers <note>original: "poteſtates"</note>, etc.* Out of which words, there are these notable things to be selected or gathered:

<margin>Colossians 2:3</margin>
First, that all the fullness of understanding consists in the revelation and knowledge of the mystery of God and his Son Jesus Christ; because in *Christ only is all the treasure of wisdom and science hidden.* And therefore it is but a folly to seek true and essential science, understanding, and wisdom from those who did not possess them.

Secondly, that the smooth-tongued orators, deceitful sophists, and vain philosophers of this world are to be avoided and in no way for the most part to be believed; forasmuch as they are only superficial and scarcely probable, being that, in essence and truth, they are nothing else—regarding their groundwork—but fiction or mere imagination.

Thirdly, that there is a philosophy, and consequently a wisdom, which is derived from the invention and tradition of men and according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ. This spurious <note>original: "spurious" meaning false or illegitimate</note> wisdom ought therefore to be forsaken, or at least not so strictly followed by those who are followers of Christ.

<margin>Colossians 2:8-9</margin>
Fourthly, that there is a true philosophy, and therefore a wisdom, which is according to Christ, forasmuch as in him *only consists all the treasures of perfect science, knowledge, understanding, and wisdom. This is framed not according to the traditions of men and the elements of this world—which is earthly <note>original: "terrene"</note>, natural <note>original: "animal"</note>, diabolical, and contradicts the truth—but according to that which descends from God the Father of lights, as St. James tells us.* <margin>James 3:15</margin> 

Upon the foundation, therefore, of this human or worldly <note>original: "mundan"</note> wisdom was the philosophy of the Grecians erected. This appears, first, because the Apostle denies it to be the true philosophy, being that it is not grounded on the cornerstone Jesus Christ. This is evident by the behavior and speech he made to the philosophers of *Athens*. For when the sect of the Epicureans and Stoics did discourse with him—after he had exhorted them from their idolatry and worshipping of false and unknown gods by the reasons of divine philosophy, and had preached to them the true wisdom (which was Jesus Christ and the resurrection of the dead), and consequently instructed them in the foundation of the true and real philosophy—some of them replied, *"What will this verbal babbler say?"* <note>original: "verball babler" translates the Greek "spermologos," a term of contempt for one who picks up scraps of knowledge.</note> and others, exclaiming against him, asserted that he was a proclaimer of new deities <note>original: "demons," used here in the classical sense of spirits or gods.</note>. <margin>Acts 17:18</margin> 

The said divine philosopher and holy Apostle replied thus: *"You men of Athens, I perceive that in all things you are too superstitious <note>In the 17th century, "superstitious" could mean "very religious" or "scrupulous in religion."</note>: for I found an altar whereon was written, 'To the unknown God'; whom you then ignorantly worship, him show I unto you, etc."* <margin>Acts 17:22</margin> Note by the way that he argues by this speech that they knew not the true grounds of philosophy, being ignorant of the true God, who is the fountain of essential wisdom. Then he proceeds thus: <margin>Acts 17:24</margin> *"God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwells not in temples made with hands, neither is worshipped with men’s hands as though he needed anything, seeing he gives to all life, and breath, and all things, etc."* 

I would have you to mark the excellency of the true wise man, namely, how he speaks the divine wisdom—and therefore the solid and essential philosophy—to the worldly philosophers of *Athens*. For he expresses in the aforementioned text that the Spirit of God or Christ (which is God) does not dwell in artificial temples, but makes every natural thing his sanctuary. Above all creatures, and by supreme excellence, he points at Man (as you shall see hereafter). And therefore he affirms that the same divine spirit of wisdom gives to every creature (for his words are, *He gives to all) life, breath, and all things.* Therefore, if he gives to all things, then there is not anything that is given its nature <note>term: "naturated" means to be endowed with a specific nature or essence.</note> by it but lives and breathes or has its existence from and in this wisdom. This is therefore rightly termed the cornerstone, forasmuch as all creatures rely on him and exist through him. And therefore it is <margin>John 1:1, 9</margin> he only who is *that light of the world, in whom is that life which gives life <note>original: "vivifie"</note> to all things.*

...the earth, then was wisdom with him, composing or making all things. By this, he argues, first, the antiquity of the eternal wisdom; and then he proves that she was the composer and maker of heaven and earth, and consequently of every thing within them, both invisible and visible. This agrees in all things with the teachings of our sacred and essential philosopher, Moses, where he first acknowledges an abyss without form. Then, he shows that the unformed matter of the abyss was, by the presence of God’s emanating Spirit, universally given form and called "waters." <margin>Genesis 1</margin> 

Then, by the acting of the divine or essential voice or word, *"Fiat"* <note>Latin: "Let it be done"</note>, which was uttered by the mouth of the Almighty, the light (or created form) was produced in the waters. Afterwards, by the will of the Creator, the word was pronounced a second time, and the waters above were divided from the waters beneath by the firmament; thus, the heavens were made by the second *fiat*. By the third *fiat*, the division of the lower waters into elements was achieved by the assistance of this one and the self-same word, or the <term>Spageric</term> <note>original: "Spagerick"; referring to the alchemical process of separating and recombining elements</note> operation of this divine and universal Spirit, *Elohim*, though acting through different properties. 

<margin>Psalm 33:6</margin> Does not David affirm as much in a few words, saying, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power" <note>original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt cæli & Spiritu ab ore ejus omnis virtus eorum"</note>? <margin>Psalm 104:24</margin> Again, "In wisdom you have made all things" <note>original: "In sapientia omnia fecisti"</note>. <margin>2 Peter 3:5</margin> And St. Peter says, "The heavens were of old, and the earth consisting out of water and through water by the word of God" <note>original: "Cæli erant prius & terra de aqua, & per aquam existentes verbo Dei"</note>. <margin>John 1</margin> And does not St. John say, "By it all things were made, and without it nothing was made"? The world was fashioned by this word or essential spirit, which was pure light, but the world did not know it. <margin>Proverbs 3:19</margin> And Solomon says, "By wisdom God founded the heavens; by his understanding he established the earth" <note>original: "Sapientia Deus fundavit cælos, stabilivit terram in prudentia"</note>. 

In conclusion, the entire harmony of Holy Scripture—which is too long for me to recite in detail here—testifies that all things, of whatever nature or condition, were made, arranged, and accomplished in, by, and through this divine power or emanation, which is God himself; for it is the divine act whose root is the Word. <margin>Romans 11:36</margin> "Of him," says St. Paul, "through him, and in him, are all things" <note>original: "Ex ipso... per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia"</note>.

But because some of the learned men of this world may reply that while it is true that God created all things by his divine Spirit or Word, it does not follow that he acts immediately and exists essentially in every thing. They argue that after this eternal Spirit of wisdom bestowed a peculiar <term>virtue</term> <note>meaning an inherent power or quality</note> on each creature during its creation, the creature can then act on its own by a free will that is separate and divided from the immediate act of God. 

I answer that, according to our established rules in divinity, the true essence of the Deity is indivisible. Therefore, God imparts no essential act or power to any creature that can be discontinued or separated from Himself. For this reason, Christ—who is the eternal spirit of wisdom—is said to fill all things. 

"Indeed," our learned opponents will say, "that is true *virtually* <note>meaning in power or effect</note>, but not *substantially* or *essentially*." I would dearly like to know—setting aside all such <term>school distinctions</term> <note>referring to Scholasticism, the medieval method of academic debate</note>, <margin>1 Timothy 6</margin> which St. Paul tells Timothy to avoid—if the power of God is not his essence, or whether the one can be divided from the other? If they reply that this power of God is not an essence but an <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</note>, they surely err. It is well known even to the Jews and Gentiles themselves that God has no "accidents" in him, seeing that he is absolutely essential and real in himself. For where his divine act is, there also is his power; and where his power is, he is truly said to be essential. Otherwise, the Word or divine act which gives life to every creature would seem to be a mere "accident" divided from the divine essence. The immortality and root of the Word prove how absurd this is. The air so altered always receives its shape or figure from the Alterer, according to the will of Him who ordains all things. Thus, the clouds, the lightnings, the thunder, the comets, the frost, hail, snow, and ice are created daily by this operating Spirit. ...it is inferred: "Neither herb nor plaster cured them, but your word, Lord, which heals all things" <note>original: "Non herba nec malagma te, sed verbo tuo sanante omnia"</note>. If the Word, therefore, heals all things, then nothing can cure except the Word or the Spirit of Wisdom, <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 12:1</margin> whose fountain is the Word, as was proved before. But seeing that this incorruptible Spirit of God is in all things, and since it is the most active and movable thing in this world, and since by his <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:24</margin> purity he penetrates through all and acts in all, what should hinder me or any other good Christian from saying that he acts in everything, and by this Word of himself, and by himself, and that immediately? Therefore, it is not any created thing acting by itself, as the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, whose philosophy dominated universities at the time; Fludd argues their reliance on "secondary causes" ignores God’s direct action.</note> doctrine most erroneously publishes to the world, seducing true Christian hearts from their Creator. This doctrine allures them to diminish God's glory—who is all in all—by assigning absolute authority to the creature, making and ordaining so many essentially distinct subordinate agents which must (supposedly) operate by their own power <note>original: "per se"</note>, such as the Sun, the stars, the winds, the elements, and all complex creatures, whether simple or complex. Truly, in doing so, they make the world believe that the instrument <note>original: "Organ"</note> acts by its own power, essentially, and not this hidden and central Word, or incorruptible Spirit existing in every thing. This Spirit is the fountain or foundation of true <term>wisdom</term> <note>original: "σοφία"</note> and the ultimate goal or "highest good" <note>original: "Summum bonum"</note> which the true philosopher or lover of wisdom aims for. Therefore, Solomon, the Prophets, and Christ, with his sanctified followers, exhort all men to be lovers of this true wisdom, in whom all action exists. This includes intellectual action, which elevates human knowledge, as well as physical action, namely operating to give life, growth, and reproduction. 

But of this, I will speak more at length in another place. I will return to my purpose and conclude this brief discourse upon the true "physick" <note>medicine</note> with Solomon’s confession, who says: <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:20</margin> "Through wisdom I knew the natures of living creatures, the raging tempers of wild beasts, the differences between plants, and the powers of roots; indeed, the worker of all things, Wisdom, revealed to me all mysteries, whether hidden or obvious" <note>original: "Per sapientiam novi naturas animalium, & iras bestiarum, & differentias virgultorum, & virtutes radicum; imo quæ sunt occulta et manifesta, mihi patefecit omnium artifex Sapientia"</note>. By this, he argues that Wisdom—that heavenly Spirit—bestowed upon herbs, animals, and minerals their virtues, both hidden and apparent. It is that eternal Word which is all in all and acts in all, and therefore can only teach and instruct by an external revelation what he internally does, and by what power he operates in each creature. 

Ancient "ethnic" <note>non-Christian or pagan</note> philosophers and physicians have found out the hidden properties in plants through practical experience, sensory observation, and logical demonstrations "from the effect to the cause" <note>original: "à posteriori"</note>. For example: 
*   of the <term>Peony</term> <note>original: "Piony"</note> to cure the "falling-sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>; 
*   of <term>Rupturewort</term> <note>original: "Herniaria"</note> to treat ruptures; 
*   of <term>Coltsfoot</term> <note>original: "Tussilago"</note> to be proper for the lungs; 
*   of <term>Eyebright</term> <note>original: "Euphragia"</note> to be good for the eyesight; 
*   of <term>Germander</term> <note>original: "Thecilea"</note> and **Oak-mistletoe** <note>original: "Viscus quercinus"</note> to prevail against the falling-sickness, etc. 

In animals:
*   the **Toad** to stop bleeding; 
*   the **Ass’s hoof**, and also the **Frog**, to cure the falling-sickness; 
*   the **Scorpion**, chiefly to cure the stings of the scorpion, etc. 

Yet, because they are ignorant of the central grounds of <term>Sympathy</term> and <term>Antipathy</term>—which consist in the "willingness" or "unwillingness" <term>Volunty</term> or <term>Nolunty</term> <note>terms describing the inherent attraction or repulsion between substances</note> of one and the same Spirit—they can give no other reason for such hidden things but only that they are "due to a hidden property" <note>original: "ab occulta proprietate"</note>. In short, they can say no more than "they are such because they are such" <note>original: "talia, quia talia"</note>. And so we receive from these learned doctors nothing else but "an unknown thing explained by something even more unknown" <note>original: "Ignotum per ignotius"</note>. 

To conclude, it is certain that Solomon learned so much of the nature of plants and other creatures by the discovery of this Spirit, that it was said of him that he was instructed by this, his schoolmistress, in the virtues of all vegetables, beginning even from the lowly hyssop and mounting up to the lofty cedars of Lebanon. Having then expressed to you in a few words the power of this Spirit in her teachings on medicine, and proved that she is the basis or ground of every healing property in the world, I will show you in the next rank her act and virtue in essential **Music**.

<margin>Music</margin> Regarding the harmony of this world, and how every earthly element and heavenly sphere is disposed by an essential kind of symphonic accord, the whole body of Scripture confirms that it is effected by this Wisdom. Again, the wise man expresses the wondrous effects of this Spirit in these words: <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 19:17</margin> "For while the elements were changed among themselves—as the sound of a musical instrument changes the nature of the tune—yet all preserved their own sound..." <note>original: "In elementa dum convertuntur, sicut in organo qualitatis sonus immutatur & omnia suum sonum custodiant, &c."</note>

Look here at the perfect and universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> fountain of all harmony, the remover of discord from both heaven and earth, and the pure essential and formal love and sympathy of this world. Therefore, by the wisest and most mystical philosophers, he is said to be the *bond or tie of the elements* <note>original: "Vinculum seu ligamentum elementorum"</note>, the band by which the clashing elements are compelled into a harmonious accord. Following the imitation of his melodious tunes and concords, all the harmonies of our external music—both vocal and instrumental—are symbolically framed. These are, in respect to the true and essential symphony of this spirit, just as a shadow is to a real object, or an image is to reality. I come now to Arithmetic and Geometry.

<margin>Arithmetic. Geometry.</margin>
As for these two arts, the wise man includes them in these few words: *You have ordered all things in measure, number, and weight* <note>original: "Omnia mensura numeroque & pondere disposuisti seu temperâsti"</note>. In these words, "measure" means the progression into length, width, and depth which this Spirit made in its outflow—moving from the point to the line, from the line or root to the square, and from the square to the cube. By "number" is meant those arithmetical dimensions in progression by which this Spirit issued out of unity into multitude—as from 1 to 10, from 10 to 100, and from 100 to 1,000. Namely, it moves from God, who is the eternal point or unity, to the first articulated number, which is 10; this represents the angelic <note>original: "æviall"</note> world, which is the first degree of composition. From 10 it goes to 100, which indicates the composition of the temporal world; and from 100 to 1,000, which points to the complex creatures made of the elements. So by this, every Christian may see how God is all, and in all, and yet beyond all; and, as the Text says, *in heaven, in the seas, in the abyss, and in hell.* For this reason, the Pythagoreans included all things under these three principles: 1, 2, and 3. By this, they attributed 1 to God in his hidden being, 2 to matter, and 3 to form, under which all things are contained.

But I will declare my mind on this more fully when I speak of the essential principles of sympathy and antipathy in the first book of the second section of this present treatise. Therefore the patient man, Job, speaking for <margin>Job 38:4</margin> JEHOVAH, says: *Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding. Who set its measurements, or who stretched a line upon it? On what were its bases fastened? Or who laid its cornerstone?* <note>original: "Ubinam eras quando fundabam terram? Annuntia, si nosti intelligentiam. Quis disposuit mensuras ejus, aut quis extendit super eam lineam? super quo bases ejus defixæ sunt? aut quis jecit lapidem ejus angularem"</note> 

By this he argues that by this Spirit—<margin>John 1:2</margin> which is the cornerstone or foundation of everything (for without it, nothing is made or can exist, as St. John testifies)—not only did the earth receive its geometrical dimension, situation, and position, but also the sun, the moon, the stars, and everything else in both heaven and earth were assigned their weight, proportion, size, and specific place in the world. Yes, truly, by this Spirit the air is carried and shaped into the forms of atmospheric phenomena <note>original: "Meteors"</note> by proportion and weight; for the sacred Text says: <margin>Job 28:25</margin> *By his wisdom, God fits a weight to the air and imparts a measurable proportion to the waters* <note>original: "Deus sapientia aptat pondus aeri & appendit aquas in mensurâ"</note> (or clouds). 

I will now show her power in the science of rhetoric and oratory, and prove in few words how she is also the most exact mistress of those arts. She is the only essential mover in the spirits of men to make them truly eloquent and persuasive; furthermore, she is the essential magnet in the orator's voice, which can draw and attract the listeners' minds to listen to and be moved by the person through whom she intends to plead.

And therefore the text says: <margin>Wisdom 10:4</margin> "Wisdom restored the earth, guiding the righteous man by a lowly piece of wood" <note>original Latin: "Sanavit Sapientia terram, per contemptibile lignum justum gubernans"</note>. By it, the art of music was revealed to Jubal; for the words are, <margin>Genesis 4:21</margin> "Jubal was the father of those who play the harp and organ" <note>original Latin: "Jubal fuit Pater Canentium Citharâ & Organo"</note>. And Tubal-Cain was the inventor of iron and brass works; for it is said: "He was a metalworker and smith in all works of brass and iron" <note>original Latin: "Ipse fuit malleator & faber, in cuncta opera æris & ferri"</note>. Again, Jabal <note>original: "Ada Ju-bal"; referring to Jabal, son of Adah in Genesis 4:20</note> was the father of those who lived in tents and the prince of shepherds. To conclude, there is no true mechanical work that did not have its origin from this Spirit, in whom alone—and in nothing else—is the gift of teaching all things. I come now to the moral and political arts, which arise from this radical Spirit.

<margin>Moral Philosophy</margin> All moral discipline also has its root and beginning from this holy Spirit of discipline, as we are taught by the whole series of Scriptures. And it was the essential voice of this Spirit which taught the Christian world, through the mouth of Christ Jesus, to embrace and follow goodness and to avoid evil. I will not say much, therefore, regarding this point, but will only speak briefly to our purpose using the words of the wise man: <margin>Proverbs 2:7</margin> "Wisdom observes the paths of justice, guarding the ways of the holy" <note>original Latin: "Sapientiâ servat semitas justitiæ, vias sanctorum custodiens"</note>. <margin>Proverbs 2:9</margin> "Through her, you shall understand justice and judgment, equity, and every good and straight path; if she enters your heart, counsel shall watch over you, and prudence shall preserve you. By her, you shall be rescued from the evil way; she will protect you from the strange woman" <note>original Latin: "Per eam intelliges justitiam, & judicium, æquitatem, & omnem semitam bonam; si intraverit cor tuum, consilium custodiet te, Prudentia servabit te. Per eam eruêris à via mala: Te custodiet a muliere extranea"</note>. <margin>Proverbs 7:5</margin> By wisdom, Solomon says, you shall understand justice and judgment, equity, and every good and straight way. If she enters into your heart, she will save and preserve you with prudence; by her, you shall be drawn from the evil way, and she will preserve you from the "strange woman" <note>In the Book of Proverbs, the "strange woman" is a personification of folly or temptation that leads one away from the path of wisdom.</note>. Also, "Wisdom teaches temperance, prudence, justice, and fortitude, than which nothing is more profitable to the life of man" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia docet temperantiam, prudentiam, justitiam, & fortitudinem, quibus utilius nihil in vita hominibus"</note>. <margin>Wisdom 8:7</margin> In another place, <margin>Proverbs 8:14</margin> "Counsel, equity, prudence, and fortitude belong to wisdom" <note>original Latin: "Sapientiæ est, consilium, æquitas, prudentia, & fortitudo"</note>. Here are expressed the four cardinal virtues, which are the pillars of moral philosophy; for in "counsel," temperance is considered, and then there is justice, wisdom, and fortitude. Again, the Son of Sirach says: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 6:31</margin> "In wisdom is the beauty of life, and those who act within her will not sin" <note>original Latin: "In Sapientiâ, est Decor vitæ, & qui operantur in ea non peccabunt"</note>. Now you know that sin is the breach of the Law, and the Mosaic Law is grounded as much upon the moral rules of behavior between man and man as it is in man’s duty toward God. And Solomon, in another place, says: <margin>Wisdom 7:11</margin> "With wisdom all good things came to me, and innumerable honors from her hands" <note>original Latin: "Cum Sapientiâ venerunt mihi omnia bona, & innumerabilis honestas per manus illius"</note>. To conclude, this is expressed to us more realistically and poignantly in the text mentioned above: <margin>Wisdom 8:7</margin> "The labors or works of wisdom have great virtues; for she teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue, than which there is nothing more profitable or useful in this life" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia labores magnas habent virtutes; sobrietatem enim & sapientiam, justitiam & virtutem docet, quibus in vita hominibus nihil est utilius"</note>. By these passages, and many more which I could produce, it is plain that the instructress and foundation of all moral or ethical doctrine is the Spirit of true wisdom, which descends from the Father of Light.

<margin>Politics</margin> As for true and sincere political government, which belongs to the kings, princes, and magistrates of this earth, we find it warranted by Scripture that wisdom is the root from which it springs, if it be good. For we find in one place <margin>2 Chronicles 1:10</margin> that "Wisdom makes a King, so that he may reign worthily over the people" <note>original Latin: "Sapientiâ facit Regem, ut digne regnet in populum"</note>. <margin>Proverbs 8:15</margin> And Solomon says, "By wisdom kings reign, and lawmakers decree just things" <note>original Latin: "Sapientiâ Reges regnant & Legum-conditores justa decernunt"</note>. Again, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 9:18</margin> "By wisdom princes rule or command, and powerful men decree justice" <note>original Latin: "Sapientiâ Principes imperant, & Potentes decernunt justitiam"</note>. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 4:16</margin> And elsewhere: "Wisdom is better than weapons of war" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia melior est quam arma bellica"</note>. And Ecclesiasticus: "He who listens to wisdom shall judge nations" <note>original Latin: "Sapientiam qui audit, judicabit Gentes"</note>. "Wisdom shall serve in the midst of the nobility and shall appear in the sight of the president or judge" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia ministrabit in medio magnarum & in conspectu Præsidis apparebit"</note>. <margin>Wisdom 8:10</margin> And Solomon, in the manner of a confession, says: "Because of wisdom, I had renown among the crowds, and honor..."

"...[I shall have] honor among the elders; though young, I shall be found sharp in judgment, and in the sight of the powerful I shall be admirable" <note>original Latin: "honorem apud seniores: juvenis acutus inveniar judicio, in conspectu potentium admirabilis ero"</note>. *For my wisdom I did shine among the people, and was honored among the elders; being but a young man, I shall be found sharp in judgment, and in the eyes of the powerful I shall appear admirable.* Again, "By wisdom I will order the people, and nations will be subject to me" <note>original Latin: "Per sapientiam disponam populos, & nationes mihi erunt subditæ"</note>. *By wisdom I will order the people, and nations will be subject unto me.* "Dreadful kings will fear when they hear of a wise man. Because of his wisdom, he will appear good in the eyes of the multitude and valiant in war; wisdom leads me so that I may manage your people justly" <note>original Latin: "Sapientem timebunt audientes reges horrendi. Ob sapientiam multitudini videbitur bonus, & in bello fortis: sapientia deducit me ut disponam populum tuum juste"</note>. *Dreadful and terrifying rulers, hearing a wise man, will be afraid. He will appear, by reason of his wisdom, good in the eyes of the multitude, and valiant in war. Wisdom guides me to manage the people justly, etc.* By these and many other passages, it appears that divine wisdom is the only guide for true government in every commonwealth; and where her rules are not respected or followed, that government must necessarily proceed from worldly wisdom, which is earthly, animalistic, and diabolical.

<margin>Miraculous and supernatural effects. Wisdom 10:16, 8:8. 1 Corinthians 2:10. John 2:8-9, 6:10. Matthew 14:25. John 9:1, 11:43, 20:19, 21:9. Luke 8:24, 8:27. Romans 15:18-19. Wisdom 10:2, 7:20. Daniel 2:22. Romans 1:21.</margin>
Lastly, I will conclude and finish this chapter with the miraculous and supernatural effects it produces, and the admirable acts which it brings to pass, beyond the capacity of man’s imagination. Thus, the man who partakes of this divine Agent and can firmly unite it to his own spirit may do wonders. "Wisdom entered into the soul of Moses, the servant of God, and he stood before terrifying kings with portents and signs; she carried Israel through the Red Sea and drowned their enemies" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia intravit in animam servi Dei Mosis; & stetit coram reges horrendos in portentis & signis: Transulit Israelem per mare rubrum & inimicos dimersit"</note>. *Wisdom entered into the soul of Moses, the servant of God; and he stood before mighty kings with prodigies and signs. He carried Israel through the Red Sea and drowned their enemies.* "Wisdom teaches a wide range of experience, for she knows the past and judges what is to come; she understands the subtleties of speech and the solutions to enigmas; she foresees signs and wonders before they happen, as well as the outcomes of times and ages" <note>original Latin: "Sapientia multiplicem experientiam docet, nam scit illa præterita, de futuris æstimat, scit versutias sermonum, & solutiones ænigmatum, signa & monstra antequam fiant præsagit, eventus quoque temporum & seculorum"</note>. *Wisdom teaches manifold experience; she is acquainted with things that are past and judges things that are to come. She understands the cleverness of speech, the solutions of enigmas or riddles, and knows signs and wonders before they appear; she is also familiar with the events of times and ages.*

And the Apostle says, "The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God" <note>original Latin: "Spiritus omnia scrutatur, etiam profunda Dei"</note>. *The Spirit searches all things, even the profound and inscrutable things of God.* It was by the power of this wisdom that wine was made from water; five thousand people were sustained by five loaves of bread; Christ walked safely upon the waters; he cured a man who was blind from birth; he raised Lazarus from the dead; he entered the room where his disciples were, "even though the doors were closed" <note>original Latin: "etiam clausis januis"</note>; he caused an infinity of fish to be caught; he compelled the wind and storm at sea to cease and be obedient to his command; and he cast out devils from those who were possessed. So also it was said, "Christ performed signs and wonders through Paul by the power of the Holy Spirit" <note>original Latin: "signa & prodigia in virtute spiritus sancti effecit Christus per Paulum"</note>. *Christ did effect signs and prodigies by the virtue of the Holy Spirit through Paul.* By this Spirit, Adam had "the power to comprehend all things" <note>original Latin: "virtutem continendi omnia"</note>, and Solomon, by it, understood the thoughts of men and knew all things that were hidden or secret. 

To conclude: Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Samuel, Daniel, Elijah, Elisha, and the other prophets; Judas Maccabeus, Christ, and his apostles—who were all observant disciples of true wisdom—brought to pass all those miracles mentioned in the Holy Testament, both New and Old, by her secret art and operation. Any person may find this to be true if they are pleased to make a proper inquiry into that holy history. But all this is most aptly expressed by the Prophet Daniel in these words: "He reveals things that are profound and hidden, and understands what lies in darkness, for light is with him" <note>original Latin: "Ipse revelat profunda & abscondita, & novit in tenebris constituta, & lux cum eo est"</note>. *He is the revealer of things that are profound and hidden, and understands the things which lurk in darkness, for light dwells with him.*

Since all this is so, it is most apparent that there is no art or science—whether it be obscure and mystical or clearly known, whether it be theoretical or practical—that did not have its root and beginning in this true wisdom. Without its action and virtue, no true and essential learning or knowledge can be obtained in this world. Instead, all will prove to be spuriously born, having their foundation not upon Christ—the true ground, firm rock, and stable cornerstone upon which all truth is built, because in him alone is the fullness of divinity—but placing the base of their knowledge upon the deceptive <note>original: "prestigious"; in this period, the word meant "deceptive" or "illusory," like a magician's trick</note> sands of imagination. Namely, they follow the inventions or traditions of men and the basic elements of this world, from which they gather the fruits of their worldly or human wisdom. This is entirely opposite in effect to true wisdom—the eternal one—which has its root and origin from God, and not from man. And therefore, regarding this kind of worldly-wise men or pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers, we may say with the Apostle: "They vanished into their own imaginations" <note>original Latin: "Evanuerunt in imaginationibus suis"</note>. *They vanished and came to nothing in their imaginations.*

### CHAPTER IV.

->Regarding false wisdom, spurious philosophy, and the philosopher; including their signs and characteristics.<-

<margin>James 3:17.</margin>
<margin>James 3:14-15.</margin>
Now that I have sufficiently explained and revealed to you the nature and essence of true wisdom—and consequently of essential philosophy and the true philosopher—it is appropriate and necessary that I describe the false wisdom of this world, along with the fragile philosophy grounded upon it. Furthermore, I will outline the traits and marks not only of this kind of wisdom but also of the philosopher who is produced and nurtured by that illegitimate <note>original: "spurious"</note> source or misbegotten offspring. The Apostle Saint James says that just as "the true wisdom which is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, willing to yield <note>original: "suasible"</note>, full of mercy and good fruit, not judgmental, and without envy <note>original: "emulation"</note> or hypocrisy," so on the contrary, "the wisdom which is not from above is earthly, animalistic <note>original: "animal"</note> or sensual, diabolical, and contradicts the truth." Consequently, it is argumentative <note>original: "litigious"</note>, immodest, stubborn, fruitless, and full of rivalry and dispute. Now, just as the foundation of the first is Jesus Christ (inasmuch as he is the true wisdom), the foundation of the other consists of the traditions or inventions of man, inspired <note>original: "animated"</note> and introduced by the devil. This led the divine philosopher <note>referring to St. Paul</note> to say, when distinguishing between these two opposites:

<margin>Colossians 2:7-8.</margin>
"In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" <note>original Latin: "In Christo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ absconditi"</note>. "I say this so that no one may deceive you with subtle or persuasive arguments" <note>original Latin: "Hoc dico, ut nemo vos decipiat in subtilitate seu suasibilitate sermonum"</note>, etc. "Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the basic principles <note>original: "elements"</note> of the world, and not according to Christ, because in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead in bodily form" <note>original Latin: "Videte ne quis vos decipiat per Philosophiam & inanem fallaciam secundum traditionem hominum secundum elementa mundi, & non secundum Christum, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter"</note>. In this speech, he seems to confirm that all wisdom and knowledge—and consequently true philosophy and all the sciences included within it—reside and are to be sought in Christ, that eternal wisdom and only cornerstone <note>original: "angular stone"</note> which fills, informs, and gives life to all things. They are in no way to be found in false philosophy, which is full of sophisticated deception and barely carries a face or shape of probability. This is because it is masked by worldly human inventions, framed according to the rules and orders of this obscure and erroneous world, and not according to the precepts of Christ, the eternal wisdom, who (as the Scriptures tell us) is "the worker of all wonders" <note>original Latin: "omnium mirabilium operator"</note>, performing all marvelous results, both natural and supernatural. For this reason, the Apostle condemns philosophy in general terms. This is not because the love of true wisdom is bad—the lover of true wisdom is indeed to be honored and esteemed—but he means that the love of worldly and human wisdom is vain. He calls it so because the pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers added "philos" <note>Greek: φιλος, meaning "love"</note> to their false "sophia" <note>Greek: σοφια, meaning "wisdom"</note>. Thus, because the word "philosophy" is a term of pagan invention, it is to be rejected in light of its erroneous and clashing rules. It is only built upon the traditions of pagan men, as it leads even Christians—much more the Gentiles—toward errors and seduces them away from the knowledge of God, rather than leading or directing them toward the true path of finding Him. For that reason, it became the occasion for widespread idolatry in this world, persuading the ignorant worldling to worship creatures instead of the Creator. For this cause, therefore, Christians were forbidden from embracing it; and so the Apostle warns us to "beware of philosophy and empty deceit," etc. Of such philosophers who do not build upon the truth, he speaks elsewhere in this way:

<margin>Romans 1:18.</margin>
"The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the impiety and unrighteousness of those men who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what may be known of God is manifest in them; for God has revealed it to them. For since the creation of the world, his invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made. His eternal power and divinity are also evident, so that they are without excuse. Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image made like corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed animals, and creeping things" <note>original Latin: "Revelatur ira Dei de cælo super omnem impietatem & injustitiam hominum... & mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei, in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum, & quadrupedum, & serpentum, &c."</note>. *God is revealed from heaven against all the impiety and injustice of those men who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness. This is because what may be known of God is made manifest to them, for God has revealed it to them. For his invisible attributes, as well as his eternal power and divinity, are understood and clearly seen through the creatures that have been made since the creation of the world. Thus, they are without excuse, because although they knew God, they did not glorify him or give him thanks. Instead, they faded away or vanished in their own imaginations, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Therefore, while claiming to be wise, they became fools and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man, birds, four-footed beasts, and serpents, etc.* Again, Solomon speaks to this very same point <margin>Wisdom 13:1.</margin> in these words: *All men are vain by nature who are ignorant of God, and who could not understand Him who truly exists from the good things they behold; nor, by considering his works, did they acknowledge the craftsman.* <note>original Latin: "Vani sunt homines omnes naturâ, in quibus inest ignorantia Dei, & qui ex iis, quæ spectantur, bonis, eum, qui est, intelligere non potuerunt, neque ex operibus consideratis, ipsum opificem agnoverunt."</note>

It is very necessary, therefore, for every Christian to be cautious when reading heathen <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy. One should consider seriously the sayings of the two aforementioned sacred philosophers <note>referring to St. Paul and Solomon</note>, who followed the rules of true wisdom, before wading too far into secular philosophy or giving it too much credit. Furthermore, let the reader recall the precepts which the first of them (I mean St. Paul) shared with the worldly philosophers of Athens. When he saw that they adored and worshipped strange and unknown gods, he taught them a new philosophy and a new wisdom—namely Jesus Christ—which was a "strange doctrine" to them. Therefore they said, *Let us hear what this babbler will say, who brings in this strange doctrine of Christ.* This shows that true wisdom never reached their ears or touched their hearts.

Let the reader observe that it was toward this kind of illegitimate <note>original: "bastard"</note> philosopher and their philosophy that the Apostle pointed when he said in the passage cited above: *Let no man deceive you with subtlety and persuasive speech. Beware of philosophy and vain fallacy, which follow the traditions of men and the elements or rudiments of this world, and not Christ, etc.* In these words, he distinguishes false philosophy or wisdom from true knowledge <note>original: "Sapience"</note>. He seems to suggest that false philosophy is merely a vain fallacy, framed according to the customs of the men of this world, such as was taught at Athens. That is to say, it relies on empty deception, subtleties, and things that seem more likely or probable in appearance than they are in reality. For that reason, it filled men with more doubts through inquiries made in "misty and foggy" passages than if they had followed the plain and simple way of teaching—that is, following the true image of the real and essential philosophy, or rather *Sophia* <note>The Greek word for Wisdom</note>.

As the Wise Man tells us, Wisdom is: *The holy spirit of understanding; unique, simple, modest, eloquent, sweet, clear, and open without ambiguity; loving that which is good, humane, kind, stable, sure, containing all virtue, making men friends of God, and entering into holy souls.* <margin>Wisdom 7:22.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Spiritus intelligentiæ Sanctus, unicus, simplex, modestus, disertus, suavis, perspicuus, amans bonum, humanus, benignus, stabilis, certus, omnem habens virtutem, amicos Dei constituens, & in animas sanctas se transferens."</note> Here we see that this description of good and true wisdom exactly matches the character described by St. James, as mentioned before. He calls it modest, kind, peaceful, <margin>James 3.</margin> persuasive <note>original: "suasible"</note>, and without envy or rivalry.

Again, as St. James says it is "from above" (namely, from the Father of Light), <margin>Wisdom 7:25.</margin> Solomon also expresses its pedigree this way: *Wisdom is the breath of the power of God, and a certain pure emanation or flow of the glory of the Almighty God, and the brightness or splendor of eternal light, and a spotless mirror of the majesty of God, and the image of his goodness.* <note>original Latin: "Sapientia est vapor virtutis Dei & emanatio quædam seu fluxus claritatis omnipotentis Dei sinceri, & candor seu splendor lucis æternæ, & speculum sine macula Majestatis Dei, & imago bonitatis illius."</note> By this definition, three things are clearly seen: first, that it is the wisdom that comes from above; second, that it is not the vain wisdom of this world (which is nothing but a fiction or empty shadow compared to this, which is the only truth); and lastly, that this wisdom brings good fruit. It grants men essential virtue and power to act both naturally and miraculously. Therefore the Apostle says: *The signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all power, in signs...* <note>original Latin: "Signa Apostolatûs mei facta sunt super vos in omni potentia, in signis..."</note>

<margin>2 Corinthians 12:12</margin>*With wonders and mighty deeds:* <note>original Latin: "in prodigiis & virtutibus"</note> The signs of my Apostleship are upon you in all patience, *in signs, wonders, and mighty deeds*. And again, <margin>Galatians 3:5</margin>*He who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles, or wonders, among you:* <note>original Latin: "Qui tribuit vobis Spiritum & operatur virtutes, seu miracula, in vobis"</note> Look here, our Christian Philosophers may see how this Wisdom brings forth power and virtue, which St. James (in the previously cited passage) calls "good fruits." For he says that the Wisdom which is from above is full of good fruits. But Paul seems to call heathen <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy a "vain fallacy." Therefore, if it is vain, then it is void of good fruit. Consequently, there is no true, fruitful philosophy, nor any truly fruitful philosopher, except that which is grounded on that true and eternal Wisdom: **Jesus**.

Besides all this, true Wisdom is peaceable, not ambiguous, and not prone to being criticized or contentiously disputed. It does not need an infinity of distinctions and <term>quiddities</term> <note>quiddities: complex, hair-splitting definitions or "the whatness" of things used in medieval logic</note> framed from the human brain. Such things actually lead the student into ignorance through their complexity, rather than clarifying the brightness of naked truth. But false philosophy is so full of distinctions, subtle and sophisticated evasions, and so subject to criticisms and disputes. It is so contentiously composed, so difficult, and in the end so fruitless, that instead of true and essential grain, we find only chaff. Instead of truth, we gather only words. Instead of essential reality, we collect barely a shadow of the Truth. In place of sincerity, we find only vanity. In conclusion, it is more often masked with a deceptive probability than it is truly discernable. For this reason, the Apostle says: <margin>1 Corinthians 2:4</margin>*My preaching was not with persuasive words of human wisdom, but with a demonstration of the Spirit and of power.* <note>original Latin: "Predicatio mea non est in persuasivis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed in ostensione spiritus & virtutis"</note>

For this reason, we find in divine wisdom the fruits of power, virtue, and miracles—such as the true and divine Philosophers produced by the "Omnipotent Cornerstone" (by which I mean the true Wisdom) in times past, making them manifest to the world. In contrast, the other philosophy can do nothing but produce criticisms, disputes, contentions, and fallacies; its fruits, in the end, are nothing but vanity. It is not I, but the Spirit of Truth that assures you of this. 

And yet now, even in this later age of the world in which Satan—the prince of this world which is darkness—has the upper hand, this earthly wisdom or "vain philosophy" (which is plastered over with dark ignorance) holds dominion. By that means, Christ, who is the true Wisdom, is daily crucified among some Christian Philosophers and buried in darkness through the misty and ambiguous clouds of that quarreling, heathenish philosophy. They so adore and follow their master **Aristotle** as if he were another **Jesus** rained down from heaven to open the treasures of true wisdom to mankind. 

But observe for a moment (I beg you) how the Apostle describes these wrangling philosophers and their sophisticated philosophy, and with what characteristics and colors he justly portrays them: <margin>1 Timothy 6:3–5</margin>*If anyone teaches otherwise and does not agree with the wholesome words of our Lord Jesus Christ* (he says) *and with the doctrine that is according to godliness, he is proud, knowing nothing, but obsessed with questions and disputes over words. From these come envy, strife, insults, evil suspicions, and the friction of men of corrupt minds who are destitute of the truth, thinking that financial gain is godliness.* <note>original Latin: "Si quis aliter docet, & non acquiescit sanis sermonibus Domini nostri Jesu Christi... existimantium quaestum esse pietatem"</note> From such people (says St. Paul to Timothy), separate yourself. 

I could heartily wish that every "Christian Peripatetic" <note>Peripatetic: a follower of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> who spends his time in disputes and criticisms after the manner of Aristotle, would reconsider. They attempt to draw out the endless bottom of truth or dive into the depths and labyrinths of reality through subtle evasions—meaning, by an infinity of distinctions that distract rather than attract a person to true wisdom (which is but plain and simple unity). I wish they would ponder this with patience and seriously remember that in the Church of God and the kingdoms of true *Sophia* (Wisdom) or, if they prefer, *Philosophia*, there is no such custom as the Apostle teaches us <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>. For this mixture of multiformed human wisdom with the wisdom of God has been the occasion of so many dissensions and discords as have sprung up among...

Now, his doctrine concerned the true philosophy, whose foundation was Jesus Christ—the true wisdom and cornerstone which sustains all, is all in all, fills all, and acts or operates all in all. They would have these act as subordinate essential agents that operate by themselves, not understanding that there is but one universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> and indivisible Agent in many dwellings, who operates by and in an infinity of organic instruments <note>original: "organicall vehicles"</note>, all in all and over all. 

And this doctrine of theirs has so infected our Christian philosophers who belong to their sect that they make distinctions regarding God’s Being, saying that He is present "virtually" <note>original: "virtualiter"</note> and not "substantially" <note>original: "substantialiter"</note> or "essentially" <note>original: "essentialiter"</note>. This is as if to say that God's power <note>original: "vertue"</note> can exist without His essence, or be divided from His divinity, which is indivisible; and so they dream of some "accidents" existing in God which are distinct from His essence. <header>Mosaical Philosophy. BOOK 2.</header>

And although things appear in their outward show to act or work by themselves in this world, our true philosopher *Paul* teaches us through his philosophy (the basis or ground of which is the true wisdom, *Jesus Christ*) that he can discern only two types of agents. The first is primary, from whom all things come, and the other is secondary, through whom all things are made. He acknowledges both to be one in essence; for because the one is an emanation out of the other, he alone—acting through himself—operates all in all. This is the perfect tenet of essential philosophy. Therefore, whatever mundane or <term>heathen</term> <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy tells us, or tries to persuade us of through subtle insinuation—which is clearly contrary to true philosophy—we ought not to believe in any case. Regarding this, the same divine philosopher seems to <margin>Galatians 1:8</margin> agree in these words: *Though an angel from heaven preach to you any other gospel than that which we have preached to you, let him be accursed. If any man preach any other gospel than that you have received, let him be accursed.* Therefore, seeing that Aristotelian learning is contradictory in several main points to the positions of essential wisdom or philosophy, a true Christian ought not to believe its main points. As *St. James* says, its grounds and character are opposite to the Holy Bible, which is the only cabinet of truth; he therefore pronounces it to be earthly, natural, and demonic <note>original: "terrene, animal, and diabolicall"</note>. 

On this point, *St. Paul* writes to his student *Timothy* in this style: *Timothy, keep that which is committed <margin>1 Timothy 6:20</margin> to you, and avoid profane and empty chatter, and the opposition of knowledge falsely so called, which some people, by professing, have erred concerning the faith.* In these words, he seems to warn his disciples not to be entangled with the deceptive charms of worldly philosophy, which contradicts the truth and is not peaceful, but troublesome and full of empty disputes and opposition. He pronounces such a philosophy to be not truly but "falsely" called a science, as are all the sciences that depend on it. Moreover, he suggests to his disciples that those Christians who profess it with too much devotion and confidence have been subtly led into errors concerning the faith. This faith is grounded upon the anchor of this invisible wisdom, which is the spiritual Christ Jesus. 

Again, in this sense, he gives this previously mentioned warning to his <margin>Colossians 2:8</margin> Colossian disciples: *Beware lest any man deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ, etc.* By this, he admonishes us Christians to shun the false philosophy of the heathens and to stick firmly to the rules and doctrine of true wisdom. Therefore, he says in the same text, "Walk rooted and built up in Christ" <note>original Latin: "In Christo ambulate radicati et aedificati in ipso"</note>. By this, he intends to show that Christ is the only cornerstone and foundation of true philosophy, given that all creatures—indeed, the whole world—is founded upon him. Consequently, the foundation of pagan philosophy is sandy and of no validity. Here the <margin>1 Corinthians 3:10</margin> Apostle says, "No man can lay any other foundation than that which is already laid, which is Jesus Christ" <note>original Latin: "Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere praeter id quod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus"</note>. 

The Apostle seems to indicate that this is completely contrary to the false grounds of the <margin>Ephesians 4:17-18</margin> heathens in these words: "I say this: that you should not walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart" <note>original Latin: "Hoc dico ut non ambuletis, sicut et gentes ambulant in vanitate sensus sui, tenebris obscuratum habentes intellectum, alienati in vita Dei per ignorantiam quae est in illis propter caecitatem cordis eorum"</note>. I must now begin to examine the specific details of the erroneous and false doctrine of <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Peripatetic: A name for the followers of Aristotle, referring to his habit of walking while teaching.</note> or Aristotelian philosophy, so that I may better expose it to the world by comparing its vanity with the goodness and perfection of the divine and sacred <term>Sophia</term> <note>Sophia: The Greek word for "Wisdom," often used in a mystical or theological sense to describe the divine intellect.</note> or wisdom.

Why should not its foundation be the true wisdom which came from God?

But before I come to answering this objection, I beg you (gentle reader) to give me liberty first to apologize a little for myself. Please understand, first of all, from my just and upright spirit, that I acknowledge and confess this "Prince of the Peripatetic Philosophy" <note>Aristotle, the leader of the Peripatetic school of philosophy.</note> to be a person of profound speculation, and that he had as deep an insight into the light of nature as any of the common rank of philosophers in his time. Indeed, he had such a sharp intellect <note>original: "ingeny"</note> and such a subtle and refined spirit, that through his worldly craft and human invention, he allured not only the pagan Greeks—who consequently termed him *Cacodæmon* <note>original: "Cacodæmon, or a deceitful spirit, or seducing from the truth"</note>—but also Christians of every sect, even until now. They are so wedded to his worldly wisdom that they admire every new student in the universities who maintains Aristotle’s actions and does not deviate from his doctrine. 

As for myself, though I may be ranked in that number, I have now collected my thoughts. By God's grace, I have attained that light of the Holy Scriptures which enables me to distinguish and discern their essential colors from the deceptive <note>original: "præstigious"</note> ones of the Pagans. I must say with Cicero, that *certain promises are to be kept, namely those that are lawful, and on the other hand, certain promises are not to be kept, namely those that are unlawful* <note>original: "Quædam promissa sunt servanda nimirum licita... Quædam promissa non sunt servanda, nempe quæ sunt illicita"</note>. Now, God forbid that good Christians should imagine that any oath made to detract from the truth of the Holy Bible should be perpetually binding, for that would be to rebel against the truth. Therefore, my essential motto in my old age—despite any allegiance I vowed to Aristotle through ceremonial rites in my youth—shall be: *Plato is my friend, Aristotle is my friend, but truth is a greater friend* <note>original: "Amicus Plato, amicus Aristoteles, sed magis amica veritas"</note>; and therefore truth ought to prevail most with me.

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:20</margin> And now, to answer the previously mentioned objection directly, we must compare the two types of wisdom proposed by the Apostles. First, St. Paul says *that God has made the wisdom of this world foolishness.* And again: <margin>1 Corinthians 3:19</margin> *The wisdom of this world is foolishness before God, for God knows that the thoughts of the wise men (or philosophers) of this world are foolish* <note>original: "Sapientia hujus mundi stultitia est apud Deum, Deus enim novit cogitationes sapientum quod stultæ sunt"</note>. For this reason, the same Apostle says in another place: <margin>1 Corinthians 2:12</margin> *We have not received the spirit of this world, but the spirit which is from God, and we speak those things which are given to us by God—not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. For the natural man <note>original: "Animalis homo"</note> does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them* <note>original: "Nos non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus... Animalis enim homo non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei..."</note>. 

By these words, we ought first to examine whether Aristotle was a "natural man" or not. If so, then what should we expect from him but mundane wisdom and philosophy? St. James terms this "natural" <note>original: "animal"</note> and earthly, which is indeed nothing in itself but total foolishness, as St. Paul tells us; for the natural man does not perceive the things of God because he considers them foolishness. The <margin>Colossians 2:8–9</margin> same Apostle bids us to beware of this kind of philosophy and wisdom, seeing that it is grounded upon the traditions of men and the elements of the world, and not upon Christ. But he points at this Greek-style <note>original: "Græcanicall"</note> wisdom more directly in these words, in which he distinguishes both it and Jewish wisdom from the wisdom of God, whose foundation is Jesus Christ: <margin>1 Corinthians 1:23</margin> *The Greeks seek wisdom, the Jews seek signs, but we preach Christ crucified* <note>original: "Sapientiam Græci quærunt, Judæi signa, nos Christum crucifixum prædicamus"</note>. He argues by these words that the Greeks search after the wisdom of the world, which consists chiefly in speculation or contemplation, just as the wisdom of the Jews is more focused on signs and visual demonstrations—for without them, they will not believe. 

Lastly, the third wisdom—the true wisdom which both the Greeks and Jews rejected and mocked—was Jesus Christ, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily. <margin>Colossians 2:9</margin> This is that real and essential wisdom which Christians ought to search after, and upon which they ought to ground their philosophy, which is divine and not human. But if they reply that perhaps Aristotle had an insight into Christian doctrine, or apprehended Christ in some manner, or at least had an eye toward the wisdom of Moses...

...and the Prophets. First, I answer that just as Aristotle lived before the incarnated Word <note>Jesus Christ</note>, it is also evident that he knew little of the Mosaical learning. I confess that his master, Plato, was more essentially grounded in true wisdom. However, Aristotle, being puffed up with self-conceit and wishing to disparage the Stoic doctrine of his master, presumed to claim all wisdom for himself. He did this by framing or fashioning a new worldly wisdom or philosophy, which was afterward called "Peripatetic" <note>the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle</note>. Through his vanity, he added many of his own inventions to a few truths, creating a gallimaufry <note>a confused jumble or medley</note> of good and bad, true and false, and wisdom and folly mixed together. This is far from the nature of perfect Christian wisdom, which must be entirely truth itself, because it is described by the Spirit of God, in whom there is nothing but truth. 

Again, if the Peripatetic, Stoic, or Epicurean doctrines had been perfect and in accord with the true wisdom of Jesus Christ, why would the Athenian philosophers have so persecuted the true and precise philosopher Paul for teaching the true wisdom of Jesus Christ? In Christ alone is the fullness of divinity, as the same Apostle teaches in various places. By this, we may perceive most plainly the kind of wisdom upon which Aristotle built his philosophy.

<margin>James 3:15</margin>
But I will come a little closer to the main point and compare the two types of wisdom expressed by Saint James, another true Christian philosopher and Apostle of Christ. He tells us in the passage mentioned above that *the wisdom which contradicts the truth is not from above—that is to say, from the Father of Light—nor is it peaceful and modest, but earthly, natural <note>original: "animal"</note>, and demonic.* 

Now, it is clear that this philosophy or wisdom of the Peripatetics is of that kind. First, it is litigious, full of disputes, fallacies, petty quarrels <note>original: "brables"</note>, and controversies, all of which are contrary to the rules of true wisdom. <margin>1 Timothy 6:4</margin>

Their method and fashion is to be constantly occupied with questions and caviling disputations in their schools. This is the foundation of so many opposing sects, both in general philosophy and in religion. From this arise disputations, strife, contention, and malice—not only in the schools between contrary factions but also among common people of different religions.

### Section I. Mosaical Philosophy.

Greek philosophy is contentious, litigious, and full of disputes, squabbles, and rivalries. For this reason, it is declared by Saint James <margin>James 3</margin> to be *earthly, sensual, demonic, and not from above.* In contrast, that philosophy which is grounded in true wisdom, which comes from above, must be *first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, envy, or hypocrisy.* For this reason, our Christian philosopher Paul warns his student Timothy <margin>1 Tim. 6:20</margin> to *shun all profane and empty chatter and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge—which some, by professing, have strayed concerning the Faith.* 

All such Christians who have their anchor-hold too firmly fastened to Aristotle’s philosophy should seriously ponder this: our eminent master Saint Paul seems to warn them with such passion that following this pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy—which consists of contentions, questions, empty chatter, and opposing "sciences" that seem true but are not (though they are falsely called so)—is the reason well-intending Christians have been deceived and have strayed from the Faith in the true Wisdom and only truth, Jesus Christ. Again, the Apostle James says <margin>James 3</margin>: *The wisdom that contradicts the Truth is not from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.* 

Now I am certain that all good Christians will maintain that the fountain of truth and verity is the Holy Bible. What will our Christian followers of Aristotle say if I prove clearly that Aristotle’s doctrine strays from the main foundations of Holy Scripture, which is the treasure of Truth, and consequently from that wisdom which is the Father of Light? It is a common phrase among our superficial scholars <note>original: "lip-learned Sophisters"</note> to say, when any contradiction is found between some axioms of Greek philosophy and sacred assertions: "Oh, this is true in philosophy, but in Scripture it is found otherwise." I say to these people: if any contradiction is found between the points of one and the other, there is a foul error, falsehood, or contradiction in one of them. Therefore, one of the two must necessarily come from an earthly, demonic, worldly, or human wisdom. Now, let every good Christian judge whether we should rather stick to God’s Word, which is the only Truth, or the claims of Aristotle, who derives his wisdom from the father of lies—I mean worldly wisdom, which for that reason is termed "demonic" or "devilish" by the Apostle. 

Others say that men are so deeply involved in the secrets of nature, or natural philosophy, that they have become atheists and will acknowledge no God. They must surely be referring to pagan philosophy and not pointing at that of Jesus Christ; for Christ's philosophy leads and directs the understanding spirit of man even to the Throne and Majesty of the true God. It persuades him to forsake the multitude of this wicked world to betake and contract itself into that blessed union from which his bright Spirit was originally derived. 

A third sort of men seem to complain and storm that any man should presume to mingle natural philosophy with divinity, or should dare to attempt to draw any axioms or authorities out of the Scriptures to prove or maintain the principles or causes of philosophy. They boldly but erroneously assert that the Bible only teaches man what belongs to salvation—that is to say, how we should fear God and behave toward our neighbors—as if the Holy Scriptures had written anything in vain! And yet it is plainly found in them <margin>Col. 2</margin> *that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden in Christ.* And it is said in another place <margin>John 14:26</margin>: *From me you shall learn all things* <note>original: *A me discetis omnia*</note>. And again: *The Holy Spirit will teach you all things* <note>original: *Spiritus Sanctus vos docebit omnia*</note>. Are we not likewise taught <margin>Wisd. 13:1</margin> *that all men are foolish who do not know the Creator by the creatures he has made* <margin>Rom. 1</margin> *and the invisible God by the visible things he has created*? 

Besides all this, man shall find therein most vividly described the three principles by which God made all things: namely, the dark Abyss or Chaos <margin>40</margin>, which they call "first matter"; the second matter, which they term "water" <margin>43</margin>; and the first Act or light, which they call their "form." Also, the true manner of the generation of meteors, of condensation and rarefaction, of generation and corruption, of action and passion, and of all other things that can be imagined in that kind of learning which the Aristotelians call "natural," is rightly (and not sophistically) expressed in this true philosophy. This is also true for every other kind of learning, whether moral or political, along with all other sciences, both liberal and mechanical, as has already been proved. What? Since, therefore, all things are effected in this world by attraction or expulsion, let us see what is *Aristotle's* opinion touching the cause of attraction, and then afterward examine whether it accords with the tenor of truth.
