...and attract water unto it. Hence, therefore, has that obvious error been introduced into this world: namely, that fire and heat suck and draw vapors and fumes toward them. However, it may be made most obvious and evident to the simplest person—provided they have their human senses about them—that the heat of the Sun and fire actually disperses <note>original: "discusse"</note> and expels things by expansion <note>original: "dilatation"</note>, rather than alluring them by way of attraction. 

For example, if the fire drew vapors toward it, then it would not permit any smoke to leave it; but the contrary is seen: namely, that it disperses by dissolving, and expels and separates by thinning <note>original: "rarefaction"</note> the subtle from the gross. It does this not with a desire to draw or attract the vapors (created by that thinning) toward itself, but to expel and disjoint them from the whole gross body it works upon. For this reason, we see the fumes and smoke fly away and be forced to avoid the action of the fire, without any inclination of the fire to retain them. Also, if we apply a wet handkerchief to the fire, we shall see that the watery substance in it will be refined <note>original: "subtiliated"</note> by the heat into a steaming vapor. But as for the fire, it is so far from attracting it that the steaming smoke will be seen to rise up in the house at random, without any evident attraction from the fire. 

The same thing happens with the Sun’s operative faculty, for it refines or thins the water and humid substances by its heat, and consequently, it draws nothing at all toward itself; rather, it disperses that which was thick into thinner portions. Now, the reason that water or gross humid substances ascend upward once they are thinned is not any attractive faculty in the Sun or stars, but a natural inclination in the thing itself. For it is a common axiom that **everything light and subtle** <note>original: "omne leve et subtile"</note> does, by a natural sympathy or appetite, **tend upward** <note>original: "tendere sursum"</note>; and therefore, by its own inclination, being so refined, it soars upward toward its natural and destined region or place, as we see in fumes, smoke, and such things. Contrariwise, **everything heavy** <note>original: "omne grave"</note> does, in like manner, **tend downward** <note>original: "tendere deorsum"</note>; all that is heavy descends by a natural desire toward the **center**. 

But so that I may more exactly and assuredly expose this error of the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: a follower of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle taught while walking about.</term> attraction of exhalations and vapors by the Sun, stars, and fire, I pray that you will simply observe our **Weather-glass** <note>This refers to an early thermoscope or thermometer, used here to demonstrate how air reacts to temperature changes.</note>, or experimental machine. We shall find there through practice that all attraction from the circumference toward the center is caused by cold, and not by heat. For by cold, the water is drawn or attracted up into the neck of the glass, and that is effected by the thickening <note>original: "inspissation"</note> of the air and its reduction into a narrower space. On the contrary, we note that if the Sun heats the head or bowl of the **matrass** <term>matrass: a long-necked glass flask used in scientific experiments.</term>, or if the warmth of a hand merely touches it, the included air expands itself and immediately flies away from the heat. It is so far from being attracted by the heat that it precipitates and forces the water downwards. 

Since this is the case—as ocular experience, the mother of fools, has taught us—let our Christian Peripatetics <note>Aristotelian philosophers who attempted to reconcile Greek science with Christian theology.</note> duly observe the "subtle wisdom" of their Master, whom they have hitherto followed. Let them see and consider how grossly he has erred in the main argument, pillar, or prop of his *Meteorology*. This being so, what can be expected other than that the whole fabric of the same should fall before the eyes of every wise contemplator? 

To be brief, these and similar errors of his have forced many of his most discreet disciples and naturalists to dissent and depart from his doctrine—concerning his opinion of the winds and thunder as well as the origin of fountains—being persuaded and allured to this abandonment by a truer spirit. # The Third Book of the First Section, touching the essential Principles of the Mosaic Philosophy.

## The Argument of this third Book.

IN this current Book, the Author teaches in a general way the true and essential principles of divine Philosophy. In particular, he expresses how various and differing the Pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers have been in their opinions concerning the beginnings of all things. Here he proves that the wisest among those non-Christian naturalists stole and derived their main grounds or principles from the true and sacred philosopher Moses, whose philosophy was originally outlined by the finger of God, as its fiery characters were stamped out or engraved in the dark <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "Hyle"; a Greek term for the primordial, unformed matter of the universe</note> by the eternal Wisdom or divine Word. He shows that although the aforementioned pagan philosophers usurped these Mosaic principles for themselves and assigned them new titles to better hide their theft, they were unable to dive into the core <note>original: "centrall"</note> understanding of them, nor rightly conceive or grasp the mystery of the everlasting Word. Consequently, they built upon these principles or foundations only a vain and worldly wisdom, carved out not from the essential rock of truth, nor relying on Christ—the only cornerstone—but shaped according to human invention and the basic elements of this world. It is much like a castle of straw or stubble: though it may be planted on a rock, it is still subject to change and is easily shaken and tottered by every gust of wind. In conclusion, our Author sets down what the true Mosaic principles are, namely: *Darkness, Water,* and *Light*. <margin>33</margin> Then, he shows that all fullness and emptiness in the world consists in the presence or absence of the formal principle, which is Light. And lastly, he shows how the two apparent active properties—namely, Cold and Heat—issue from the two aforementioned fountains of Darkness and Light, just as the two passive natures, Moisture and Dryness <note>original: "Drought"</note>, derive their origin from those active properties.

## CHAPTER 1.

->*In which the uncertainty of the ancient Greek and Arabian philosophers is set down, regarding their opinions on the principles or beginnings of all things.*<-

It is an evident argument that the pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers were not well settled on the foundations of their philosophy. Instead, they wavered in their imaginations concerning the true principles of nature, since within each of their sects, they maintained and upheld a variety—and sometimes even a plain contradiction—of opinions about them. 

For example, Thales of Miletus, who was enrolled among the number of the wise men of Greece, held the opinion that water was the beginning of all things. But Anaximenes and his disciples affirmed that an infinite air was the first cause or origin of every existence. For this reason also, Anaximander esteemed this universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> air to be God. Again, on the other side, Zoroaster claimed that all things take their beginning from fire and light; likewise, the Pythagoreans say that there is one universal fire in and over all things in this world. 

Truly, each of these opinions, if they are duly considered, will be found to approach and have a near relation to the Mosaic truth. For a divine fire or light issuing forth from darkness, or the dark abyss, did suddenly by its bright presence reveal and make manifest the hidden and invisible waters. The subtler part of these waters is the vast spirit of the air. For this reason, both Thales and Anaximenes seem in some way to agree on one subject. And yet, if we penetrate more deeply into the matter, we shall perceive that these two focused only on the material or passive principle, since from it, the substance of heaven and earth and everything within them has its existence or material being. 

On the other side, Zoroaster did not choose fire for the primary beginning of all things without reason, because it did proceed and appear in action before the waters or moist nature were made manifest—just as action goes before passion, or the cause precedes the effect. And yet, nevertheless, he erred in this assertion because the active principle can in no way be rightly considered except in its relation to a passive origin. 

The Stoic Zeno, therefore, being more cautious than the rest, establishes his opinion concerning the first principle by a firmer tie or obligation. He said that the substance of the fire, being converted into water by the air, is the beginning of all things. But Empedocles would be sure to lay his foundations more securely (as he vainly imagined) than Zeno; for that cause, he ordained the four elements to be the radical principles of all things, of which two are agents <note>acting forces</note> and two are patients <note>recipients of action</note>.

Now, the main error of these philosophers in their judgments concerning the principles was that they did not mark or consider that the divine power or sacred word was more ancient and of a greater antiquity than any of their aforementioned principles. If they had understood this through a riper contemplation, they would have confessed—being instructed and directed by reasons produced from the eternal unity, or essential point and beginning of all things—that the divine light or sacred emanation (which Scriptures entitle by the name of the Holy Spirit of Wisdom) was the actual beginning of all things. 

Nevertheless, before it, there was another property in one and the same sacred essence, which was termed the divine power <note>original: "potentia divina"</note>. This preceded its act or emanation, just as the Father in time, order, and being is justly said to exist before the Son, or the Creator before the creature. Thereupon, the wise man says in <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:4.</margin> "Wisdom was created before all things" <note>original: "Omnium prior creata est sapientia"</note>. 

And yet, it is most apparent that some of the Greek and Egyptian philosophers—namely Plato, Pythagoras, Socrates, Hermes, and others—did so instruct their understandings, partly by observing the doctrine of their predecessors and partly through the experience they gathered in their long travels and journeys <note>original: "peregrinations"</note> among the Ethiopians, Egyptians, Hebrews, Armenians, Arabians, Babylonians, and Indians. For Plato, Pythagoras, Hippocrates, and others traveled over all or most of these countries to augment and increase their knowledge, as historians <note>original: "Historiographers"</note> worthy of credit have related. Because of this, they undoubtedly discerned—though from afar and, as it were, in a cloud—the true light in...

## CHAP. II.

*What the Mosaic principles or beginnings were in general: How they were produced and extracted out of Nothing. Then, what is meant by that word "Nothing." And lastly, the first principle—which is the dark Abyss or Chaos without form—is particularly described.*

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>
The Mosaic principles are very plain and evident to all those who wisely contemplate and observe the words of the most excellent philosopher, Moses, in his first chapter of Genesis. For before there is any mention of that <term>spagyrical</term> <note>original: "Spagiricall"; referring to the alchemical process of separating and recombining elements.</note> separation which was effected by the Word of God or the divine Spirit <term>Elohim</term> <note>A Hebrew name for God.</note> in the six days' work of the Creation mentioned and expressed there, it is said that darkness was upon the face of the <term>Abyss</term>; and that the Earth was without shape and form <note>original: "Terra erat inanis & vacua"</note>. Here it appears that the Heavens and the Earth were not as yet enacted or given form, but were one deformed, rude, and undigested mass. Consequently, all things were enfolded <note>original: "complicitly comprehended"</note> in one dark Abyss, but they were as yet nothing in their unfolded, visible state <note>original: "explicitly they were as yet nothing"</note>. 

As an example, we see that a great tree—with its body, branches, bark, leaves, and fruit—is enfolded within a grain or kernel; but visibly it is no such thing, existing only somewhat in the imagination. Saint Augustine compares this "Nothing" to speech: while it is in the mind of the speaker, it is as nothing to the person it is spoken to—that is to say, it is something in potential power, and nothing in essence. But when it is uttered or spoken, then that which was before enfolded in the mind of the speaker <note>original: "in animo loquentis"</note> is now clearly apprehended by the hearer. Plato compares it in this state of its nothingness to a vision in a dream, which when a man awakes proves to be nothing but a mere imagination. But because this statement—namely, that "God created all things out of nothing"—has puzzled the minds of many understanding persons (since it could not be perceived how this word <insert>{</insert> "Nothing" <note>original: "Nihil"</note> should be understood), I purpose in few words to discuss it and express my opinion on what is meant by it.

The "Prince of the <term>Peripatetics</term>" <note>Aristotle and his followers.</note> says: "Nothing is made from nothing" <note>original: "Ex Nihilo nihil fit"</note>. This is a learned sentence and an infallible axiom from so learned a personage, if the sense of the word were always to be interpreted in one and the same way. But I say, being founded on good grounds, that there may be those who (either by presumption or through ignorance) are of the opinion that in these words—"God created all things out of nothing"—the word "nothing" <note>original: "Nihilum"</note> ought not to be taken or interpreted as a "negative nothing" <note>original: "Nihilum negativum"</note>, or such a total void that falls outside the capacity or understanding of human reason or intellect. Such a kind of "nothing" was never intended to be the first matter of the Creation. For it appears, both by the infallible sense of Holy Scripture and the sacred light of nature, that <margin>46</margin> the first essence and matter of all things was from all eternity in God, and with God, one and the same thing; and this we prove out of Scripture in this manner. 

<margin>Genesis 1:1.</margin>
Moses says: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" <note>original: "In Principio creavit Deus cœlum & terram"</note>. In this speech, the word "Beginning" <note>original: "Principium"</note> is not to be taken for a negative nothing. For the Scripture tells us in plain <margin>Romans 11:36.</margin> terms that "of him, and through him, and in him are all things" <note>original: "ex ipso, & per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia"</note>. Therefore, if all things proceed from God the Creator, who is the highest of Entities, it follows that they do not proceed from a negative nothing. And again, Scriptures say, as Saint Jerome writes: "Almighty Lord, your hand created the world" <note>original: "Omnipotens Domine, manus tua creavit orbem terrarum"</note>; or, according to Tremellius: "the world out of [matter...]" <margin>Wisdom 11:18.</margin> <note>original: "mundum... ex materia"</note>

<summary>Fludd argues that "Nothing" in the context of creation refers not to a literal void, but to the unmanifest potential of all things existing within God's essence before they were given form. He maintains that the Bible contains a comprehensive "meteorological philosophy" that explains the natural world through divine principles.</summary>

### CHAP. III.

->Of the material fruit or principle which issued and was revealed by the Spirit<-
->of God out of the dark Abyss, and how the substantial machine<-
->of the world was framed from it.<-

All things were implicitly contained or comprehended in the divine powers (as is already shown). In regard to human capacity, this was without form, because it was contained within one formless or invisible water, which was therefore called the Mother of the Elements and the Seed of all things. For just as the whole plant or tree is contained in a small kernel or little misshapen seed, and is in no way subject to man's perception before it sprouts forth, even so all things were in the beginning potentially in the water. The water was also an invisible thing, without form or shape, veiled over with deformity; for darkness was upon the face of the abyss. This was termed the "first matter," which had no formal action that man could imagine, and therefore was said to be only in potential <note>original: "puissance"</note>. 

A wise Philosopher, deeply experienced in the mystical works of the Creation, speaks in this manner: "The first matter out of which the water issued was *nothing* <note>original: "nihil"</note>, and out of it was created the matter of the waters." This ought not to be understood in a human way—namely, that God created the waters out of a literal "nothing"—and yet it was spoken rightly, because in the beginning, nothing was visible. But if wise men would elevate their thoughts above common understanding to find the origin of the waters through contemplation, they would not deny that before the creation of the waters, there was a certain matter in the highest mystery. That is to say, in the divine power <insert>44.</insert> or dark and unformed abyss, which was the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> treasury or storehouse out of which the waters flowed during creation. 

This is partly confirmed by Scripture in various places. The Apostle *Paul* teaches us in the place mentioned before, saying: *By faith we understand that the worlds were prepared by the word of God, so that from invisible things, visible things were made.* <note>original: "Fide intelligimus aptata esse secula verbo Dei, ut ex invisibilibus visibilia fierent"; Hebrews 11:3.</note> By this it is evident that the things which fall under man's sense and knowledge <note>original: "kenning"</note> were not at first subject to man's sense, and therefore were regarded as if they did not exist. Saint *Paul* also says in a similar way: *God chooses those things which are not, so that those things which...* <note>original: "Deus eligit ea quæ non sunt, ut ea que"; 1 Corinthians 1:28.</note>

But when it has shown itself so that it is something and truly subsists, then the dark **Aleph** <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, representing the beginning or unity.</note> is converted into the light **Aleph**: for it is written, *As his darkness is, so is his light*." <margin><insert>37.</insert></margin> 

Nothing is the beginning but wisdom or sapience, and it is the infinity of the three highest numerations of the Kabbalistic tree, which you are accustomed to call the three persons in divinity. This is an absolute essence which, while it is pulled back into the abyss of darkness and rests still and quiet—or, as they say, having respect unto nothing—is for that cause termed by the Hebrews *Ain*, that is to say, *Nihil*, or nothing, or no entity. This is because we, being affected with extreme shallowness or poverty of wit and capacity in the understanding of divine things, judge those things which do not appear just as we are accustomed to do of such things as do not exist at all. 

But when it has shown itself to be somewhat indeed, and that it does really exist as something in human apprehension, then is dark *Aleph* converted into light *Aleph*: for it is written, *As his darkness, such is his light*, or the express words of the Prophet are, *Darkness is to him as light itself*, <margin>Psalm 139:12.</margin> darkness is unto him as Light. 

By this it is evident that though darkness or invisibility appears to our senses to be nothing in comparison to that which is made manifest in light, yet in truth all things are real and essential before God. Therefore, that "nothing" or deformity (out of which the waters, which are the material principle of all things, were originally extracted) seems to him—in whose divine power they remain—a material existence. For as much as nothing is in God but what is essential reality, or a something in being, but *of him, by him, and in him are all things*, <margin>Romans 11:33.</margin> as we are taught by Holy Scripture. 

Therefore, both the dark matrix or womb of the waters, and the watery infant or humid nature which sprung out of the belly of the gloomy abyss or Chaos, were really in God before they appeared to sight. That is to say, they remained in the Almighty’s power or will <note>original: "volunty"</note> and were to be disposed of by him as he pleased, no differently than the plan of a building is first in the mind of the builder.

Secondly, it was the same eternal wisdom, or Spirit *Elohim*, who, acting as it were the part of a midwife, delivered and brought forth this birth, giving it action and form. Again, we may learn from the same chapter of Moses that the waters were the subject of that separation which was effected by the **Spagiric** <note>Alchemical; referring to the process of separating and recombining elements.</note> or fiery virtue of the said Spirit or divine Word.

There was a middle kind of them which, participating in both extremes, was termed the firmament, whose main office <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> was to divide and separate the water from the waters. ### CHAPTER V.
#### Of Fullness and Emptiness, and what true fullness and voidness or nothingness is.

Now that we have briefly discussed and set down the nature of both the two constituting or composing principles, and also the privative and decomposing nature, it is necessary for us to know the property and sense of **Fullness** <note>original: **Plenitude**</note> and **Emptiness** <note>original: **Vacuity**</note> according to true wisdom or Christian philosophy. And first, I will speak a word or two about that **Emptiness** <note>original: **Vacuity**</note> which is so detestable and hateful in the works the Creator has made. Both the fathers of the philosophers and those who have been experts in theology have called it by the name of *Nihil* or **Nothing**. Moses calls it a deformed darkness, or a dark abyss. Hermes calls it a fearful or horrible shadow, void of shape or form. The Cabalists call it a potential being, which is as yet nothing in actual existence. Plato makes it a thing scarcely credible, and therefore hardly to be imagined, and likens it to a mere dream which, when a man is awake, proves to be nothing. St. Augustine says: "When I conceive of anything without form, I first understand nothing more than I understood before; just as by seeing nothing, darkness is seen, and by hearing nothing, silence is heard" <note>original Latin: *Cum aliquid informe concipio, prius nihil intelligo quàm intelligebam, quemadmodum nihil videndo videntur tenebræ, nihil audiendo auditur silentium*</note>. By this, it appears that he compares this "Nothing" to darkness and silence. Job therefore says: "God stretched out the North over emptiness and the void, and he hung the earth upon nothing" <note>original Latin: *Aquilonem Deus extendit super inane & vacuum, & suspendit terram super Nihilum*; Job 26:7</note>.

Job 12:22.

And again, elsewhere: "He reveals the foundations out of darkness and brings the deadly shadow out into the light" <note>original Latin: *Revelat fundamenta è tenebris, & educit in lucem umbram Lethalem*</note>. By all this, he argues that **Emptiness**, **Voidness**, **Nothing**, and **Darkness** are one and the same thing: namely, **Vanity**, **Nothingness**, or **Void**, because all fullness and completion <note>original: *plenitude*</note> is from God in his active property. But God had not yet shone forth upon the world, and therefore as the first deformed matter of the world was void and destitute of all activating grace and formal goodness, it was said to be **Vain**, **Empty**, and **Darkness**. For this reason, Moses said that before the act of Creation, "The earth was void and empty" <note>original Latin: *Terra erat inanis & vacua*</note>, because it was not yet endowed with the beams of Light, Life, and Form. "Darkness was upon the face of the Abyss" <note>original Latin: *Tenebræ fuerunt super faciem Abyssi*</note>, before the all-shaping and creating Spirit of the Lord was carried over the waters. But after the Spirit's appearance, it is said that God called that which appeared dry out of the water "Earth"; and God saw that it was good, and it produced the tender herbs and seeds of every kind, and so on. Therefore, the Earth that was "empty and void" <note>original Latin: *inane and void*</note> before the revelation of God’s Spirit has now become full of divine Light and multiplying Grace. Consequently, it was no longer void and empty—that is to say, destitute of essential being—but became fertile and fruitful, being now replenished with divine fire and the incorruptible Spirit of God, according to that saying of Solomon: <margin>Wisdom 1.</margin> "The holy spirit of Wisdom fills the earth" <note>original Latin: *Spiritus Disciplinæ sanctus implet orbem terrarum*</note>. And again: <margin>Wisdom 12:1. John 1.</margin> "The incorruptible Spirit of God is in every thing" <note>original Latin: *Incorruptibilis Spiritus inest omni rei*</note>. "By this light" <margin>Ephesians 4:10.</margin> (says Saint John) "the world was made" <note>original Latin: *Per hanc lucem mundus est factus*</note>. And the Apostle says, "Christ fills all things" <note>original Latin: *Christus implet omnia*</note>.

By this we may perceive that all fullness comes from the divine Act. Conversely, "vacuity" or emptiness occurs when that formal life is absent from the waters. This is the reason that a <term>Vacuum</term> (void) or emptiness is held to be so horrible a thing in Nature. Because the utter absence of the eternal emanation is intolerable to the creature; every thing desires fervently to be <term>informed</term> <note>original: "informed," meaning to be given an essential form or soul</note> by a natural appetite and affection. Therefore, it is abominable to every natural thing to be utterly deprived of being. For this reason, it follows that unless God had filled all things in this world with his Spirit, emptiness and empty deformity would have possessed the world. But because He, by His presence, created all things from nothing through the illuminating presence of His emanating Spirit—and by this His Spiritual Word He maintains and sustains them all—it follows that there is nothing in this world which is a "void," in vain, or empty. This is maintained by the assertion of the Wise Man <note>Solomon, in the Book of Wisdom</note> mentioned before: <margin>Wisdom 11:18.</margin> "The hand of the Almighty," he says, "created the world from formless matter" <note>original Latin: *Manus Omnipotentis mundum ex informi materia creavit*</note>. That is, out of an empty and void matter, and consequently out of "nothing" <note>original Latin: *Nihil*</note>; for it had no name, since it is "form" that gives a thing its name and essence.

By this, therefore, it may appear how vain the concept of "Vacuum" or "Vacuity" held by the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>followers of Aristotle</note> is, compared to that which is held to be "void and empty" by the true Wise Man. They consider their "vacuum" to be a mere imaginary place in the air, not filled by any bodily existence, not even by air itself—even though it would be capable of receiving some watery existence, namely air, water, or earth. And so they dream of an imaginary <term>Chimera</term> <note>a mythical monster; here meaning a wild or impossible fantasy</note>, which in truth is of itself absolute nothing. It is impossible that any place should be formed in the Universe which can be void in that manner, and consequently, it is not worth dreaming about. But our "Vacuum" and "Void" is a potential matter, or earth, or Abyss without form; namely, that which is only "in potentiality toward reality" <note>original Latin: *in potentia ad actum*</note>, waiting to be brought into "Act" by the presence of Divine Light.

It is no marvel that Aristotle did not think of this kind of emptiness and fullness, since in one place he says, "From nothing, nothing is made" <note>original Latin: *Ex nihilo nihil fit*</note>, and in another place he affirms Light to be an <term>Accident</term> <note>a property that does not exist on its own, like color or shape</note>. Therefore, it did not appear to his senses that such an "accident" could take away emptiness or vacuity and fill all things essentially by its presence. But I will combat our Christian Peripatetics with their own weapons, who hold it as a maxim that "the existence of an accident is to be within a subject" <note>original Latin: *accidentis esse sit inesse*</note>. I will therefore assail them with this syllogism:

If Light is an "Accident," then its existence is to adhere to, or to be in, some "Subject." But the existence of true Light is to exist without any adherence to matter or "Subject" <note>because it existed before matter was formed</note>. Therefore, it is no accident.

The first part of the argument <note>the Major premise</note> is proved by Aristotle's own axiom, which is: "The existence of an Accident is to be in, or to adhere to, some material Subject" <note>original Latin: *Accidentis esse est in esse, aut adhærere subjecto alicui*</note>, or else it cannot be. The second part <note>the Minor premise</note> is maintained by the words of <margin>1 John 1:5.</margin> Moses: Light was created the first day before any creature, and therefore it did <margin>John 1.</margin> not have any preceding actual matter or "Subject" to be in or adhere to. Besides, it is <margin>Wisdom 7.</margin> beyond imagination that God should create "Accidents" before any Essential or Substantial creature. Again, God, who is the Fountain of Light, is said to be "Light in whom is no darkness." And again, the Word is defined in another place to be "Light," and the Spirit of Wisdom is said to be the bright splendor and shining forth of the Almighty. And therefore it was most absurd in Aristotle, and even in some of...

### CHAP. VI.

->*How the two essential but opposite active properties first arose, and afterward how so many passive natures issued from the aforementioned principles. By the power of these properties, all changes and alterations were and are carried out in this sublunary world.*<-

In this place, I will relate to you the births and beginnings, first of the two opposite active natures (or essential virtues) which proceed from the two radical or main principles mentioned before. Then I will describe to you the conditions of those two passive ones, which are derived from the effects of those two mutual actions. You must know, therefore, that just as the "potential" or dark principle is contrary and opposite in its essential property to the "actual" emanation of light, so too has each of them manifested or brought forth into this world two offspring or essential properties. These are opposing in condition and total adversaries to one another in their nature. These two active virtues are *Cold* and *Heat*. I purpose to speak of the manner of their production and their individual conditions in this chapter, starting first with Cold.

It is clear from what has already been said—and shall be more fully expressed in the first book of my *Sympathetic History*—that darkness is the immediate effect of the divine "Nolunty" <term>Nolunty (Latin: *noluntas*) refers to God's "non-willing" or withdrawal, the opposite of his active "Volunty" or will.</term>, or latent Divinity, and consequently of God's restrictive property or divine power. Therefore, it is the mother of privation, death, emptiness, nothingness, lack of form, and so forth. For the property of the dark Nothing (or the deformed abyss) is naturally to rest and not to act or operate. The reason for this is that its entire appetite is to be focused in and around the center, beyond which there is no motion or action, and not to expand itself toward the circumference, as the Spirit of Light—or God in his active will or manifest nature—is accustomed to do. For this reason, the dark principle claims for itself, by a natural instinct, rest and quietness. This property begets or produces an essential virtue of its own condition: *Cold*. Cold is chosen as a champion to resist the assaults of its opposite, *Heat*, whose companions are motion or action (for the restless antagonist and provoker of Cold is Heat). Unless it is stirred up by the assaults of Heat, Cold does not move, but seems to wait upon its drowsy mother, Darkness and privation, whose children are fixation and rest. These sleep in and cling fast to the center, and therefore are unwilling to look outward toward the circumference.

<margin>In the *Pimander* <note>A foundational text of Hermeticism.</note>.</margin>
<margin>Reuchlin, *De Arte Cabalistica*, Book 3.</margin>
In truth, cold is an essential act proceeding from and attending to the divine power, which in this property pulls its beams back from the circumference into itself. This agrees with the saying of the philosopher Hermes: "The One begets the One and reflects into itself" <note>original Latin: *Monas generat monadem & se reflexit in se-ipsum*</note>. This means it would not shine outward, but retained its activity centrally within itself, and so seemed to rest in itself. This was the same as the teaching of the Cabalist <term>A student of the Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</term> Bahir: "When the divine wisdom was retracted into the abyss of darkness, remaining still and idle and regarding nothing, it is called *Ain* <note>Hebrew: אֵין</note>, that is, Nothing; in which state it is called the dark *Aleph* <note>The first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, here representing the first principle of God.</note>" <note>original Latin/Hebrew: *Sapientia cum esset in abysso tenebrarum retracta, immanens ociosaque & ad nihil respiciens אֵין, i. e. Nihil, dicitur; in quo statu Aleph tenebrosum dictitatur*</note>.

In this contracted, or rather secluded and private state of the divine unity, it operates according to this negative property or condition through its essential agent, Cold. This proves that Cold is not an "accident," as the empty doctrine of the Peripatetics would persuade us. It is apparent to every wise man that no accidental qualities are in or can come from God, since the divine Nature is purely a simple, essential, and formal purity, existing in himself and of himself,

said to be *one simple spirit, yet manifold* <note>original: *Spiritus unicus multiplex*</note>—one simple spirit in essence, but manifold in respect to his essential properties. Now, it is made evident by its effects that this essential property, or nature of Cold, is the formal instrument (or instrumental virtue) by which God operates in his hidden and potential state. He uses it to resist heat, action, or motion, and to deform or destroy that which he effected in his manifest <note>original: "patent"</note> nature through his Heat or active property. 

For what the spirit of wisdom in its manifest nature performed through its hot spirit or blast from the south or easterly wind—namely, thinning <note>original: "subtiliating"</note> and rarefying the waters into thin air, making that which was gross subtle, and making that which was opaque and dark transparent <note>original: "diaphan"</note> and invisible—the self-same spirit, assuming his hidden and cold property, deforms and undoes. By blowing or breathing from the North, the same thin and rarefied air is made thick, dense, and visible, which was previously made invisible through rarefaction. That which was made transparent, light, and clear by the dissipating of its parts is now, by the contractive virtue of the Northern properties, reduced into an opaque or dark substance that is in no way transparent. 

That which was active, movable, and lively by the addition of heat has now become stagnant <note>original: "stupid"</note>, still, and deadly by the invasion of cold. That which was light and had no sensible weight is framed into a heavy and ponderous body or consistency, as we see when the air is turned into snow, hail, ice, and frost by the northern blast. Now, that it is only one and the same spirit in essence which blows from the four

By this, he argues that it is only one spirit, though it assumes a four-fold property at its pleasure. 

And now, to confirm that everything said here is true, simply observe the words of the royal Psalmist: *The Lord sends forth the snow like wool,
<margin>Psalm 147:16-18.</margin>
scatters the frost like ashes, and casts down the ice like chunks <note>original: "gobbits," from the Latin *frusta*</note>; who is able to withstand his cold? From these words we may observe many notable things: 

First, that God, in his hidden or latent property, uses his essential action of cold to contract toward the center those things which were previously expanded toward the circumference. 

Secondly, that the property of cold is attributed or ascribed to God in his northern action; therefore it is said, *Who is able to resist his cold?* For this reason, it is evident that it is an essential virtue in the divine power <note>original: "puissance"</note>. 

Thirdly, that it must be the act of unity in his dark, hidden, and privative property—both because it darkens things that are transparent, clear, and light, and because it deprives those things of life and motion which acted, moved, and lived through essential heat. Lastly, it is an utter enemy to the action of heat, which accompanies the revealed, emanating, and life-giving <note>original: "vivifying"</note> divinity. 

Fourthly, that the effects of cold are undone by the act of the revealed nature of God, which is the Word; for the text says, *He sends out his word, and dissolves or melts all these* (namely, the snow, frost, and ice). 

Fifthly, that all this is effected by one and the same spirit in essence, but of diverse and opposite conditions, to perform the will of the Father who sends it forth. 

Again, that the cold property of the wind is the essential depriving virtue—the numbing <note>original: "stupefying"</note> and contracting act of God—appears by this passage from

I conclude, therefore, that cold is the essential act of the divine power or eternal wisdom <note>original: "sapience"</note>, shrouding itself in its mantle of darkness. It therefore manifests the divine will in that specific state through its effects—namely, that it draws from the circumference toward the center. Consequently, it is the reason for the gathering together of things (whether they are of different or similar kinds), and is therefore the only essential agent or efficient cause of thickening <note>original: "inspissation"</note>, contraction, tightening <note>original: "constriction"</note>, fixation, immobility, weight <note>original: "ponderosity"</note>, rest, darkening <note>original: "obteneration"</note>, death <note>original: "mortification"</note>, deprivation, and such like.

His emanation from the center toward the circumference, and revealing himself upon the dark face of the Abyss, causes the invisible non-being <note>original: *non Ens*</note> or potential nothing <note>original: *potentiall Nihil*</note> to appear in action. This state is first animated by his bright presence in the form of waters. He is said by the Wise Man <note>Referring to Solomon in the Book of Wisdom</note> to be *more mobile than all mobile things, piercing through or reaching everywhere because of his purity* <note>original: *omnibus mobilibus mobilior, ubique penetrans seu attingens propter munditiam ejus*</note>. 

Just as the other privative or "Northern" property produced rest and an absence of operation—through attraction or contraction from the circumference toward the center—so in this, his positive or "Southern" and "Oriental" property, he procreates motion. By dilating himself, or sending out his active beam, brightness, or emanation from the center toward the circumference, he is accompanied by the essential act of heat <note>original: "calidity"</note>, which operates continually upon the effects of cold by resisting, dissolving, and destroying them. 

Thus, this formal champion of Light, namely Heat, wars perpetually against the cold guardian of Darkness. For the one can have no dominion in the air until the other is exiled little by little. Therefore, just as the Light principle (with all its branches) is said to be the father of position, act, form <note>original: "information"</note>, fullness, motion, life, health, and heat, so also does heat operate according to the nature of its restless and ever-operating father, which is Light. It works to destroy the effects of darkness and cold, as we see in the nature of the hot winds, specifically those of the South and the East. 

For the Northern cold wind gathers, contracts, hardens, thickens, or condenses the air, making it heavy, fixed, immovable, and opaque; it changes the air by thickening <note>original: "inspissation"</note> into the nature of heavier elements. Conversely, the hot winds or spirits dissipate, dilate, soften, rarefy, and make thin, light, volatile, movable, and transparent whatever the cold winds had altered. All of this is effected by the alchemical <note>original: "spagerick"</note> or separative act of God’s Spirit or Word.

Therefore the Prophet said in the text mentioned before: *Sending forth his word, he melts them; as soon as he blows his wind, the waters flow* <note>original: *Emittens verbum suum liquefacit ista, simul ac efflat ventum suum effluunt aquae*</note>. This means that God, by sending forth his Word—that is, causing his bright virtue to shine forth—did undo or melt the snow, frost, and ice which God, in his hidden or contractive property, had caused under the form of an angelic wind. Therefore it is said: as soon as he blows forth his breath or wind, the waters flow. That is to say, the snow is melted, and from a fixed and opaque substance, it becomes movable, lively, flowing, and transparent <note>original: "diaphan"</note>. 

So also the heat of the Easterly wind destroys and dissipates the watery effects of the Westerly wind. Therefore the Prophet says: *Afterward, when the East wind comes, the wind of the Lord from the desert, his spring shall fail and his fountain shall be dried up* <note>original: *Postquam veniente Euro, vento JEHOVÆ è deserto, exaruerit scaturigo ejus & siccatus fuerit fons ejus*</note>. This implies that the water was changed by the heat of that wind into air through rarefaction or refinement <note>original: "subtiliation"</note>. 

Thus you have understood how these two opposite virtues—Cold and Heat—spring from one and the same Spirit in its radical essence. Through this essence, the Spirit operates actually and essentially by a double property, producing opposite effects in the universal <note>original: "Catholick"</note> element of the sublunary world to fulfill the will of the Creator in the air, and upon the earth and seas. 

Now I will speak a word or two about the procreation or generation of such passive natures as are brought forth by the mutual action and opposition of the two aforementioned essential virtues. These virtues have their root or beginning either in the Divine Nature’s negation <note>original: "Nolunty", from the Latin *noluntas*, referring to God's "hidden" or "unwilling" state of contraction</note> and privative existence, or in its affirmation <note>original: "Volunty", from *voluntas*, referring to God's "willing" or active emanation</note> and positive emanation.

These passive qualities essentially depend upon the former ones, and belong to them in the same way the female or passive belongs to the male or active. First, I will tell you my thoughts regarding the birth of humidity <note>moisture</note>, and afterward I will speak of dryness <note>original: "Siccity"</note>. 

We must imagine that when there was no formal Light to bring form to the shapeless Abyss or Chaos—and consequently no Heat to act and make a division of Light from Darkness—then all the dark Chaos was inclining toward drought and wetness, congealed with cold. For cold has an infinite power and dominion where heat is absent. We see this around the Northern Pole: all the waters are frozen into a dry and cold clod or heap because of the absence of the Sun's heat. In the same way, where the Sun or the burning Easterly wind sends forth its breaths <note>original: "spiracles"</note> of heat directly, cold is banished, and the Earth is turned into a dry, thirsty, and spongy mass. Even so, and after the same pattern, are those earlier states; or rather, these modern examples follow those ancient patterns. For the Chaos was a confused, cold, and dry heap, until the Light did appear and began to operate. Also the

Light in itself, as it was considered without any action upon the passive mass, was of a fiery condition—that is to say, only heat and dryness <note>original: "drouth"</note> appeared in it. It follows, therefore, that just as cold is in effect nothing other than the act of divine power made potent and evident by the absence of Heat, so also is dryness nothing but an apparent passive nature. Dryness always accompanies the two aforementioned active powers in their absolute purpose when moisture is totally absent. 

Now, moisture is like a hybrid <note>original: "mongrell"</note> begotten between the two opposite active forces, which is proved in this way: The North wind, by its dominion, turns the Air into snow, hail, ice, or frost—that is, into a cold and dry substance. But when the Southerly or Easterly winds begin to take dominion, then their blasts gradually penetrate those dry masses or substances, undoing them and converting them into a moist or humid nature. This follows the meaning of the words of David: *As soon (he says) as he blows forth his wind, the waters flow. As soon as he sends forth his Word, they are liquefied.* 

So, moisture is nothing more than a mixture of heat and cold in one solid substance, which is fluxible in potentiality <note>original: *potentia*</note>; then, little by little, the cold and dryness depart and become faint, depending on whether the power of the wind is more or less vigorous in Heat. For we must observe this: just as cold makes things immobile and fixed, it is an evident sign that the Southern or Eastern Heat has taken possession of the Mass when, by their action, it begins to moisten, to revive, and to move again. Nothing effects that function except Heat. 

In this very same manner, the uncreated and all-creating Spirit of Light, moving upon the face of the dark abyss, operated within it and caused the congealed Mass to soften <note>original: "relent"</note>. It was then called "waters" by Moses, and the "moist nature" <note>original: *humida natura*</note> by Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure linked to alchemy and philosophy</note>. And so they continue to this day, being altered from one nature to another according to the will of God, which he accomplishes through his ministers, the Angelic winds, causing the spiritual waters to change and wheel about from one nature into another. We must observe in these changes that even the visible waters were first made and derived from the invisible waters, according to St. Paul's doctrine mentioned before. For Heaven existed before the Sea and Earth, which were, in a sense, the feces, dregs, or grosser part of the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> sublunary element.

### *A visual demonstration, confirming the Divine properties or virtues mentioned above.*

Before we proceed to our visual demonstration <note>original: "ocular Demonstration"</note>, which shall be performed using our experimental instrument <note>Fludd is referring to his "weather glass" or thermoscope, a primitive thermometer used to show the expansion and contraction of air</note>, we must first consider that the universal Air or sublunary Heaven is the subtler and more spiritual portion of those waters which are under the Firmament. Moses mentions this division; therefore, every particular part of it corresponds to the whole. Consequently, the air included in the glass of the instrument is of the same nature as the whole universal Air. Because of their continuity, as the whole air outside fares, so does the part included within. 

Again, just as the Spirit which walked upon the waters animated, vivified, informed, and dilated them—giving them motion—so also by his absence (either by hiding his act or contracting his emanating beams into himself), the waters are also contracted, condensed, and darkened. This is apparent in the property of the Northern wind, which proceeds from the privative <note>A "privative" action is one defined by the absence or taking away of a quality—in this case, the absence of heat</note> or contractive action of this Spirit. 

But as the waters by their existence fill the vaulted cavity of the world, so also does the all-informing Spirit fill every corner of them. Inasmuch as it operates "all in all," but with a diversity of properties (and is therefore termed "manifold wisdom" <note>original: *multiformis Sapientia*</note>), it sometimes operates in its privative property in these lower waters, as was already told you—namely, when the wind blows from the North and West. At other times, it operates in its positive nature, such as when it breathes from the South or East. In the first case, by its cold action, it contracts from the circumference toward the center; in the latter—namely, by its hot property—it dilates from the center to the circumference. 

Seeing then that water is the universal passive substance out of which the shape of the whole world and everything in it was carved and fashioned (as St. Peter tells us), and that the eternal, creating, and all-acting Spirit of the Lord is the universal actor which moves "all in all" in the waters (as Moses intimates to us), and that it does so through an infinity of organs—such as Angels, Sun, Moon, Stars, and Winds...

...fire, and so on, as we find in many places of Scripture. It must necessarily follow that God is the active force behind both the contraction and expansion of air, both generally in nature and specifically within this glass instrument. Therefore, just as the sun, the hot winds, fire, or the natural heat of the human body derive their power to expand things from his radiating and activating power—altering the cold air, winds, and water from their passive state—so it follows that both the expansion and the contraction of the air inside the glass are direct acts of this Spirit’s active or passive property. 

For when this Spirit blows from the North or West, the air is compressed more or less into a smaller space inside the glass. This is proven <margin>The North wind</margin> because the water is drawn higher into the neck of the glass, so that a physical vacuum is not allowed to occur in nature <note>original: "corporall vacuity"; Fludd is referencing the scientific principle that "nature abhors a vacuum"</note>. Furthermore, it is most apparent that the air in the glass is compressed even further whenever the Northern cold dominates the outside air, because the air is gathered into a tighter space or passage than it occupied before the water rose up. 

On the other hand, if hot winds or the summer sun heat the outside air, then the trapped air will also expand, and in its expansion, it requires a larger space. That the air is expanded by heat is plainly demonstrated by the fact that the water level is pushed down many degrees lower than it was before. Again, if you place your hand on the top of the glass bulb, the water will sink because the air will immediately expand. 

Now, the Scriptures confirm in many places (both previously mentioned and those that follow) that the spirit of life which gives this heat to humans or animals comes from this eternal Spirit which, as the Apostle says, "gives life to all things" <note>original Latin/English: "doth vivifie all things"; likely 1 Timothy 6:13</note>. Again, the Prophet calls this "one Spirit from the four winds, to breathe into the dead bodies so that they might live again" <margin>Ezekiel 37:9</margin>. 

Thus, you see it clearly confirmed by visual demonstration that cold contracts, thickens <note>original: "inspissate"</note>, and makes the trapped air dense. This is proven by the drawing up of the water and the shrinking of the air. Conversely, you see that heat expands and disperses air, as shown by the expansion of the air in hot weather or by placing a hand on the bulb <note>original: "bolts head"</note>, which is made evident by the water being pushed down.

Please note (I beg you, those of you who will not be overly biased toward the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</term>) two notable errors of the Aristotelians. The first is revealed in their maxim that "heat gathers together things of a similar nature" <note>original Latin: *calidum doth congregare homogenea*</note>. Now you see it visually demonstrated here that heat does the exact opposite: it scatters and disperses the air (which consists of similar parts) and therefore does *not* gather it together. Instead, it is cold that congregates, compacts, and gathers similar things together, as well as dissimilar things. For you can see in our instrument that cold contracts and gathers the air—and even the water—into a tighter and narrower space. Therefore, their claim is also unsound when they say that "cold only gathers together things of different natures" <note>original Latin: *frigidum doth onely congregare heterogenea*</note>.

Their other obvious error is also revealed by this visual experiment. They claim that the sun, stars, fire, and all heat draw vapors and moisture from the earth and water toward themselves. However, we find the opposite through our experimental glass. By simply placing a warm hand on the glass, the air immediately expands; far from being attracted to the heat, the air actually flies away from the hand. This is proven by the pushing down or "precipitation" of the water, as we have said. 

Thus, we have sufficiently described the state of the first and second principles of all things in this book, though only in brief terms. My intention is to discuss them more extensively and in greater detail in the first book of my *History of Sympathy and Antipathy*.

I will now proceed to the next book, where I plan to address the mystery of thinning <term>Rarefaction</term> and thickening <term>Condensation</term>, along with the variety within the heavenly structure and the transformation of the one universal earthly element <note>original: "catholick sublunary Element"</note> into four different states of being. Finally, I will conclude with the fundamental primary cause of creation, birth, decay, and resurrection.

# The Fourth Book

->The Argument of this Book.<-

In this book, the universal mystery of <term>rarefaction</term> <note>the process of making a substance less dense; expansion</note> and <term>condensation</term> <note>the process of making a substance more dense; contraction</note> is explained. It is also proved here that the world was made by these two processes: the heavens were established in their proper order, and the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> element was altered and changed in a fourfold manner and condition.

## CHAPTER I.

->*In this chapter, the common or universal subject of condensation and rarefaction is once again recounted or repeated. Additionally, the two essential opposite properties or virtues—which are derived from the Eternal Principle in its negative and positive nature—are proved to be the immediate causes of both those alterations in the general element of the Waters.*<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'I' decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
I have made it (as I imagine) most plain and evident to your understanding—not only by the testimony of ancient philosophy and the infallible wisdom of Holy Scripture but also by visible demonstration—that the common or universal matter and subject of all things was the Waters. These Waters were enacted and created by the bright Spirit of the Lord before all other things. 

Since this is so, and because all condensation and rarefaction require a subject or material substance in which they are performed, it follows that the only matter which endures or undergoes the act of either process must be water, or a humid and moist nature. This is because water is the only substantial material that fills the entire vast cavity of the world. Consequently, it is the material existence from which both Heaven and Earth, and all things within them, are framed and were originally shaped. 

Water is therefore the main subject of condensation and rarefaction. By these means, all things in this world are made to differ from one another and are disposed and ordered by God according to weight, number, and measure in their proper ranks and places. That is, they are placed in a higher or lower region according to the dignity that the universal or eternal Creator <note>original: "catholick or eternall Actor"</note> bestowed upon them during their creation. 

The common matter of <term>incrassation</term> <note>thickening or becoming more solid</note> and <term>subtiliation</term> <note>becoming thinner or more refined</note> having thus been made manifest, we must now find the universal actor or operator in this work. I indicated to you before that this actor was the sacred emanation of that divine splendor which operated from the very beginning, operates at this present moment, and shall hereafter work all that which shall be effected in the heavens above and the earth beneath. 

This assertion of mine accords well with this axiom of the Apostle, which I have repeated often (and not without just cause):

He is that all-informing and operating Spirit who acts and accomplishes his pleasure in all and over all through his various organs, whether they be angelic, celestial, or elementary. These organs, according to their different dispositions, are moved by this internal act to operate in this world the will of the Creator, both positively and negatively, as shall be told to you in the chapter following.

->### CHAPTER II.<-

->*How this Divine Spirit, or Ruach Elohim <note>Hebrew for "Spirit of God."</note>, being but one in Essence, works through both his Angelic and Astral organs in this sublunary <note>The physical world below the moon; the earthly realm.</note> world in a four-fold manner.*<-

The Eternal spirit of wisdom, who is the initial principle of all things, and in whom and by whom (as the Apostle teaches us) the <margin>Colossians 1:16</margin> *Angels, Thrones, powers, and dominions were Created,* operates through his Angelic Organs of contrary strengths within the universal Element of the lower waters, causing both the effect of Condensation and that of Rarefaction. Now, that this one spirit works in and through spiritual and Angelic Organs—specifically in the actions carried out by the properties of the four winds—is proved from the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, where we find these words: *I saw four Angels standing on the four corners of the Earth, holding the four winds of the Earth, so that they should not blow on the Earth, nor on the Sea, etc.* <margin>Revelation 7:1</margin> By this it is evident that these Angelic Presidents over the four winds were the Ministers and Organs through which the spirits or blasts of the winds were emitted or held back according to the will of that eternal spirit, who guides them when and where he pleases. 

But we find by daily observation that the essential power in the Northern spirit <note>The North Wind.</note> is cold, and therefore contractive or attractive from the circumference toward the center, and consequently a cause of freezing and condensation. By this kind of Angelic power, the divine spirit works his negative effects and acts of thickening <note>original: "Inspissation"</note> and solidification <note>original: "fixation"</note> in the sublunary Element, causing terrestrial and earthly effects. 

But on the contrary, we find that through the Southern and Easterly Angelic spirits, the all-creating and operating power causes Rarefaction and thinning <note>original: "Subtiliation"</note> in the said inferior waters through their essential action, which is heat. For this reason, the hot winds undo by rarefaction all that which the cold Northern winds achieved by freezing. It appears, therefore, that the "increased spirit"—which moves preeminently in the angelic creature *Michael* (whose name includes *El*, or "Strong God" <note>original: *Deus fortis*</note>)—is that same princely spirit specified by the Prophet Ezekiel (as has already been proved). He dwells in the great Angel who, rising up from the East, commanded the four governors of the winds and their legions. By this it is manifest that they all receive their action and power from him, and are ordained to be employed only at his will—either to cause privation or presence, and consequently to produce condensation or rarefaction in the world at his pleasure. Specifically, they produce "position" and "information" <note>term: "information" here refers to the act of giving "form" or life to matter.</note> by his light and heat, and "privation" or "deformation" by his dark and cold property. <margin>Psalm 103:20</margin> And upon this, the kingly Prophet <note>King David</note> speaks thus: "The strong angels of God, who execute his word and listen to the voice of his command, are his ministers who perform his will." <note>original Latin: *Angeli Dei validissimi robore, efficientes verbum ejus, auscultantes voci ejus, ministri ejus facientes placitum.*</note> And again, "Who makes your angels winds or spirits <margin>Psalm 104:4</margin> (for the Hebrew word *Ruach* <note>original: רוח</note> signifies wind, spirit, or breath), and your ministers flames of fire." <note>original Latin: *Qui facis angelos tuos ventos, et ministros tuos ignem urentem*</note>

By this it is evident that the Eternal Breath is what animates the Angels. The Angels give life and vigor first to the stars, and then to the winds. The winds first give form to the elements—or rather, they alter the universal sublunary element <note>The "catholick sublunary element" refers to the basic underlying matter of the world below the moon.</note> into various natures, which are termed "Elements." Then, by the mixing of various "windy forms" in that one element, they produce meteorological compositions <note>term: "meteorologicall compositions" refers to "meteors," which in this period included all atmospheric phenomena like rain, snow, wind, and lightning.</note> of various natures, according to the diversity of the windy forms that alter it.

But so that I may discuss these matters more appropriately, and also address many difficulties and doubts that have greatly troubled the philosophers and theosophers <note>term: "theosophers" were those who sought divine wisdom through mystical insight or philosophical study of God's works.</note> of our age regarding the principal "tabernacle" <note>A dwelling place or container.</note> of this all-acting and creating Spirit in the world: before I proceed any further in this my history of Condensation and Rarefaction, I will express my opinion on that point at length. This clarification <note>original: "enucleation"</note> will be very relevant and necessary for opening up this main business, because in it consists not only the world’s creation, but also the imperial government of the world’s Spirit and the formal manner in which meteors are produced.

Regarding the person: surely the whole Christian Church in his days would not have chosen a man of lowly skill in the Hebrew language to undergo a task of such importance—being for the primary good of the whole Christian Church—as was the translation of the Bible out of Hebrew into Latin. And from this, the 'Alphabetical Cabala' <note>original: *Alphabetaria hac cabala*</note> or 'reception' sprang, by which he revealed or disclosed the great secrets of divine things, etc." 

If Reuchlin meant this regarding *St. Jerome*, as many learned men imagine, you will not deny that he was deeply well-versed in the profound and secret meaning of the Scriptures; therefore, he was a man who should not be so easily deceived or deluded in his interpretation. Again, no one can deny that the Pope and the whole Christian clergy assisted him in this business with all the ancient books or manuscripts that might direct him to the true way or sense of interpretation. Thus, he did not lack the support of ancient authority, but could discern between the true and corrupt text in his interpretation. 

Therefore, so that we neither accuse the later interpreters for their exposition, nor detract from *St. Jerome’s* labors (which deserve an everlasting monument), we must instead attribute the error to the corruption or alteration of the Hebrew text. This is because the entire harmony of the Scriptures, and the main subject of the Psalm in which it is recited, tend and incline toward the interpretation of *St. Jerome*, as I will specifically prove and express to you by these following arguments:

3. Then, from the resolution of the ancient theologians, along with other circumstances belonging to them. 
4. Fourthly, from an astronomical observation and the dignity and excellence of the solar creature. 
5. Fifthly, from an arithmetical consideration. 
6. Sixthly, from the point and circle in Geometry. 
7. Seventhly, from the consonance of the greatest perfection in music or harmony. 
8. Eighthly, from a physical or natural regard. 
9. And lastly, by the assertions of the wisest and most divine philosophers, which accord exactly with the harmony of the Scriptures. 

I shall speak of each of these in their order.

By this, it is argued that this heavenly mass is made into a tabernacle for the Spiritual Sun—the beautiful and divine Spirit of Light. This does not mean the spirit is limited to the Sun; as the Scriptures say, the Holy Spirit was abundantly in the physical Christ, and yet it was not denied to fill the earth and heavens as well.

# Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

The fifth argument shows how, from an **arithmetical perspective**, Divinity must necessarily dwell in the Sun. Specifically, just as there is only one unity from which the entire multitude of stars in heaven derive and draw their formal essence, so too are all numbers produced from a single arithmetical unity. The number two is simply the form of one and the same unity conceived twice; adding one more unity makes three, and so on to infinity <note>original: "in infinitum"</note>. In exactly the same way that one candle lights another, and then a third, and continues to infinity, so does this one heavenly Candle <note>The Sun</note> fill all the starry candles in heaven with light and beauty. Yet, it still retains its accustomed unity in perfection, power, and glory without any loss.

By the sixth argument (which is **geometrical**), considering that the Sun is a most bright circular body, it must necessarily have a central point within its circumference where all its illuminating power resides. This is because the circumference is nothing more than a radial expansion of a point-like and essential virtue from the center to the edge. This is the meaning of that philosophical axiom: *Virtue and truth reside in the middle* <note>original: "In medio consistit virtus & veritas"</note>. Now, if that wonderful beauty and clear brightness found in the Sun did not extend from the center, it would not proceed from an internal principle <note>original: "à principio interno"</note>; it would then require some other external source of light, just as the Moon does. However, that is proven to be false, as no body in the world is found to be equal to it in brightness. This is an argument that it possesses a central divinity, or divine virtue, within it. Like the soul in the center of a living creature, this divinity gives life and acts from the center toward the circumference. By making the surface of the body a fiery and bright "colored thing" <note>original: "coloratum"; Fludd uses this to mean a physical object made visible by light</note>, it causes its radiant outflow to extend to all the limits of the vast world, according to the infinity of its central agent. This is why God is said to be the center of all things, whose circumference is nowhere—that is to say, He is in and over all, and beyond or outside of all. 

Nor should it seem strange to anyone that I say the uncreated light is visible through the "tabernacle" <note>The Sun</note> which it inhabits, since the Scriptures testify *that he is a consuming fire* <note>Hebrews 12:29</note>. And again, *that the spirit of wisdom excels the sun and stars in brightness* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 7:29</note>. It is also said, *He is attired with light as with a garment* <note>Psalm 104:2</note>. To conclude, He is the fountain and father of light <note>original: "fons & pater luminis"</note>, and therefore no light, whether visible or invisible, can exist in this world that does not come from Him. Does not St. Paul seem to assert *that all visible things were first made from things that were not visible*? This argues that all visible light originated from the invisible light whose fountain is God; this invisible light continues in essence within its likeness in created things, as shall be shown presently.

The seventh argument is confirmed by an **observation in music**: namely, that the divine Spirit has chosen the Sun for his dwelling place because of its position in heaven. Consider that God, as He is said to exist in Himself, is described by Scripture as seated *in the heaven of heavens*, and in another place, *in the highest heavens, yet he respects and looks down upon the earth*. In that regard, we may compare Him—if it be permitted to compare sacred things with worldly ones <note>original: "si sacra cum mundanis componere fas sit"</note>—to a **unison** in harmony. If a string of a musical instrument is struck while open, it sounds a unity from the bridge of the instrument to the nut or head. So, we imagine that a string <note>original: "chord"</note> may be extended from the world’s circumference (the highest heavens) to the center (the earth). Furthermore, if we press the string exactly in the middle, each half-string, when struck, will sound as an **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note> to the whole. This middle point will prove to be the center or perfection for each end of the string, which then points out the circumference.

Now, the harmonious octave is the most perfect accord of all others. Therefore, it signifies that the middle point between the light (or heaven) and the earth is the seat of the greatest perfection. This corresponds to the unison as 1 does to 2, which is in a double proportion <note>original: "in proportione dupla"; the 2:1 ratio of an octave</note>. It follows, therefore—and is apparent by its effects—that the Sun is placed in this central seat, which corresponds to the whole as 2 does to 1, because it is the opinion of all astronomers that the Sun is placed in the middle, or center, of the heavens. 

Now, I ask you to observe how this perfect accord was mystically shaped out of the divine and fundamental unity, which said, "Let it be done" <note>original: "Fiat"</note>, and it was done. Unity said, "Let it be done," and so this unison caused a divine emanation, which created the number 2. This had the same relationship to unity as the octave (perfection) has to a unison. Now, this bright emanation, by which all things were created and framed in true harmony, chose for itself...

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 4

In this world, the perfect seat of its royal regard toward all creatures is at the point of the **octave** <term>original: "diapason," the interval representing the most perfect harmony</term>, which is always in the middle of the unison, and therefore in the center of the heavens. But it appears to the eyes that the Sun is positioned in the middle of the seven planets; and again, it appears by the divine glory which shines from it that it is a seat of divine perfection. Therefore, the **Platonists** <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato who believed in an ideal world of forms</note> have imagined that the Solar orb or sphere is the seat of their **soul of the world** <note>original: "anima mundi"</note>. Now, as this royal and most harmonious octave contains within its capacity the other two inferior accords in music—namely, the **perfect fifth** <term>original: "diapente"</term> and the **perfect fourth** <term>original: "diatessaron"</term> (for the octave is composed of these two united)—it is likely that the whole harmony of the heavens, and consequently of the world, is put into practice in this created instrument. The actor or player upon it is the eternal Spirit, who sounds out every minute from this, His glorious instrument, strains of life, life-giving, multiplication, peace, or preservation for all creatures. For this is the office of the eternal Christ in this world—I mean the divine Word—in whom, as the Evangelist John testifies, is life. But of this, more in the next section.

Eighthly, it is proved by a physical or natural perspective: for we observe, and not we only, but the beasts themselves—and even the very herbs and vegetable plants of the earth—feel and, as it were, confess that the Sun is the chief treasury of life-giving power <note>original: "vivification"</note> and multiplication in this world. Consequently, it is apparent that when the Sun approaches near us, the herbs and trees which seemed dead before now revive, put on their green coats, and flourish with their blossoms and flowers. But contrariwise, when it departs to the other side of the **Equator** <note>original: "Æquinoctiall"</note>, they put off their flowers and green apparel and begin to mourn, as it were, for his departure. But, says St. Paul, **God gives life to all things** <note>original: "Deus vivificat omnia"</note>. And therefore, if the Sun by his presence brings the virtue of life-giving to the world, it is apparent that it has this gift from the Spirit of God, which is the Spirit of life. Being abundantly poured by God into this heavenly vessel, it effects these life-giving acts in the world, just as the same spirit, being fluently infused into Christ, Moses, Elijah, and other Saints upon earth, effected wonders upon the earth in healing, reviving from death, etc. Does not the <margin>Ecclesiastes 1</margin> sacred text also aver that **God has poured out His wisdom upon all His works according to His gift** <note>original: "Sapientiam Deus effudit supra omnia opera sua secundum datum suum"</note>? Why then should any man have any doubt or question regarding the Spirit's habitation in the Sun in abundance? 

This, therefore, is the chief subject of this Psalm of David: to express that the glory of God appears palpably out of the creatures of heaven. Indeed, out of every creature the eternal Spirit shines or expresses His glory more or less and is to be discerned within it according to the gift given to it. <margin>Job 26:13</margin> Thereupon Job says, **God has adorned the heavens with His Spirit** <note>original: "Cælos ornavit Deus Spiritu suo"</note>. By which words it is manifest that it is the essential Spirit of God which gives, by the abundance of His presence, the luster and glory to the Sun. For that reason, the Sun is termed—and not erroneously—by the Platonists (who therein have imitated the divine poet Orpheus), the **Eye of the world** <note>original: "Oculus mundi"</note>, because in and by it, as in a certain clear and smooth looking glass or mirror, all things are seen and discovered. 

Again, the philosopher Heraclitus says: **"If you take away the Sun from the world, what is our little body if the soul is missing? There is no beating vein or pulse to be discerned in it, there is no judgment to be perceived in it, and there is neither vital breath nor respiration in it"** <note>original: "Si solem è mundo sustuleris, quid est nostrum Corpusculum, si desit anima? Nulla ibi contractatur vena pulsatilis, sentiendum nullum inest judicium, Nullus in eo vitalis halitus aut respiratio"</note>. For this reason also, it is termed the **Heart of heaven** <note>original: "Cor cæli"</note>, because just as the lively fountain of blood exists in the heart to water and moisten the other members of the body, so also it appears by effect that the virtue, growth, and conservation of all things, both inferior and superior, issues and springs from the Sun. It imparts and inspires life, light, and heat to inferior things by its light, and bestows small light to the superior ones. Now this light is a certain simple act which converts all things to itself by a life-giving heat, which penetrates <margin>John 1:4. 1 Timothy 6:13. Acts 17:25. Judith 16:17. Wisdom 7:22. 1 Corinthians 12. Wisdom 7:24.</margin> all things and refines <note>original: "concucteth," an alchemical term for ripening or perfecting through heat</note> their virtues everywhere, while also dispersing and expelling all darkness and obscurity. 

Whereby it is apparent that if life in general is in the Word, as St. John says; and if this universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> spirit of life gives life to all things, as St. Paul and Judith affirm; and if the spirit of wisdom is brighter than the sun, and is a simple and pure spirit which is more movable and active than all things, and therefore...
