# Sect. 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

<insert>See Note 4</insert>

...therefore he operates all in all. And if he penetrates all things because of his purity, as *Solomon* says, and all these properties are found in the solar virtue <note>original: "solar vertue"; the power or life-force emanating from the Sun</note>, what should dissuade a person from thinking that the Hebrew text was not rightly understood by *Jerome* <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> when he interpreted it as, *He has set his tabernacle in the sun* <note>original: "Posuit tabernaculum suum in sole"</note>? 

Truly, it was necessary for man to understand this, given that until this very hour, there are few who will acknowledge that the Spirit of God operates and works immediately in his organ, the Sun, and through the Sun. Instead, being seduced by pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"; referring to non-Christian or classical Greek philosophy</note> learning, they admit many subordinate agents or efficient causes, *acting by themselves* <note>original: "per se"</note>—that is, causes distinguished from the essential act of God. This is the reason for idolatry: the worshipping of the creature instead of the Creator, and the neglect or ignorance of the Creator within the creature. 

For although it is said by Solomon, <margin>Wisdom 16:28</margin> *that we ought to anticipate the sun's rising to give God thanks* <note>original: "Quod solem prævenire oportet ad benedictionem Dei"</note>, and again we read that *when we pray, we should turn our faces toward the east, or the rising sun,* yet we ought to imagine that he teaches this doctrine for the sake of the Creator who dwells in that bright tabernacle, and not for the sake of the tabernacle or the creature itself. 

It was into this very error that the Egyptians fell; by adoring this illuminated creature instead of the Illuminator, they built a temple and city in honor of the Sun. For this reason, the <margin>Isaiah 19:18</margin> *chariots and horses of the sun, which the ignorant Jews had set up before the gate of God's temple, were justly pulled down, for they did not distinguish the Creator from the creature.* 

This error—which to this hour clings to those schooled in the Aristotelian <note>original: "Aristotelically learned"; those following the logic of Aristotle, which often separated God from the natural mechanics of the world</note> ways of this world—is described in its true character by that Evangelist who assured us that all life is in the Word. This Word or light, he says, is in the world, and the world <margin>John 1:4, 10</margin> *was made by it, and the world did not know him. But as many as did receive or acknowledge him (namely, that he made all, and was all, and in all) were numbered among the children of God.* 

Therefore, all true Christians ought to understand that he fills all, gives life to all, sustains all, and operates all in all. Without this understanding, they cannot be esteemed the legitimate children of God. They ought not to be so ignorant of the Creator within the creature, since his glory shines out of them and may be perceived by them to a greater or lesser degree. It is wrong to think that he is absent even from the most beautiful creature in the world, for he is present with all; for it is said, *that he fills all*. 

This is not "virtually" or "accidentally" <term>In traditional philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to a thing's nature (like the color of a shirt), whereas "essence" is what the thing actually is.</term> as some worldly-wise <margin>Ephesians 4:10</margin> men claim through their pagan distinctions—distorting the truth of the Scripture by doing so—but he is there in essence. In plain terms, it is said in one place: *Christ is in all, and over all; in him are all things.* But Christ, who is the true wisdom, is the powerful <note>original: "vertuous"</note> or essential emanation from the Father, and therefore no "accident." <margin>Colossians 1:3; Wisdom 7:25; Wisdom 12:1</margin> In another place: *The incorruptible Spirit of God is in all things.* But that Spirit, which has no corruption in it, preserves from corruption, and truly gives life, is no accident, but a perfect essence. 

In another place: *Of him, by him, and in him are all things* <margin>Romans 11:36</margin>; therefore, this is meant essentially, and not accidentally. In another place: *God is all in all.* And again the Apostle says: *Of God the Father are all things <margin>1 Corinthians 8:3</margin> by our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things.* All of this cannot be understood in any other way than as God’s essence being in and over all, because in himself he is only essential; therefore, no "accidents" can be attributed to him. 

Consequently, we may conclude that God’s Spirit is essentially in his creatures, and for that reason, we ought simply to consider him and acknowledge him in his works. For any person who calls themselves a Christian and does not know this is but a Christian in name, and is therefore vain and miserable. This is partly confirmed by the words of St. *Paul*, and partly by those of *Solomon* mentioned before: *The anger of God (says St. Paul) is revealed from heaven upon the impiety and injustice of those men who keep the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is made manifest to them, for God has revealed it to <margin>Romans 1:16</margin> them. For the invisible things of him are discerned by the creatures of this world, through those things which are understood by creation, as are also his everlasting power and divinity. So that they are inexcusable, because when they knew God, they did not glorify him or give him thanks, but faded away or vanished in their own imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened; and therefore, while saying they were wise, they became fools and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of a corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of serpents, etc.* 

By this, he argues first that God ought to be studied and known in his creatures, and that we ought to acknowledge and credit all their glory and power to his Spirit, or the divinity within them, and not to mistake the Creator for the creature. For he seems expressly to argue and signi—

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book. 4.

...signify <note>original: "nifie"; likely a continuation of "signify" from the previous page</note> that his everlasting virtue and divinity is within his creatures, and that it appears out of them. For his words imply that his invisible qualities are perceived through the things that are created, as are his everlasting virtue and divinity. And why not? Since in the Word there is and was from the beginning life, or the life-giving Spirit, and life is in the creatures; therefore, the Word is there, and consequently the incorruptible Spirit. Solomon confirms the previously mentioned passage in Wisdom 13:1 <margin>Wisdom 13:1</margin> with this: *All men are foolish by nature who are ignorant of God; they cannot understand him who truly is by looking at the good things he has created, nor do they recognize the craftsman by considering his works.* By this, he argues that divinity within the creature may be perceived through the appearance of the creature. Therefore, it is evident that the Prophet <note>referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms</note> spoke correctly when he affirmed that *the heavens declare the glory and majesty of God* by the beautiful appearance of that glorious Spirit which animated <note>original: "inact"; to put into action or give life to</note> them and adorned their beautiful eye—I mean the Sun—with such divine, life-giving, and illuminating virtue, which possesses and inhabits it in abundance. 

And therefore I conclude that the Prophet spoke rightly and instructively to an ignorant world: the bright Spirit of God dwells in the sun of heaven as if in a Tabernacle <note>a temporary dwelling or tent, often referring to the biblical dwelling of God's presence</note>, and from there, he imparts and distributes his gifts of form, life, growth <note>original: "vegetation"</note>, and reproduction to every creature. And yet, I will not agree with Aristotle <note>the ancient Greek philosopher whose views dominated medieval science</note> that *the Sun and man beget a man* <note>original: "Sol & homo generant hominem"</note>; rather, I believe that the life-giving Spirit—which is powerful in the Sun and present in every specific creature—is the only one who gives life to all things. He sends his breath <note>original: "spiracle"</note> of natural heat and life through the Sun in an ordinary course to help and assist creatures to live and multiply. Yet, he is not confined only within the Sun, but works "all in all," both inside and outside of it, since he fills all things. This is sound doctrine because it attributes all life-giving actions—whether direct or indirect—solely to him who acts and effects all things, and not to the created instrument through which he operates. To do otherwise would be to take away from the Creator to give credit to the creature for what it does not truly possess. 

As for the later interpretation which says, *He made the sun a pavilion or tabernacle in the heavens* <note>original: "Soli posuit tentorium in cælis"</note>, what benefit, I ask you, can that teaching bring to man? The first interpretation teaches man that the Spirit of God is within this bright heavenly creature, and therefore teaches us to worship the Lord and not the palace. Ignorance of the divine Spirit's presence in beautiful creatures has caused infinite errors in the world. Therefore, this is an interpretation of great importance and instruction.

The second interpretation is so trivial that it requires no such elaborate <note>original: "curiosity"</note> expression to signify that the Sun has its seat or place in heaven. Honestly, what child does not know this by looking up, without any instruction from the Prophet? How is that relevant to the preceding text, *The heavens declare the glory of God*, etc.? Why would he mention the Sun immediately afterward? Just to tell us the Sun was in heaven? Everyone knows that. No, it was to show that the beauty of the heavens was derived from that glorious Spirit of God who mainly had his residence or dwelling in the "sunny Tabernacle." This was so that blind, worldly men might recognize that it was God within that beautiful creature, and not the creature itself, which sent down so abundantly those virtuous influences and lights poured out from the vessel of the Sun. Because people misunderstood this knowledge, many of God's creatures (whom he created in his own image) have been led into error and drawn ignorantly to worship the Sun and other stars as gods—which, in truth, are nothing of themselves. *By his Spirit he adorned the heavens* <margin>Job 26:13</margin> <note>original: "Spiritu suo ornavit cælos"</note>, says Job. He does not say "by the Sun," but *by his Spirit*, which made the Sun its Tabernacle. 

And now to our last argument, in which I will show you how that exposition by Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> seems to be confirmed by the assertions of certain wise philosophers. One says (and Saint Augustine agrees with this opinion): *Every thing claims for itself as much divinity as it is capable of receiving light* <note>original: "Qualibet res tantum sibi Dei vindicat, quantum capax est luminis"</note>. But the Sun is the brightest creature in the world; therefore, it possesses the Spirit of divinity in abundance. Many philosophers agree on this, not straying from the teachings of Scripture: namely, that *in light is divinity, and in divinity is light* <note>original: "In lumine numen, in numine lumen"</note>. And Plato said: *Do not speak of God without light* <note>original: "Ne loquaris de Deo sine Lumine"</note>. Does not Scripture confirm all this by saying that *God is light* <margin>1 John 1; Psalm 104:2; Deuteronomy 9:3</margin>, and that *he is clothed or wrapped in light as with a garment* <note>original: "vestitur seu amictus est Lumine quasi vestimento"</note>?

[instru]ment. <note>The text likely completes "instrument" or "establishment" from the previous page.</note> Indeed, he is truly said to be a ***consuming fire***. I conclude, therefore, that **Jerome** <note>original: "Jerom"; referring to St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> has translated that passage according to its true sense. Consequently, we may understand the reason for **rarefaction** <note>the process of making a substance less dense; thinning</note> and **condensation** <note>the process of making a substance more dense; thickening</note> based on the presence or absence of the Sun. We must confess, after a proper examination of the case, that the only Agent of these two operations in the waters or **universal element** <note>original: "catholick Element"; here meaning the all-encompassing substance of air or water</note> is the presence, action, and emanation of the Eternal Spirit, or otherwise his absence and rest. 

This is easily demonstrated by our **experimental glass** <note>This refers to a thermoscope or "weather glass," an early version of the thermometer that Robert Fludd famously used to demonstrate his cosmological theories.</note>: for the nearer the Sun is to us, and the deeper we are in Summer, the more the air in the glass will be **dilated** <note>expanded through rarefaction</note>. This is proven by the fact that in summertime, the water in the glass is pushed down and forced to its lowest point. Conversely, the further the Sun is from us, and the deeper we are in winter, the more the air is condensed in the glass; this is made evident by the rise or elevation of the water in the neck of the **flask** <note>original: "mattrass"; a long-necked glass vessel used in early chemistry</note> or glass. 

We do not say that the entire cause of condensation and rarefaction comes only from the Spirit in the Sun; the same Spirit is just as present in this lower **elementary region** as he is in the **ethereal** <note>heavenly or upper</note> regions. He holds the power and life of the winds under his rule, by which he raises or lowers the waters in the glass in both winter and summer. Consequently, he causes the condensation and rarefaction of the air, both inside the instrument and outside of it. By that means, he causes a **daily** <note>original: "diuturnall"</note> change in the general **sublunary** <note>below the moon; earthly</note> waters, or the universal element of air, shifting it through a four-fold nature from one condition to another. This mutation or alteration of the lower moist nature from one form into another is commonly called "the Elements," as shall be explained hereafter. But first, we will look at the structure of the heavens and show how they were framed through condensation and rarefaction, performed by this one eternal **Spirit of God** <term>Ruach Elohim</term>.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*In what manner this Eternal Spirit, or Ruach Elohim, framed the Heavens and shaped or made its Stars through his act of Condensation and Rarefaction.*<-

<margin>2 Peter 3:5 <note>The original margin notes 3:4, but the quote is from verse 5.</note></margin>
<margin>Pimander 3 <note>Refers to the *Poimandres*, the first tractate of the *Corpus Hermeticum*.</note></margin>
<margin>Wisdom 11:20</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 11:3</margin>
It is the Apostle Peter’s assertion that ***the heavens and the earth were made of the waters and by the waters, by the Word of God***. So we see that the Word is the Agent in the condensation of invisible waters into visible waters, and then of these visible waters into a visible earth. Thus, the world was generally divided into thicker and thinner regions by that divine Spirit, the **Spirit of God** <term>Ruach Elohim</term>, which was carried upon the waters. 

This is well argued by **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> in these words: *"Once things were distinguished and balanced, which were carried by a fiery Spirit, the heaven shone forth into seven circles"* <note>original Latin: "Distinctis libratisque rebus, quæ igneo Spiritu vehebantur, emicuit cælum, septem in circulos"</note>. Here he signifies that it was a fiery Spirit, and a little earlier he calls it the **Holy Splendor** <note>original: "Splendorem Sanctum"</note>, which sustained and bore up every circle or sphere of the heavens in its proper place. Regarding this, the Wise Man says: *"You have ordered all things in measure, number, and weight"* <note>original Latin: "Omnia mensura, numeroque, & pondere, disposuisti seu temperasti"; from Wisdom of Solomon 11:20.</note>. That is to say, he disposed them in a distinct measure and proportion, in heaviness and lightness, and in a proper and convenient number—namely, into seven distinct spheres and an infinity of condensed bodies. 

For although all the heavens are composed of air and fire—and for that reason it is called **Ether, as if it were fiery air** <term>Æther quasi igneus aer</term>—yet by the rule of St. **Paul**, who teaches us ***that things which are visible were first made of things that are invisible***, we are instructed that both the visible bodies in heaven and all visible lights were first made of invisible waters and invisible formal Light. This Light has its root in God, the bright eternal Unity of all created numbers. Therefore, just as **Aristotle** says that ***Stars are the denser parts of their sphere*** <note>original Latin: "Stellæ are densiores partes sui orbis"</note>, so I say that while the substance of the heavens is invisible because of its thinness (rarity), the stars are visible because of their thickness (density). It was condensation that caused visibility, and rarefaction which is the cause of invisibility. Yet, despite this, we do not conclude with Aristotle that the stars are simply the denser parts of their orbits, but rather Lights which were included in the spirit of the dark shadow of the abyss. This spirit, in separating Light from Darkness, soared upward by virtue of the included Light, and so, according to the proportion of that eternal formal fire, which...

...which it retains to this day as its cornerstone. It is sustained and elevated in its proper place, no differently than we see an artificial **firework** <note>original: "squib"</note>—according to the proportion of its artificial and fading fire and the **weight** <note>original: "ponderosity"</note> of its body—raised in the air to a certain height during the force of the gunpowder. It moves neither lower nor higher than its essential energy permits, and there it remains until the force of the corruptible and wasting fire is spent, at which point it falls back down. 

But the light of a star carries and raises up its spiritual body according to the proportion of its mounting light, which soars as high as its power and the weight of its body will permit. Thus, it hangs perpetually at a certain distance from the center because its fire is of an eternal and incorruptible nature, and will not fade like the artificial fire of a firework. 

Now, all the illuminating energies and animating forces or flames imparted to the universal waters were bestowed upon them by that bright <margin>Wisdom 7</margin> **universal** <note>original: "catholick"</note> Spirit or emanation. This Spirit was sent forth by God to be carried upon the waters and—as Scripture affirms—is brighter than the Sun or stars. Therefore, none of those lights are separate in essence from that glorious and glittering Spirit, whose beams were dispersed over all the waters in the abyss to give them life and being. 

For this reason—because each light had a different proportion of essential brightness and measure of **physical density** <note>original: "corpulence"</note>—each celestial body varies in its type of virtue, motion, and influence from the others. However, because the extracted **quintessence** <note>the purest or "fifth" essence of a substance</note> (or the purer material essence of the entire Chaos) was united with the purity of light that issued from the creating Spirit into an **Angelic state** <note>original: "Angelicall alterity"</note>, both of those natures combined into a single mass. This mass soared out of the dark abyss into the center of the heavens, where it claimed the **Royal Throne of the Sun** <note>original: "Phœbean Throne"; referring to Phoebus Apollo, the Greek god of the sun.</note>. That spherical mass is to this hour called the Sun of Heaven. As the created fountain of light, it ignites and essentially enlightens all the rest of the stars in the heavens above, as well as the **Elements** <note>the four basic elements: earth, water, air, fire</note> and the creatures made of those elements below. 

So, after the universal light was contracted on the fourth day of Creation, the Sun was ordained to be the primary organ of life and growth in the starry world. It sends and showers down its influences and fiery **breaths** <note>original: "spiracles"</note> of life, preservation, growth, and reproduction upon the earthly earth and waters.

<margin>Theological Resolutions, Treatise 2, Part 2, Section 2, Question on the works of the First Day.</margin>

Thus, in a few words, you have the reason for that **condensation** <note>thickening</note> and **rarefaction** <note>thinning or expanding</note> by which both the invisible heavenly substance and visible celestial bodies were made. This seems to agree with the opinions of the learned theologians, **Basil** and **Damascene** <note>St. Basil the Great and St. John of Damascus, early Church Fathers</note>, regarding the causes of the divine Spirit's action in condensation and rarefaction before the Sun appeared in the heavens. They argue that the day’s rarefaction (or clear heaven) was caused by an emission of light ordained by the divine will of this omnipotent Spirit. Conversely, they believe the night’s condensation and the opaque or condensed bodies in the heavens were caused by a contraction of light, also brought about by the sacred Spirit’s will. 

Thus, through the confession of certain primary Fathers of the Church, we see the cause of the cold, condensing night and the hot, rarefying day before the Spirit was gathered into the tabernacle or quintessence of the Sun. This Sun was extracted by the **alchemical** <note>original: "Spagerick"; referring to spagyrics, the branch of alchemy involving the separation and recombination of natural elements.</note> or separating action of the divine Spirit out of the huge, deformed waters of the abyss. 

Therefore, this must also be the reason for condensation and rarefaction to this day. When the Spirit in the Sun is far from us—as if it were contracting its beams toward itself or absenting itself from our hemisphere—the cold waters incline toward the nature of their mother, Chaos. Because of this, the nights and darkness are long, and the light and day are short and faint in heat. In that season, the common **earthly** <note>original: "sublunary"</note> element is subject to condensation and **thickening** <note>original: "incrassation"</note>. It is therefore constrained or contracted into the consistency of frosts, snow, hail, ice, and cold showers. 

Again, when the Sun is near to us, it expands itself. By its heat and presence, the cold waters become hot, the days are lengthened and fortified, and the heat is made strong. Then the common earthly element is ready for expansion and **thinning** <note>original: "subtiliation"</note>, being easily ignited and set on fire with lightnings, **flashes** <note>original: "coruscations"</note>, and such things. But I leave the history of the condensation and thinning of the ethereal Spirit to descend to similar actions or conditions in the earthly element.

## CHAP. V.

->How the lower waters, or universal sublunary element, were distinguished, ordered, and shaped into various distinct spheres; which are called particular elements, and that by the aforementioned all-working Spirit, or divine Word.<-

---

<margin>See *Pimander* 3. "The moist nature from which the elements [come], etc." *Pimander* 1. Genesis 1. 2 Peter 3:6.</margin>
Since it has already been most certainly proved that the universal substance of the world's machine <note>original: "machin"; referring to the universe as a complex, God-designed mechanism</note> was made of only one thing—namely, a matter produced out of the potential depths of the dark chaos or abyss by the <term>spagerick</term> <note>original: "spagerick"; an alchemical term referring to the process of separating and recombining elements to achieve a pure state</note> virtue of the divine Word—which matter *Moses* termed "Waters" and *Hermes* called the "moist nature" (from which, as both *Moses* and *St. Peter* assert, the heavens and the earth were made of old), it must follow that the universal sublunary element was derived out of this universal mass of waters. This element is commonly called by the name of *Air*, just as all that moist substance in the celestial orb is called *Ether*. Now, this general element is altered and changed from one shape into another by the breath of the divine Spirit, the <term>Ruach Elohim</term> <note>Hebrew: "Spirit of God"</note>. For that which we see as visible water was first made from the air, which is an invisible water; likewise, visible water is made into earth through condensation. This is proved, first, by the words of *St. Paul*, who says: <margin>*Hebrews* 11:3.</margin> *By faith we acknowledge that it has always been thus with the world through the Word, so that from those things which could not be seen, those things were made which can be seen.* <note>original Latin: "Per fidem agnovimus quod semper ita actum sit cum mundo per Verbum, ut ex iis quæ videri non poterant fierent ea quæ possunt videri"</note> And again, *Solomon* says <margin>*Wisdom* 11:18.</margin> that the world was made of a matter that was not seen. But besides these proofs, we are taught by chemical experience that earth is nothing other than coagulated water, and visible water is nothing other than invisible air reduced to visibility by condensation; nor is fire anything other than rarified <note>thinned out or heated</note> air. In conclusion, all the sublunary waters were in the beginning nothing but an invisible, moist, or watery spirit, which we call by the common name "Air." Consequently, the universal sublunary element was originally nothing but one air, since heaven was made before the seas or the earth, as *Moses* teaches us. 

Therefore, by faith we must believe, according to *St. Paul's* doctrine, that all visible things—and therefore the seas and the earth—were first made or produced out of things not visible; that is to say, aerial or heavenly. For it is one universal air that fills the vast cavity or vault of the world, which is called "Heaven" because of its lightness, thinness, or invisibility; conversely, the earth and seas are so named because of their weight, density, and visibility. Since it is evident that the universal sublunary air is the main material ground and substance of that which the world calls elements, and that it is altered and changed from one state into another by the Word or divine Spirit, the <term>Ruach Elohim</term> (by which I mean the eternal wisdom), let us consider how this potent Spirit effects such ever-changing transformations <note>original: "Protean transmutations"</note> within that same uniform, invisible, thin water or air. Through this, a clear rotation is made within it, from one nature into another, which are therefore termed distinct elements. 

We must consider, in the first place, that this was that life-giving Spirit which the Prophet called from the four winds, saying: <margin>*Ezekiel* 37:9.</margin> *"Come, O Spirit, from the four winds and breathe upon these slain, that they may live again."* <note>original Latin: "Veni, Spiritus, à quatuor ventis & insuffla interfectos istos ut reviviscant"</note> Therefore, this one Spirit, the <term>Ruach Elohim</term>, was the royal commander of the four winds, and consequently could contract the air by his windy instruments and dilate it again at his pleasure. It was He, and no other, who animates the four winds and directs the Angels—who are his under-governors of them—to alter and change the invisible air into visible shapes, whenever and however He pleases. First, regarding His general act in ordering the air into various shapes, it is said: <margin>*Jeremiah* 51:16, *Job* 37:21, *Job* 26:8, *Job* 28:25.</margin> *"God draws the winds out of his treasuries."* <note>original Latin: "Deus ventos depromit e thesauris"</note> And again: *"The air is suddenly gathered into clouds, and the passing wind drives them away. Now, the principal organs by which this Spirit moves and acts—turning and changing this universal aerial subject from one thing into another—are the angelic winds, which He has ordained to blow from the four quarters or angles of the earth with different properties.

This alters and changes the moist, passive nature from one condition into another according to His will.

The Southerly wind brings forth vapors, clouds, lightning, and thunders. The Westerly wind brings cold rains and, as it were, snowy dissolutions. # Mosaical Philosophy. Book 4.

<margin>Hebrews 11</margin> ...as mentioned before, that *visible things were first made from things invisible?* The change of all things, whether visible or invisible, is therefore carried out by the condensing or contracting faculty and property within the all-acting Spirit. Conversely, the reduction of things from a visible state back into an invisible one is caused by the rarefying or dilating action of the very same Spirit—identical in essence, but differing in its property. Therefore, just as air was changed into water, and water into earth, by degrees of cold, so too is earth insensibly changed into water, and water into air, by various degrees of heat.

For *if this were not the case*, how would it be possible that the vast amount of water falling from the clouds does not continually increase the volume of the seas and diminish the air? Or why would burning such vast amounts of coal and whole mountains of wood not make the earth smaller in consistency, if there were not a constant supply and transformation of air into water, and water into earth? Though this divine nature performs these effects secretly and imperceptibly, the results prove it true. For when wood and coal are consumed, we find that their earthly bulk or bodily mass is almost entirely resolved by fire and heat into watery smoke and misty air. 

The philosophical axiom states that "everything is resolved back into its first matter or principle." It is therefore apparent that both the water and the airy smoke, which make up the earthly bulk of a great oak or a mountain of coal, were originally made of the invisible air. Again, if this were not so, the sulfur, stones, and dust—which both the authority of the Bible and common experience teach us descend from heaven—would increase the size of the Earth more and more, since they fall in various places daily. But leaving these theoretical proofs, I will move on to such visual demonstrations as I have learned from my experimental glass.

->**The Demonstration**<-

We find that from the lower region of the <term>weather-glass</term> <note>original: "Calender- or Weather-glasse"; an early instrument (thermoscope) used to show changes in temperature via the expansion and contraction of air</note> to the summit or top of its head, there is nothing inside but a portion of the common invisible element: air. Yet, even in this small model of air, we find strange mutations or alterations caused by the power of the four winds that blow in the open atmosphere. 

When the hot Easterly wind blows, the air expands and extends itself all along the neck of the glass, pushing the water down to the lowest degree because of its expansion. In this state, the air approaches the nature of fire; for fire is said to be nothing other than extremely expanded air—though, in truth, it is the abundant presence of the bright "form" <note>the divine, life-giving light</note> that expands it so much. 

However, if the South wind blows, the air will not be so extremely expanded, but will take on the middle nature of air, and therefore it will draw the water up by several degrees. But if it happens that the Westerly wind holds sole dominion in the sublunary element <note>the region below the moon; the Earthly realm</note>, then the air in the glass grows thicker, and for that reason, it attracts the water higher. This is because cold has a great power over the air, and its nature is to condense and thicken.

Lastly, if the cold Northern winds govern or control this universal sublunary element, then the contained air will be contracted or squeezed into a very narrow space. This is proven by the fact that the colder the wind is, the higher the water will be elevated in the glass. It is therefore made clear that the more the air is contracted, the more it is thickened, and consequently, it must become heavier <note>original: "ponderous"</note> relative to the space it occupies. All the air that weighed a certain amount in half a yard of space weighs at least that much in only two inches of space after contraction.

Thus you see that, in truth, there is fundamentally only one universal sublunary element. Although the angelic spirit that blows from the four corners of the heavens informs and alters it in four different ways, this led the Ancients to imagine in their fantasies four distinct elements of equal birth and being from the beginning. But you can see clearly from what has been said that this position of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>followers of Aristotle</note> and other sects is false, even though it has gained a universal name and dominance in this world among both the learned and the ignorant. These people base their sayings on the doctrine of the worldly learned, who are corrupted and seduced from the truth by pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> disciplines. 

In the final part of this book, I will now explain to you how all generation and corruption in this world is made, and that the lowest depth, or the **end point** <note>original: *terminus ad quem*</note> toward which the motion of corruption tends, is simply the basic element of nature. From that principle, after being altered in four ways, a new generation begins.

### CHAP. VI.

->*The true Mystery of Generation and Decay (also a touch of Re-generation or Resurrection) is expressed here, according to the doctrine of Holy Scripture.*<-

As we have plainly, though in few words, described for you a dark negative <note>original: "privative"</note> Principle—namely that which seemed to be without form before all beginnings, and therefore kills and deprives things of life, being as it were outside of all existence in regard to our capacity, because the active, life-giving light does not shine forth but is hidden in the center. So also have we manifested to you another Spiritual Principle, which is Light, now shining out of Darkness; and this is the only thing which shapes, enlivens, and animates all things with life. I told you that all was but one essential Unity: For the three Divine Persons were but one and the same in essence, and therefore that Light was to him as Darkness, and consequently he was the beginning of all beginnings. That is to say, he is the principle of both loss <note>original: "Privation"</note> and decay, as well as establishment <note>original: "Position"</note> and creation. One of these is the act leading toward life—namely the uncreated Light—and the other is the passive subject of life or death—that is, the waters. For the waters were derived out of Darkness, and therefore, because of their darkness, they participate in their suffering <note>original: "passion"</note> as much in the negative as in the positive principle. For that reason, the Actor in both extremes is God, who is Unity; he, by withdrawing his life-giving Spirit from the creature, causes death and loss, and consequently leaves nothing in it but the marks of decay and ruin. On the contrary, by continuing his incorruptible Spirit in the creature, it remains by that presence without decay. Also, after God withdraws his Spirit from the creature, then the creature dies; if he sends his Spirit of life into the creature again, it revives and rises again. This was the reason, in one sense, for the Resurrection of our Savior, who for that cause was termed the *Firstborn of the resurrection from the dead* <note>original: "Primavus resurrectionis à mortuis"</note>. And in another sense, it was the cause that Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note> raised the widow's child from the dead; and that the bones of Elisha <note>original: "Elizeus"</note> caused the murdered Amalekite <note>original: "Amalikite"</note> to rise again; as also that Christ caused Lazarus to revive when he was dead, as shall be shown hereafter. I will therefore express to you from the Scriptures: first, that God (to whom the act of taking away is as familiar as that of giving, if we only consider the watery or passive composition, because it participates in both extremes) is the only Actor in death and decay as well as in life and creation. And then secondly, I will briefly prove to you the manner in which the self-same Unity in essence operates thus contrarily in the watery or physical subject of all things.

"Good and evil are from God" <note>original: "bonum & malum à Deo sunt"</note>; Life and death, good and evil, are from God. Now for the second point, namely, to show how the Lord operates by one and the same Spirit toward life, death, and resurrection, we may easily understand it if we consider that it was the all-enacting Spirit of wisdom which first informed the world with life and being. This Spirit gave life to every creature and preserves it from death and corruption as long as it remains and operates in a life-giving way within those creatures. Therefore, it is said: <margin>Judith 16:14</margin> "Let every creature serve God, for you spoke and they were made; you sent your Spirit and they were created" <note>original: "Deo serviat omnis creatura, quia dixisti & facta sunt, misisti spiritum & creata sunt"</note>. Again: <margin>Acts 17:25</margin> "God, not needing the aid of anyone, gives or bestows on all creatures life, and breath, and all things" <note>original: "Deus non aliquo indigens dat omnibus vitam & inspirationem & omnia"</note>. In another place: <margin>Isaiah 42:5</margin> "God gives breath to the people who are on the earth, and spirit to those who walk upon it" <note>original: "Deus dat flatum populo qui est super terram, & spiritum calcantibus eam"</note>. And it was for this reason that the Psalmist says: <margin>Psalm 30:5</margin> "Life is present through the benevolence of Jehovah" <note>original: "Vita adest benevolentia JEHOVÆ"</note>. <margin>Psalm 41:2</margin> "God is the restorer of life" <note>original: "Vita restaurator est JEHOVÆ"</note>. <margin>Psalm 87:7</margin> "All the fountains of my life are from God" <note>original: "Vitæ meæ fontes omnes à Deo"</note>. <margin>Psalm 90:17</margin> "The prolonging of life is through the benevolence of Jehovah" <note>original: "Vitæ prolongatio est benignitas JEHOVÆ"</note>. From this it is apparent that the presence of the life-giving Spirit of God is the cause of life, multiplication, and preservation. Therefore Job said: <margin>Job 10:12</margin> "Your visitation preserves my spirit" <note>original: "Visitatio tua conservat spiritum meum"</note>.

Conversely, the absence of that same spirit, to a greater or lesser degree, is the occasion of sickness, death, destruction, or corruption. Therefore it is said: <margin>Deuteronomy 31:17</margin> "God forsakes the wicked, and hides his face from those who are impious, so that many evils and troubles may encumber them" <note>original: "Deus malos relinquit, & abscondit faciem suam ab impiis, ut obveniant iis mala multa & angustiæ"</note>. But the specific causes of life, death, and resurrection are expressed in these words of the Prophet David mentioned before: "O Lord, how glorious are your works? In wisdom you have made them all; the earth is full of your riches; so is the wide sea, and innumerable creeping things within it. You give to them, and they gather it; you open your hand, and they are filled with good things; but if you hide your face they are troubled; if you take away their breath they die, and return to dust. Again, if you send out your Spirit they are re-created and revive, and you renew the face of the earth, etc." <margin>Psalm 104:24–30</margin> <note>The text cites verse 20, but the passage describes Psalm 104:24–30.</note>

See here: the essential reason and central method of <term>Generation and Corruption</term> <note>The natural process of coming into being and decaying.</note> is exactly described and set forth by the Psalmist. Namely, that by the presence and kind action of the incorruptible Spirit of the Lord, life is continued; and on the contrary, by its absence, departure, or by it being taken away from the creature, the creature dies and decays. For as long as the incorruptible Spirit of the Lord acts and works in the creature, it is not possible for it to die or decay; but when the Spirit departs, death and corruption must necessarily follow. Also, when it remains in the body but rests from its action—or, as it were, withdraws its active beams from the outer edges <note>original: "circumference"</note> toward the center (which the Prophet calls "the hiding of God's face")—then the creature is troubled, which is the same as saying it is sick. But if the Spirit is totally taken away, then the creature is forced, for lack of it, to expire and die. To conclude, if the Spirit returns and shines forth again upon the creature, then it revives again, as happened to **Lazarus** and to the widow's child whom the Prophet raised.

By this it is apparent how death is nothing else but the absence of the <term>essential form</term> <note>The inner divine spark or blueprint that gives a thing its identity and life.</note>. Consequently, it is made evident that the life-giving form comes immediately from God, and is not that imaginary one which the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, whom the author believes rely on abstract logic rather than spiritual truth.</note> have fumbled after. I prove it clearly from these passages, though the previous text expresses it plainly enough: <margin>Genesis 6:3</margin> "My Spirit shall not remain perpetually in man," says the Lord, "because he is flesh, and his days shall be a hundred and twenty years" <note>original: "Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum quia caro est, eruntque Dies ejus centum viginti annorum"</note>. This argues that it is the Spirit of God which makes man live, and that by its absence, death must follow. 

But because the overly curious will hardly approve of this translation by <term>Jerome</term> <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note>, claiming that the nature of the Hebrew text is understood differently, I will maintain and confirm it by a similar passage of the same nature in **Job**: <margin>Job 34:14–15</margin> <note>Text cites Job 34:3, but quotes verses 14–15.</note> "If God, setting his mind upon man, should receive or draw back to himself his spirit or breath of life, all flesh would fail and die, and man would likewise return to ashes" <note>original: "Si Deus apponens ad hominem animam suam, Spiritum aut flatum ejus ad se reciperet vel traheret, deficeret & expiraret omnis caro, simul & homo in cinerem reverteretur"</note>. So we see that it is the Spirit of God which gives life, not only to man, but also to every other creature; and that it is meant by the

The real life-giving <note>original: "vivifying"</note> Spirit of God, which explicitly gives life to man, is confirmed by Job in another place: "The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty has given me life" <note>original: "Spiritus Dei fecit me & inspiratio Omnipotentis vivificavit me"</note>. Therefore, it follows that if the presence of this Spirit causes generation, life, and preservation, then by necessity its absence must cause corruption, death, and destruction. For when the Spirit of the Lord is removed from the physical mass of a creature, it leaves it deformed, like another chaos, or an "earth without form and void" <note>original: "terra inanis & vacua"</note>, being destitute of the Spirit of life which caused it to act and exist in its specific nature. Since this incorruptible Spirit preserves the physical mass from decay by its own incorruptible virtue and power, it follows that when the Spirit has departed—or is entirely withdrawn into itself without any external action—the mass must immediately die and return to a state of absolute nothingness <note>original: "privative nothing"</note>.

Now, there is a difference between resurrection from death (or rather, a deadly sleep, for Christ’s words regarding Lazarus were that he was not dead but sleeping) to a temporary life, and resurrection to an eternal life. Just as nothing hinders death more than the presence of the incorruptible Spirit, so too nothing hinders the perpetuity of living more than a corruptible body—that is, a body subject to death or decay. Therefore, that body must die so that it may shed its corruption and put on incorruption. This is achieved by

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:36</margin>
the purification and separation of the decayable attachments <note>original: "corruptible additaments"</note>. This is effected by loosening the bond of the alterable elements and freeing the spiritual part of the physical composition from its long captivity so that it may become pure and clean. Once this is done, the union of the incorruptible Spirit with it

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:37, 38, 39</margin>
will make everything spiritual. According to the doctrine of Saint Paul: *That which is sown will not be brought to life unless it dies. And that which you sow is not the body that shall be, but God gives it a body as He pleases. Therefore, just as the body is sown in corruption, so it rises in incorruption; as it is sown a natural or physical body, so it is raised a heavenly and spiritual body.* Thus, the body must die so that it may cast off corruption—meaning the decayable portion of the impure elements—so that, having been

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:50</margin>
made spiritual, it may remain with the Spirit of life forever. For this reason, Paul affirms *that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God*, because in their physical nature they are subject to decay, and therefore cannot inherit the land of immortality. Rather, it is the pure spirit of the blood and flesh which rises (after they have discarded their coarse physical shell <note>original: "grosse tabernacle"</note>) into incorruption, being animated by the incorruptible Spirit of the Lord. This Spirit causes only a temporary life in the natural or compacted physical mass, but an eternal life in the spiritual and refined body, which is opposite in condition to the natural body, as

<margin>1 Corinthians 15:44</margin>
the Apostle justifies; for through purification, it is changed from a physical body into a heavenly and spiritual one. Do we not see by this same example how even a grain of wheat is so raised in power after it has endured decay? Once freed from the coarse physical bond, it would mount and soar upward toward the heavens, were it not that the spirit, though set at liberty, is still detained by the physical material that hinders its ascent. Nevertheless, it is so improved after its decay that its power is increased by many degrees, as seen in the abundant multiplication produced by its expanded spirit through the abundance of that incorruptible spirit it puts on.

Regarding the other kind of resurrection, which is to a temporary life, this occurs because the body is not fully decayed. There is no loosening of the physical bonds through total dissolution, which would allow the spiritual body to be purified and completely separated from the physical dregs that come from the lower waters. In such cases, the hidden spiritual body is not yet at liberty to embrace the spirit of life with eternal ties. This was the kind of resurrection

<margin>Luke 7:14</margin>
which Christ performed for the widow's son who was being carried to his burial, when He said, "Young man, I say to you, Arise; and he that was dead sat up." <margin>1 Kings 17:22</margin>

Now, if we compare our principle of generation and corruption with that of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, we shall find as much confusion in theirs as there is a plain explanation in ours. For they define generation to be *a change of matter from its original substantial form into another substantial form* <note>original: "mutatio materiæ a forma substantiali pristina in aliam formam substantialem"</note>. Also, they claim corruption is *the change and loss of a substantial form which was first in the matter, but now is no longer in it* <note>original: "mutatio & amissio formæ substantialis quæ prius inerat materiæ, sed nunc non inest eidem"</note>. <margin>J. Velcurio, Book 2, Chapter 13, Physics Commentary. J. Velcurio, Book 3, Chapter 14, Physics Commentary. <note>Johannes Velcurio was a 16th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note></margin> Thus you see how they name a "substantial form," but what it is, and how it enters the body to cause generation, or in what manner <margin><insert>Word</insert></margin> it departs from it again to cause death and corruption, they do not explain. Therefore, we have *the unknown explained by the even more unknown* <note>original: "ignotum per ignotius"</note>. In truth, it is the Spirit of God which gives form and life to <note>original: "informeth and vivifieth"</note> all things, causing by its presence both generation (which Aristotle observed) and resurrection (which he never knew or could discern by his worldly philosophy), just as its absence causes corruption, deprivation, and death. So, in this change or passage of the creature from one state to another, we find that just as it was made—and all other things out of one dark and deformed potential principle—by the shining forth of actual Light, which gave form and created all things out of nothing, making them live and exist, so also by the absence of that all-forming Light, each thing becomes dark, dead, and destitute of its essential form, until a new Light manifests itself in a way that changes the watery substance <note>original: "alienate the watery Subject"</note> from the form and shape it had at first. Thus, the body or carcass of a dead man is in the state of an unformed chaos, because it has lost its accustomed human substantial form or action. It is no different than if the Lord took away his Spirit from the world: all things would return again to nothing, or to an unformed chaos or dark abyss, as it was at the beginning. But when the effective action of a new form breaks forth out of the dead carcass, causing the whole mass to become full of worms <note>original: "verminous"</note>, then we may say that the corruption of the one is the generation of the other—a principle that always holds true when the elementary material is still present. <margin><insert>Hell is in the change into the worm that dies not; for long before the fruit generates—Lice become food for birds to eat, mangled in various ways; a first generation is preserved which contains the seed forever!! The conscience is the hell, hot and so urgent in minds.</insert></margin> Thus "Privation" <note>The absence of a form.</note> is the middle ground between them both, and is like a vacuum, a "Nothing" <note>original: "Nihil"</note> or non-entity between two formal states. But I will demonstrate the mystery of generation and corruption in this manner:

Now that the progression or ranks of the world's creation and its simple members have been shown to you—which consist of four ranks, a state in which the world must endure until it is refined with fire—I will make my progression from these simple members of the world's existence and proceed to the order of degrees in composition. These have their beginning and foundation from those members, namely from the first degree or rank in generation or composition, unto its completion. And just as between the beginning of a mixture and its perfection there must be a middle stage <note>original: "medium or mean"</note>, which must be *imperfectly mixed* <note>original: "imperfectè mixtum"</note>, so between a simple element and a perfect body, an imperfect composition must occur—namely one of a meteorological nature <note>Referring to atmospheric phenomena like vapors or rain.</note>. As for example, in the generation of a man, the beginning (which is founded on the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> watery element and takes its place in the first rank) is sperm; for it is a watery or fluid substance, but little altered. And just as the whole fabric of the world and the seeds of all things were in the water...

implicitly <note>original: "complicitly," meaning folded inward or existing potentially</note> contained, and yet nothing appeared externally but water. So in the seed <note>original: "Sperm"</note>, though nothing appears in the first degree manifestly <note>original: "explicitly"</note> but the seed itself, yet the whole man—namely the bones, flesh, blood, sinews, and the like—are implicitly contained, and will by degrees appear manifest. Specifically, in the sixth rank, it will be altered from a fluid <note>original: "humour"</note> to a solid, with a clear distinction of the three principal members <note>likely referring to the heart, liver, and brain</note>; in the seventh, it takes an embryonic shape; and in the eighth—which completes a "cube" from the material root of 2 or the square of 4 (which is characterized in the universal element <note>original: "catholick Element"</note> by the impressions of the four winds)—it becomes a perfect creature.

Yet it contains implicitly a cloud, water or rain, fire or lightning, and a heavy stone, along with salt and such things, which by degrees appear manifestly through the power of the four winds. Thus, a vapor occupies the first rank, the cloud the sixth, the lightning and cloud the seventh, and the earthly stone represents an exact rotation of all four "windy" <note>original: "ventous"</note> forms into one mixture, which represents the eighth place in composition or generation. 

But when a man comes to corruption <note>decay or death</note>, then his parts proceed in reverse order <note>original: "resolution backwards"</note>: namely from 8 to 7, from 7 to 6, and from 6 to 5, until he returns to the point of the simple seed-like element from which he began. There, a new generation begins in another form, for all-acting Nature is never idle. Similarly, a stone is resolved into water, and water into a vaporous cloud, and the cloud into the air from which it came—which is the simple universal element that allows no further or deeper breakdown through corruption.

Now, the only Operator in both these works is the Spirit of God. In generation, it shines forth from the center of the universal elements or the interior of the seed toward perfection, and continues its action until a perfect man is produced. *Job* confirms this as follows:

<margin>Job 10:10-12</margin>
> <note>original Latin: "Nonne sicut Lac fudistime? & sicut caseum coagulasti me? cute & carne texisti me, ossibusque & nervis induisti me: cum vita benignitatem exercuisti erga me. Et visitatio tua conservavit spiritum meum:"</note>
> "Did you not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese? Did you not cover me with skin and flesh? You clothed me with bones and sinews; you showed me your kindness in my life, and your visitation preserves my spirit."

Conversely, when the Spirit of God withdraws his beams from the outer circle of generation and composition back toward the center of simplicity, he ceases to "visit" the spirit of the creature. Consequently, it must fade, and in its decay, return to the principle from which it came. From there, if the same Spirit is pleased to shine forth again, a new generation begins where the corruption or dissolution ended.

# CHAPTER VII.

### That God (contrary to *Aristotle's* assertion, and the opinion of various other Pagan <note>original: "Ethnick," referring to non-Christian/Classical philosophers</note> Philosophers) does not operate by necessity for the creation and continuation of his creatures, but by his own will and benevolent inclination.

<margin>Johannes Velcurio, Book 1, Chapter 5, *Commentary on Physics*.</margin>
**WE** properly term that *Necessary* which can be no other way; on the other hand, we consider that to be voluntary, as well as *fortuitous* <note>happening by chance</note>, which may be otherwise. Now, a great dispute has arisen and sprung up among the Pagan philosophers as to whether God operates in this world voluntarily, or by necessity, or as if by compulsion. The majority of them are firmly of the opinion that God acts in this world—both in the generation and preservation of things, as well as their corruption—by necessity, and not by any voluntary motion. From this it must follow that he was forced to do or effect what he does from all eternity by some other nature which was either co-eternal with him or pre-existent; or else that he was pushed forward against his will to effect this or that by some creature which he had made. 

I will briefly express to you how erroneous and far-fetched all of this is from the rules and center of truth. For first of all, what (I ask you) is of greater antiquity than God, seeing as he existed before anything else? In geometry, what comes before, or is in measure smaller than, a point? Or which among all the numbers of arithmetic is as ancient as unity <note>the number one</note>? Therefore, it must follow that God is free and voluntary in his actions, since he existed of himself and did exist without regard to any other principle—whether preceding or co-eternal—from the very beginning. He was therefore sufficient in himself, and of himself, to work and operate by himself from all eternity.

But the principal reasons for the aforementioned Pagan opinion are twofold: first, because God acts and operates by his own essence <note>his fundamental nature</note> and not by any acquired virtue; second, because the effects in the world seem to be necessary, and therefore they conclude that they cannot come or proceed from any contingent <note>uncertain</note>—that is to say, fortuitous or voluntary—occasion of another. 

Regarding the first point, it seems to me they argue against themselves; for as he acts by his own essence or substance, it is evident that he is moved of his own accord, and consequently not by any external compulsion or internal necessity. Moreover, within the scope of unity, there can be no compulsion or coercion, because Unity cannot "suffer" <note>original: "suffer," meaning to be acted upon or changed by an external force</note>. Again, it is not possible that he should be urged to work by any external or foreign cause, because he remains primarily fixed and steadfast in himself, and of himself. He works as the original fountain of all things by himself, emitting his

To the second point, I say that necessary effects in no way imply any necessity in the first efficient cause. This is because secondary causes (which *Plato* and other wise men called handmaids or servants) act at the command and prompting of him who is the unity of all multitude, and therefore all in all, or by a necessary order. Thus, any necessity found in worldly created things depends upon the will <note>original: "volunty"</note> and command of him who made them, an order which he accomplishes and finishes at his pleasure. Therefore, we find this written by the wise man:
<margin>Wisdom 16:22.</margin>
*He makes the fire mild and gentle, lest it should burn; and then again he makes it burn in the midst of waters <note>original: "Ignem mitescit ne combureret, modò ignem ille facit ardere inter aquas, &c."</note>, yes, and in the clouds of hail and snow, without melting them. Again, He makes the fire forget its destroying property, so that the righteous may be nourished by it.* It was also an evident proof that God does not work out of necessity upon this creature of fire when the three servants of the living Lord were untouched by the fire of the Chaldean furnace, although it was heated seven times. This is also confirmed by the history where it is said that in the time of *Joshua*, the Sun stood still for a whole day's space; as also that in the days of *Hezekiah*, the Sun was made to go backward fifteen degrees on the sundial <note>original: "Horologe or Diall"</note> without any evident reason in nature.

Moreover, it is proved and verified in that wonderful eclipse of the Sun which happened at the death and passion of our Savior, wherein the Sun of heaven was totally obscured. This also occurred beyond the expectation or understanding of the astrologers and naturalists of this world; for at the instant of that eclipse (or "passion of the Sun"), the Moon was neither in the "head" nor "tail" of the Dragon <note>These are the lunar nodes, the points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic; a solar eclipse normally only happens when the Moon is near these points</note>, as *Firmicus*, that great expert in astronomy, witnesses. Therefore, it was brought about against the common course of nature. All these events could never have happened if God acted out of necessity in this world. It follows, therefore, plainly, that God operates in this world by his own free will, not out of necessity, to effect the ordinary or annual course of things according to the laws and necessities of nature—all of which he also effects voluntarily and of his own free will, namely for their creation and preservation as well as their final corruption.

But come here and listen, O you vain philosophers who would have God—who is the actor and ordainer of all things—be bound by the laws of necessity. What honor and glory can any man justly attribute to God for his wisdom, justice, and mercy <note>original: "clemency"</note> if he were constrained by necessity, not only to create all things in this or that manner, but also to nourish and sustain them, and afterward to bring them to corruption? What thanks, service, or adoration would we owe him if what he did for us was done out of necessity? Why, *Aristotle*, according to your assertion, should we offer sacrifice to the roots of nature? Or what would it avail us mortal men to pray and pour out our supplications to God (a duty which *Plato, Porphyry, Iamblichus*, and *Proclus* nonetheless teach us is most necessary) if he could not be appeased <note>original: "propitiated"</note> by praying, since he works only by necessity? Or why did *Socrates* and *Pythagoras* (who, by the testimony of the Oracle, were esteemed the wisest persons of their time) customarily pour out their prayers to God, if God were only constrained to act and operate whatever he did in the world?
<margin>Psalm 30:8.</margin>
Or why does the Prophet proclaim *that God alone is to be called upon and prayed to <note>original: "Quod Deus sit solus inclamandus & deprecandus"</note>*, if there were any necessity in God to act in the generation and conservation of things? Yes, truly, it is clearly demonstrated by what has already been said that God, by means of prayer, is customarily inclined to mercy <note>original: "misericord"</note> and pity, and that it is in his free will to deal either in severity or mercy with the world and its creatures. Consequently, he is not urged by necessity to operate or bring forth effects, as certain vain pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers have claimed. Among these, I must name a remarkable person and a follower of *Aristotle's* doctrine, namely *Galen*, that prince of the pagan physicians, who speaks atheistically in these words:
<margin>*On the Use of Parts* <note>original: "De usu partium"</note>, Book 2, Chapter 14.</margin>
*Moses thinks that God can do all things, even if he wished to make a horse or an ox out of ashes. But we do not think so; rather, we maintain that nature cannot do certain things, and that God does not even attempt them at all. Instead, from those things which he can do, he chooses what is best. Now indeed, since it would be better for the hairs in the eyelids always to be equal in size and number, we do not claim that because he willed this, they were immediately made so—for he would not have been able to do that. And we maintain that even if he had willed it a thousand times, yet never* <note>original: "Moses arbitratur omnia Deum posse facere, etiamsi ex cineribus equum aut bovem facere velit. Nos autem non ita sentimus, sed confirmamus quaedam naturam facere non posse, eaque Deum nè aggredi omnino; sed ex his quae facere potest, quod melius est eligere. Jam vero cum pilos in palpebris satius esset equales semper esse magnitudine & numero, non ipsum quidem hoc voluisse affirmamus, illos mox factos fuisse, neque enim id facere potuisset, affirmamusque si eos etiam millies voluisset, nunquam tamen..."</note>

# Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

...such things would be, if they had been produced from soft skin. *Moses* imagined that God can do all things—yes, even if he wanted to make a horse or an ox out of ashes. But I am of another opinion: for I say that Nature cannot do some things, and that God does not attempt those things at all, but instead chooses and makes a selection of the best of such things as he is able to accomplish. Now, since it would be better if the hair in the eyebrows were always equal in size and number, I affirm that it is not he who willed it so; and even if they were made immediately, he could not do it. I say that if he willed them to be so a thousand times, they would never be such if they had been produced out of soft skin. 

<note>The author is quoting an opponent, likely Galen, who argues that God is limited by the physical properties of matter.</note>

Look how atheistically he speaks! See how he would restrain the omnipotence <term>all-powerful nature</term> of God and limit his actions with the heavy shackle of necessity—even claiming God is powerless!

But there are certain other philosophers who behave themselves more modestly regarding the aforementioned doubt. For *Avicenna* <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> affirms that these actions are neither out of necessity nor violent, but consist of a middle ground between the two; and based on that, he concludes that it depends on the "volunty" <term>free will</term> of the Agent. In this resolution, he seems not to vary much from the Scriptures, which say:

<margin>Tobit 13:5</margin>
> *God has chastised us for our iniquities; he will save us for his mercy's sake.* <note>original Latin: "Deus castigavit nos propter iniquitates nostras, ipse salvabit nos propter misericordiam suam."</note>

By this, this "chosen vessel" <note>A biblical term for a servant of God.</note> suggests that there is a free will in God to punish and to have mercy. But this is expressed in plain words in this manner:

<margin>Daniel 4</margin>
*God operates according to his will, as much among the powers of heaven as among the inhabitants of the earth.* <note>original Latin: "Deus juxta voluntatem suam facit, tam in cœli virtutibus, quam in habitatoribus terræ."</note> In these words, the Prophet evidently shows that every operation in this world is brought about by the Will, and in or by the Word or Spirit of the Almighty. Therefore, it is not out of necessity, as *Aristotle*, *Galen*, and many other ethnic <term>pagan/non-Christian</term> philosophers have claimed, to the disparagement of God and the tarnishing of his omnipotence. 

However, it is most evident that there is an undoubted necessity in the "organic causes" <term>the physical instruments or mechanisms of nature</term> and in the effects that result from God's acts within them. Therefore, the Prophet *Baruch* says: *The sun, moon, stars, lightnings, winds, clouds, etc., obey the will and command of God; that is, they are stirred by his Word and by necessity provoked to carry out his pleasure.* <note>original Latin: "Deo obediunt per omnia, Sol, Luna, Sydera, Fulgur, Ventus, Nubes, &c."</note> It does not follow, therefore, that he who commands must be forced to act in that commanding way, since he does it as a "first mover" who has no other actor before him or existing eternally with him. Consequently, he operates out of a free will which is fundamentally grounded in himself. On this point, the Apostle says:

<margin>Romans 9</margin>
*Who is able to resist the will of God?* <note>original Latin: "Voluntati Dei quis resistat?"</note> And the Prophet:

<margin>Isaiah 46:10</margin>
*My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be accomplished.* <note>original Latin: "Consilium meum stabit, & omnis voluntas mea fiet."</note> And *Job*:

<margin>Job 23</margin>
*Whatever God willed to be done, that he accomplishes.* <note>original Latin: "Deus quodcunque voluit hoc facit."</note> Therefore, he does not act involuntarily or out of necessity, but voluntarily and according to his free will.

We conclude, therefore, that since what is "necessary" is that which cannot happen otherwise but must be so, then that which is "contingent" may happen or be brought about differently—such as something that is either accidental or voluntary. Now, that the acts of God in this world are voluntary, and therefore cannot be tied up with the bonds of necessity, is proved by this: namely, because things can happen differently than they usually do by the laws or rules of nature. For example, when it was the will of God that the sun should stand still, or move backward, or that it should be eclipsed when the moon was in none of the points of the "animal intersection"—that is, neither in the "head or tail of the Dragon" <note>Archaic astronomical terms for the lunar nodes, the points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic; eclipses usually only happen at these points.</note>, etc.

# The Fifth Book of this Present Section.

## The Argument of this Book.

*After the author had expressed the original nature of the two essential properties—namely Heat and Cold—and had proved their main effects to be Rarefaction <term>the thinning of matter</term> and Condensation <term>the thickening of matter</term>, by which the heavens and elements were framed: he proceeds now in this book to the mystery of meteorological impressions <note>Atmospheric phenomena like rain, wind, and clouds.</note>. These represent the first degree of "composition" <term>the mixing of elements</term>, showing that their construction is the act of the Divine Spirit, performed within the universal element of the world's lower region. Consequently, these phenomena do not proceed from the accidental and external grounds or beginnings that the Peripatetics <term>followers of Aristotle</term> falsely suspect. For this reason, he has compared the meteorological doctrine of Aristotle with that of the Holy Scripture. Finally, by bringing pagan philosophy concerning these airy impressions to the "Lydian trial" <note>The Lydian stone was a touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here, it means a test of truth.</note>, or touchstone of Truth, he finds them to be false, counterfeit metal—indeed, mere dross—compared to the golden Truth.*

By that means, he may at last discern with open eyes that main difference which exists between the wisdom and philosophy of this world—which in truth (for the Spirit of God has pronounced it so) is mere foolishness—and that of God, which is the real and essential truth. Thus, you may discern, and that in few words, the manner or order of my method in this book, not intending to be over-tedious to you in it, but to finish briefly that *meteorological* wisdom which, in regard of its own worth, deserves to be enrolled in the everlasting monument of a far larger volume, and to be polished or burnished over with the luster of a more elegant style and refined manner of speech.

# Mosaic Philosophy. Book 5.

...will express what the pagan Peripatetic <note>original: "Peripateticks"; the followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> philosophers, and their Christian followers, have determined and do determine concerning them.

The Peripatetic philosophers are of the opinion that the wind is a hot and dry exhalation—one that is difficult to ignite—which arises out of the earth and soars up into the middle region of the air. From there, it is immediately repelled downward because of the coldness of that region. As it strives upward again, partly due to its own lightness and partly because of other rising exhalations it meets during its violent and forced descent, it moves sideways in the lower region of the air. It stirs and agitates this air so that it does not rot <note>original: "putrifie"</note> for lack of motion. This is the summary of their opinion concerning the generation of the winds. I will, therefore, examine this Peripatetic or Aristotelian definition, or rather description, of the winds.

First, I do so because the false <note>original: "spurious"</note> Christian philosophers, as if incited by a kind of unbridled madness, do not hesitate to defend and uphold this opinion with their best efforts—in public schools, private studies, and their writings—and with such confident obstinacy as if it had been divinely revealed to the world or pronounced by the sacred Oracle of Truth itself.

Secondly, I examine it because the place where this imaginary exhalation is said to be created, and from which it is derived, is believed by them to be the earth. The destination to which it desires to ascend is (according to their doctrine) the middle region of the air, which it is not permitted to enter or penetrate because of the cold temperature. Thus, the middle area is the place where it moves naturally upward and by compulsion (or against nature) downward. Finally, by the jostling or struggling together of other rising exhalations and the forceful descending fumes, it moves "laterally"—that is to say, toward the right or left hand—in the lower region of the air.

Thirdly, they seem to assert, as appears by this definition, that the agent, mover, or efficient cause of this exhalation moving downward and sideways is twofold: namely, the cold of the middle region of the air, which forces and presses that barely imaginable fume downward toward the earth; and the other is the troop of other rising exhalations or subtle smokes that successively rise out of the earth. In their upward motion, these meet the fume that is forced to descend; they strive and, as it were, wrestle with it, and consequently create a noise in the air which is called the Wind.

And this is the Peripatetic philosopher's "windy fiction," which in the end, after a proper examination, will prove to be but a bubble or a vain puff of wind; that is to say, merely words without any substance. Now, the final end or cause why nature has ordained these windy motions in the air is (as their definition testifies) so that by this manner of ventilation, the air may be preserved, cleared, and purged from all rot and corrupt disposition. But whoever gives credit to this pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> definition—especially if he is a true lover of wisdom—I counsel him first to examine every particular part of it. Having made a diligent inquiry, let him see and discern whether these ideas agree with the laws of true reason and wisdom.

In the first rank and order, therefore, let us observe whether there is any probability of truth to be found in the first part of his description. By it, we are told and taught that the material substance of the wind is a hot and dry exhalation arising and surging out of the earth. But by Holy Scripture (which all true Christians ought to believe above all things), we are taught that the wind has its origin or beginning from the Spirit or breath of JEHOVAH:

<margin>Exodus 15:8.</margin>
"By the breath of your nostrils the waters were gathered together, you blew with your wind, and the sea covered them" <note>original Latin: "A flatu narium tuorum coacervatæ sunt aquæ, flavisti vento tuo & operuit eos mare"</note>, says Moses.

<margin>Job 37:9, 28:25.</margin>
And Job says, "God produces the ice with his breath; when God blows, the frost and ice are created" <note>original Latin: "Glaciem edit Deus vento suo, flante Deo concrescit gelu"</note>. And "God gives weight <note>original: "proportion"</note> to the air or wind" <note>original Latin: "Deus facit pondus vento"</note>.

<margin>Psalm 104:4.</margin>
And the Prophet David says, "Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers flames of fire" <note>original Latin: "Qui facit angelos ventos, & ministros suos ignem urentem"</note>. Upon this, learned persons and Doctors who have dived deeply into the mysteries of true nature assert that the external part of the Angels is air, or the subtle, moist nature of the world, and that their internal or formal portion is a hidden divine fire.
