The second part of this definition suggests to us that the place where that exhalation (the material cause of the wind) is created and from which it is derived, is the earth. However, the definition says the place or seat toward which it tends is the middle region of the air; and the medium and space in which it moves—upward, downward, and sideways—is the lower region of the air. 

In this assertion by this pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosopher, I will make plain and prove evidently that several gross errors and palpable absurdities will be found. But so that we may better conduct our inquiry and hunt after the truth of the matter—that is, for the sake of a more exact examination—it will be necessary for us to divide this clause into three parts. In the first, we ought seriously to consider whether the matter of the winds is extracted out of the earth or not. In the second, we must see if that substance only soars up and makes its way to the concave surface of the middle region of the air. In the third, we must ask whether the place in which the wind moves is only the lower region of the air. 

Regarding the first question or doubt, we say that either the sacred Bible (which is the fountain of truth) is false, or this specific part of the second member of the definition must be most erroneous. For, Saint John says: <margin>John 3:8.</margin> "The wind or spirit blows where it wishes, and you hear its voice, but you do not know from where it comes or where it goes" <note>original Latin: "Spiritus ubi vult spirat, & vocem ejus audis, sed nescis unde venias, aut quò vadat"</note>. 

When this is rightly pondered by wise men, they must conclude one of two things: either Aristotle saw further into the mysteries of God and nature than the Evangelist—who was a true and sincere Christian philosopher and theologian <note>original: "Theosopher"</note>—in which case Saint John must be proved a liar in his doctrine (which would be a great impiety for any Christian to imagine); or else the assertion of Aristotle must clearly be found false and in all things contradictory to the truth. 

Aristotle says that the matter of the wind moves from the earth and ascends into the middle region of the air, and from there is repelled downward. But Saint John says that the wind does not move by force—that is to say, by external compulsion or accidental pushing—but voluntarily, according to its own pleasure and appetite. His words are, "It blows where it wishes" <note>original Latin: "Spiritus spirat ubi vult"</note>; and although its voice and noise are familiar to the ears, it is nevertheless not known from where it comes or where it goes. 

This doctrine of the Evangelist, which differs so greatly from that of Aristotle, is maintained in various places of Holy Writ. For the royal Psalmist, along with the Prophet Jeremiah, says: <margin>Psalm 135:7. Jeremiah 51:15.</margin> "He brings forth the winds out of his treasuries" <note>original Latin: "Depromit ventos è thesauris suis"</note>. But the Scriptures prove that the earth is not the seat or place of God's treasury, stating: <margin>Deuteronomy 28:12.</margin> "The LORD will open to you his best treasure, the heavens, giving rain to the earth in its due time" <note>original Latin: "Aperiet tibi JEHOVAH thesaurum suum optimum, cælos, dando pluviam terræ suo tempore"</note>. He does not say the earth, but the heavens; so between these two there is a great difference, as between night and day. 

Therefore, it is evident that the heaven, or the universal element of air, is the secret cabinet of these "mighty meteorological works of God" <note>original Latin: "meteorologica Dei magnalia"</note>. Regarding this, it is said in another place: <margin>Psalm 78:23. # Section 1. *Mosaical Philosophy*

The Prince of our philosophers <note>original: "Prince of our Philosophers" refers to Aristotle</note> will not blush (forsooth) to say that the wind is something merely accidental, and that it has its motion only from external principles, and not from that central and internal agent which is the actor and operator of, and in, all things. Consequently, he argues it could not blow or breathe where it pleases, nor yet hear the voice of the Lord when it was commanded to come from the four winds. He, according to his fancy, says that this invention of his is extracted out of the earth, when the Scriptures say that it is the most lively and agile creature of God, which he brings out of the heavens (which are his treasury); for in this, both the Prophets, *Jeremiah* and *David*, agree. But in this part of his definition, he concludes that the lateral motion of the wind is caused through that resistance and impediment made by such exhalations as ascend. Oh, poor argument for so mighty a philosopher! As if such a fanning motion as that is—from the north to the south, and so forth—could be so certain and direct in its course while being guided by so uncertain an agent as an accidental striving and contention between ascending and descending fumes?

<margin>Ezekiel 37.</margin>
I beseech you tell me (my clever Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripateticks"; followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note>), what manner of exhalation rose out of the earth and shouldered or shoved and resisted one another in that emission of Spirit which happened when the Prophet said, *Come from the four winds, O spirit* <note>original: "A quatuor ventis adveni, Spiritus"</note>? Methinks I see the Christian disciples of *Aristotle* to be completely mute and destitute of tongues to answer. And if they should say that it was a miraculous wind and not a natural one, I answer that I know no more efficient causes in nature, or out of nature, but only one. Therefore it is said regarding the production of meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and snow.</note>—namely, in the common course of this world's nature—God blows from the north; God produces frost, snow, and ice by his breath; God thunders from heaven; God melts the thick clouds into rain; God sends lightning from his throne and coals of fire out of his mouth; God makes the dark clouds his hiding place; God comes from the south in thunder. The voice of the Lord makes the cedars of mount *Lebanon* to stoop and the hinds to miscarry their young. God is a consuming fire. Who can stand or resist the cold of God? and so forth, in many more places in both the New and Old Testament. And, to conclude, that God operates all in all, and that he gives life to all, etc. 

But our Peripatetic philosophers come with their school-tricks and idle distinctions and say, "It is true indeed that he is the *principal efficient cause* <note>original: "causa efficiens principalis"</note>; but there are many secondary and subordinate causes in nature which act of themselves." I say, plain dealing is a jewel, and truth—being one simple essence—hates double-dealing. Let us imitate her in plainness and simplicity of understanding. We cannot attain this unless we abstract our minds from the subtle multiplicity of worldly philosophy and vain fallacy (of which St. *Paul* bids us to beware); for in multitude lurks an infinity of errors, but in unity consists that unique verity which is true wisdom. Why then should we distract men's thoughts from the simple sense of Scripture by a multiplicity of distinctions, which seem to twist it like a nose of wax a hundred different ways?

It would be impossible for this difference and variety to occur if all winds were framed and fashioned only in one way—that is, if they moved sideways by compulsion, as Aristotle tells the story.

<margin>Psalm 91.</margin> I come now to the last clause or member of the Peripatetic definition, which touches upon the final end or reason for the production and creation of the winds. His opinion is that nature produces this manner of ventilation for the purging and purifying of the air, and for its preservation. But we are taught by experience that this is not true; for we, along with Galen and Hippocrates, discern that the southerly winds are contagious and pestilential <note>original: "pestiferous"</note>, because they make the air thick and cause it to become putrid and rotten by their malignant heat and loose humidity. This we also have confirmed by the sacred text. <margin>Habakkuk 3.</margin> David says, *Do not fear the pestilence or the destroying demon in the noonday* <note>original: "Ne timeto a lue seu demonio vastante in meridie"</note>. And Habakkuk says: *When God came from the south, the pestilence went before him, and the burning plague followed at his feet* <note>original: "Deo a meridie veniente praecessit (vel ante-ivit) eum pestis & antrax ad pedes ipsius"; the original text uses "anthrax" or "antrax" to mean a carbuncle or inflammatory tumor</note>. 

Indeed, all winds in general—as well as the other meteors of heaven—are ordained by the Creator as much for a whip and scourge as to assist, preserve, and save the creature, as we are certified by many places of Scripture, <margin>Job 37:14.</margin> and as Job has taught us in express terms. Therefore, Aristotle has erred in his judgment concerning the final cause of the winds, just as he did in the rest of his theories.

We may justly conclude from this that the definition provided by our pagan Peripatetic—whom we Christians adore and follow with such devotion and reverence—is altogether false and of no validity. This is because the winds are creatures of a nature more essentially eminent and divine than either Aristotle or any of his faction ever understood. They are not things without internal lights and essences, and they do not consist only of external and accidental motions—that is to say, they are not made of fumes or exhalations arising by accident or chance out of <margin>Zechariah 6:1.</margin> the earth. But, as Zechariah teaches us, they are created and animated by an angelic spirit and stand before the Lord of all the earth. They are hidden in the power or treasury of their Lord, from which he calls them at his pleasure to accomplish his will upon the earth and upon the seas—either *for vengeance or punishment* <note>original: "ad vindictam seu punitionem"</note>, or else *to show mercy and kindness to his creatures* <note>original: "ad misericordiam & benignitatem creaturis praebendam"</note>.

***

*The true and essential definition of the wind is expressed in various ways in this chapter, according to the sense and assertion of the Holy Scriptures.*

Tell us essentially what the wind is, or how you define or describe it rightly by the warrant of Holy Writ?" To this I answer that it may be described in many ways under one and the same essence. First of all, we may describe it, and not irrelevantly, in this manner:

# Sect. 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

The wind is an airy spirit, of a medium <note>original: "mean"; here meaning intermediate or average density</note> consistency, inspired and animated by the breath or inspiration of JEHOVAH, which he draws forth from his treasury to execute his will and pleasure, either by way of a curse and vengeance, or of blessing and mercy <note>original: "misericord"</note>.

Every part of this definition is proven by appropriate passages of Holy Scripture. First, that its external nature is air of a medium consistency is made manifest by the fact that the words "air," "wind," and "spirit" are expressed in many places in Scripture by one and the same Hebrew word, namely, ***Ruach***. Again, that its internal or moving soul and central action is the divine Spirit or inspiration is proven and confirmed by the passages cited before: *By the breath of your nostrils the waters were gathered in a heap; you blew with your wind, and the sea covered them* <note>original Latin: "A flatu narium tuarum coacervatæ sunt aquæ, flavisti vento tuo, & operuit eos mare"</note>. So it appears there is no difference between an angelic creature and the air when it is so divinely inspired; for the air is said to be the external or manifest form of an angel (both good and bad), animated by God to carry out his will, either to punish or to extend and show forth his kind mercy or clemency. Meanwhile, its internal and hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> portion is the immediate breath of God. Therefore (as I said before), they are termed by **St. Denis** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher</note> ***Algamatha***, that is to say, clear mirrors or looking-glasses which receive the light of God. Is it not expressed in plain words by **David**, *That he made his angels winds* <note>original Latin: "Quod angelos suos fecerit ventos"</note>? Here, by "his angels" is meant the emissions from his throne; when these are incorporated with the air, they are termed angelic natures. Again, JEHOVAH said of the Angel who went before the Israelites to lead them in the wilderness, *Do not provoke him, for he will not bear your errors, because my name is in him* <note>original Latin: "Nolite exacerbare eum, nam non feret defectiones vestras, quoniam nomen meum est in eo"</note>; that is to say, the bright impression of my Word. For the Son of Sirach said that Wisdom went before them in a pillar of cloud, and was a light to them in the night and a shadow in the day to keep them from extreme heat. 

For this reason, the same Angel is called in many places of that book sometimes **Jehovah**, in regard to his inward and uncreated essential act, and sometimes **Angel**, in regard to his "alterity" <term>alterity: the state of being "other" or a separate created being</term> or his composition of two parts—that is, as he was a creature. Therefore, just as God is "identity" (namely, an absolute, simple, pure, and uncreated essence), an Angel is termed **Alterity** by the wiser Rabbis, because he is composed of the uniform inspiration of God and the humid or airy nature of the world. This is to say, he is made of a created spirit or a created air, which made the Psalmist say what was cited above: *Who makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire* <note>original Latin: "Qui facit angelos ventos, & ministros suos ignem urentem"</note>. Consequently, they neither understand God truly by and in his works as he ought to be known, nor can they rightly conceive the mystery of his creatures, whose cornerstone is the brightness of the all-animating and informing Word.

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5

...which interpretation we have maintained to be good in the preceding book of this discourse: *God set his tabernacle in the sun* <note>original Latin: *Posuit Deus tabernaculum suum in sole*</note> <margin>Psalm 19:4</margin>. By this it is evident that it was the pleasure of God, the Creator of all things, that this vessel should be rich and abundant in his Spirit. Being placed in the center, heart, <term>diapason</term> <note>original: "diapason"; here meaning the point of perfect harmony or the central "note" of the universe</note>, or perfect point of the world, the sun might—by its virtuous harmony and life—order and govern the animal course and temporal disposition of things that are born and decay on the earth, in the seas, and in the universal sublunary element, namely, the universal air. As air is the vehicle of life in every creature below the moon, it is also necessary to consider that the air is animated and inspired by the sun, just as the higher angelic natures receive their light and being from the Creator, before whose face they are always present. I do not say that the Sun itself gives life, but rather the increased virtue within the Sun, which God has elected as the palace or treasury-house for His power. And therefore it is said that *the sun is full of the glory of the Lord, or of his divine virtue and essence* <note>original Latin: *Sol est gloriæ Domini, seu virtutis & essentiæ divinæ, plenus*</note>. And again it is termed *an admirable vessel, the work of the Most High* <note>original Latin: *Vas ad mirabile, opus Excelsi*</note> <margin>Ecclesiasticus 43:2</margin>.

Now, we are taught that this divine virtue in the Sun guides the air and makes it a general angelic spirit or wind—that is, an air animated by divinity which is apt to move according to the motion of the Mover—by these words of Solomon: *The Sun illuminating all things in its circuit, the spirit moves on and returns in its circles* <note>original Latin: *Sol lustrans universa in circuitu, pergit Spiritus & in circulos suos revertitur*</note> <margin>Ecclesiastes 1:6</margin>. This argues that the Sun, by his presence, animates and makes the air mobile and agile by thinning and quickening the spirits within that air, which was previously quiet and still. 

Now, I would not want any man to mistake me and think I mean that the whole Spirit of the Lord is confined only within the Sun; for, as I said, Scripture reports that Christ was rich and full of the Spirit. So God imparted to the Sun an abundance of his illuminating, positive, generative, and life-giving virtue; and yet, nevertheless, He fills all things—but not in only one manner, nor in the same property or proportion. For according to the common course He has ordained for the ordering of the yearly seasons, where the Sun (His actual tabernacle) is more or less absent or removed, there the <term>divine power</term> <note>original Latin: *potentia divina*</note>, or the cold "privative" Spirit of God, is more or less in operation, for there it acts universally. 

As for example: when the Sun is absent and under the earth, it causes darkness, coldness, dullness of air, and a heavy <term>thickness</term> <note>original: "spissitude"; density or thickness</note> to be present. For example: when the Sun is beyond the <term>Equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note>, moving toward the Tropic of Capricorn, cold, frost, snow, ice, short days, and thick, cloudy, and rainy air are present, and southerly winds are most frequent. For then the "privative" property of God <note>referring to the qualities of darkness and cold as the absence of light and heat</note> has dominion over the northern hemisphere. At this time, the plants, herbs, and trees are naked; having their spirits and humors congealed, they appear as if dead; the earth loses its <term>greenness</term> <note>original: "viridity"</note> and, like a sterile and barren widow, begins to mourn. 

But as soon as the sunny chariot, with its princely Lord, approaches our hemisphere and enters into this northern world by the fiery and martial gate of *Aries* (the Ram), which occurs in the Springtime, then these almost dead creatures—having been previously mortified by the cruel cold of northern privation—begin to revive. The nights grow short, the cold diminishes, and the congealed and fixed spirits in the plants relent, liquefy, and become animated and flowing. The birds rejoice and are quickened, and the dull and senseless air is refreshed little by little, taking flight into the southern regions for reasons I will show you in my demonstrative positions immediately following. 

And yet, despite the absence of the bright and active Spirit in the Sun, it follows that the one and self-same Spirit which fills all may alter His privative property when and where He pleases. For we often see, quite contrary to the common constitution of the year, that thunders and lightnings are produced in the middle of the hardest winters; and the winds which are most active—namely, the east and south—blow beyond expectation. All of this is performed by Him at His pleasure, who operates all in all, how, by what means, and where and when He chooses. This, therefore, being well pondered, I enter into the state of this, my demonstration.

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical exploration of how the Sun's presence or absence affects the air, transitioning from the general nature of the Sun to the specific mechanics of wind movement.</meta>

Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

### *The demonstration or proof of how the annual winds are moved by the life-giving spirit which is in the Sun.*

I have told you that the whole effect of divine action in the moist nature of this lower world consists of <term>congelation</term> <note>original: "Congelation"; the process of thickening or freezing</note> and <term>rarefaction</term> <note>original: "Rarefaction"; the process of air becoming thinner and expanding</note>. The first was caused by the depriving and northern action of God’s Spirit, which operates through cold; the other by His positive operation, which is guided by heat. Now, as these two have their dominance or decline based on the presence or absence of the Sun, so also is the universal air colder, thicker, more opaque, and sluggish or dull when the Sun is farthest away. Conversely, the air is hotter, thinner, brighter, more transparent, agile, and active when the Sun is nearest. Mark, therefore, the properties of the air contained within the glass vessel of the <term>Calendar-Instrument</term> <note>An early meteorological device similar to a thermometer</note>, and remember that it is but one and the same Spirit in essence that works both deprivingly and positively. For it was one and the same Spirit which was called by the Prophet from the north and south, for the Text says: *Come, O spirit, from the four winds* <note>original Latin: *Veni spiritus à quatuor ventis*</note>, etc. Therefore, it is this Spirit that governs the universal air below the moon, both deprivingly and positively. And although this Spirit is most plentiful in the Sun, it is nevertheless everywhere, and is able at all times and in every place to express itself in both properties. I come, therefore, to the main point.

In the first chapter of the first book of this present section, I most clearly demonstrated to you that the air contained in the <term>Weather-glass</term> <note>An early form of thermometer that measured the expansion and contraction of air</note> has, in every respect, a relation to the air or universal element of the great world. There it is also proved that the airy, moist nature exactly fills every place of the vaulted world where the earth or water are not—lest any void should be found in its hollow—just as the expanded air in the head and neck of the **Weather-glass** fills its cavity. Therefore, as the air inside the glass works by expansion at the presence of the Sun—namely, in the summer season when the external air is heated—so too, and in the exact same manner, will the air of this Northern Hemisphere be expanded when the Sun is present. Indeed, the nearer the Sun is, and the more direct its beams are, the greater the general air's rarefaction will be, and consequently that of the particular air which is in the glass.

On the other side, when the Sun is absent from the <term>Boreal</term> <note>original: "Boreall"; meaning northern</note> hemisphere—namely, when it moves beyond the <term>Equinoctial</term> <note>The Equator</note>—then the common air in that hemisphere will grow cold and be contracted and condensed. Consequently, the particular air in the glass will be contracted in the same proportion, which may easily be measured or understood by the degrees the water rises in the glass, just as the expansion may be observed by the water's descent. Once this is well understood—that the cause of this expansion is the presence of this divine action in the sun’s "tabernacle," and the reason for the condensation is the absence or distance of that action (the operating and emanating Spirit)—it follows that the presence of the divine power is darkness. For (as we said) the absence of heat is the presence of cold, which is the essential worker in the divine power; and again, the presence of heat is the absence of cold. So also the absence of positive light creates depriving darkness, and the absence of depriving darkness brings the presence of positive light.

We may easily, therefore, gather the reason for the annual winds and perceive what their external nature is, and how that air is animated by the life-giving Spirit which is sent out from the Sun. Consider, therefore, that when the Sun is present with us, summer is created by his presence; the air is warmed by the bright beams of his Spirit, and by warming it is thinned. ### Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5.

He assigns no internal cause of motion to the cloud, regarding it as something dead and without an active spirit.

For this reason, several doubts present themselves for every wise man's consideration. These must be thoroughly resolved and determined before he will be able to rightly judge the truth of the matter. Namely:
1. First, whether the heat of the Sun draws and attracts vapors out of the earth and waters into the middle region of the air to compose and shape a cloudy meteor. 
2. Second, whether the coldness of the middle region of the air is the cause of the condensation, or thickening, of a thin vaporous substance into the consistency of a well-compacted cloud. 
3. Third, whether clouds are only moved by external efficient agents—namely, by the winds and Sun—as if they lacked any internal active principle or central agent, or if they are instead moved and animated by an internal spirit. 

I intend to answer each of these three questions or doubts in the order they are proposed.

Regarding the first objection, I say: It is a most false and erroneous tenet of the Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripateticks"; followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> that the Sun, stars, or fire draw any vapors or exhalations toward them. It is proven by experience that they actually expel and scatter away from them such things as are rarified <note>made thinner or less dense</note> by them, rather than drawing and alluring them. Nor is it true, as most men falsely dream and surmise, that the Sun draws fumes upward, or that fire sucks the vaporous substance of thinned water toward itself. Rather, their function is to rarify and refine the waters and to turn the moister part of the earth into vapor. Then, it is naturally characteristic of those light substances, by their own inclination, to ascend and mount upwards without any other external agent. 

We have plainly demonstrated all of this with our experimental instrument <note>likely a thermoscope or early weather glass</note>. If you place your hand upon the bolt’s head <note>the glass bulb at the top of the instrument</note> or round glass, the air inside will expand <note>original: "dilate"</note> and immediately fly away from the warming agent that expands it; therefore, that agent is even less likely to suck or draw the air toward itself. By this it is evident that while it seemed to worldly-wise men that because a vapor or fume ascends, that motion from the Earth must proceed from the attractive power of the summer heat; in conclusion, this is proved to be completely false and erroneous. The nature of heat and light is entirely contrary to attraction. Heat expels by expansion, dissipates, and enlarges, which is contrary to the nature of attraction, gathering together, and condensation—which are the properties of cold, as is demonstrated by our experimental machine.

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5.

...no further. But I will tell you about an experiment of my own, which led me toward the truth concerning the generation of mists and clouds. When, in my travels, I journeyed from Venice to Augsburg in Germany, I traveled between the high mountains and rocks of the Alps. On a certain day when the heavens were perfectly clear, with no cloud to be seen on the horizon, and the sun was shining brightly (as it usually does in those times), I noticed a certain fog or mist beginning to rise little by little on the top of a steep mountain where the sunbeams beat down strongly. It thickened more and more until it grew from a slight vapor into a mist, and from a foggy mist finally into a thick cloud. All this while, the air was clear everywhere else, except only on that side of the hill—from the top to the bottom—which we were watching. 

It made me marvel a little, and therefore, alighting from our coach, I took some grass and threw it into the air to see which way the wind blew. I found it to be blowing directly against that towering hill, which rose toward the heavens above its neighbors. <margin>11. 32. 34</margin> Whereupon I immediately concluded that the stages of progression—from a vapor into a mist, from a mist into a fog, and so on until the consistency of a cloud—were caused by the compression of the common air. This air was driven by the wind little by little against the lofty rock or mountain. Because the mountain hindered its passage or flight, the air behind was pushed into the air in front. By thus adding and compressing parts of the air into other parts, a perfect cloud was made, shaped exactly to that part of the mountain. Immediately afterward, when it became heavy and capable of reflecting the sun's rays, it turned itself into rain for a space of four miles on this side of the rock, while all the rest of the air remained clear and without any cloud. <margin>mist & cloud</margin> 

By this, I immediately understood that clouds were not created in the <margin>clouds</margin> manner described by the Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripateticks"; followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note>—that is, by vapors rising out of the earth and waters—but by the thickening or condensation <note>original: "inspissation or incrassation"</note> of the thin and invisible air into a thick, dense, and visible cloud, according to the previously mentioned passage from Job:

> *Suddenly the air shall be condensed into clouds, and the passing wind shall drive them away.* <note>original: "Subitò aer condensabitur in nubes & transiens ventus fugabit eas."</note>

But then I was a little puzzled when I remembered that mountains and high rocks cannot always be the cause of clouds by resisting and stopping the escaping air, since we find that clouds appear everywhere—even in flat deserts and open seas where there are no hills. After I had considered this for a little while and weighed this objection, I quickly conceived a certain answer and resolution to this doubt. I considered that there is no wind blowing in the heavens with dominance that does not also have some opposite or crosswind blowing with it, though it is not noticed because the mightier wind obscures the action of the weaker one—just as a candle is scarcely noticed in the open sun. 

I will prove by common experience that two or more winds blow at one and the same time. Being often on the seas, I have observed that when the predominant wind has decreased a little in force by fits and pushed the ship's sail only weakly, an opposite wind has immediately revealed itself and moved the sail the contrary way, until the original wind rose again and filled the sail back toward our intended destination. But we also have Scriptures to testify that opposite winds often blow at the same instant. First, the same Spirit was called from the <margin>Ezekiel 37. Daniel 7.</margin> quarters of the four winds by Ezekiel and Daniel:

For by **Neptune**, he means the presiding spirit <term>original: "president"</term> of the western <note>original: "occidentall"</note> winds, which are cold, moist, and watery; and by **Phœbus**, he intends the eastern <note>original: "orientall"</note> presiding spirit, whose blasts are hot, dry, and fiery; while **Mars** signifies thunder and lightning. The poet **Ovid** also notably expresses the combat that takes place among the winds in these verses, speaking in the persona of **Boreas**, the North Wind:

> *I am the same one who, when I have found my brothers in the open sky—for that is my field—struggle with such great effort that the middle air sounds with our collisions, and fires forced out of the hollow clouds leap forth.* <note>original: "Idem ego quum fratres cœlo sum nactus aperto / Nam mihi campus is est, tanto molimine luctor / Ut medius nostris concussibus insonet Æther / Exiliantque cavis elisi nubibus ignes."</note>

> *When I meet my brothers in the air,*
> *(Which is my field) I wrestle with such ire,*
> *That middle heavens echo at our fare,*
> *And hollow clouds vent forth flashing fire.*

By "Brothers," **Boreas** (the North Wind) means the southern blast and the other cardinal winds. When Boreas meets them in the air, their contentious struggling and wrestling produce thunder, whirlwinds, and similar tempestuous storms. Therefore, we should have no doubt that two or more winds can blow at the same time—either from opposite directions or crossing each other in the open air. This causes the invisible air between them to be thickened or condensed by compression. It changes from the state of ordinary air into a barely visible vaporous substance, then into a more visible misty thickness, and finally into a fully apparent and visible cloud. Nevertheless, that cloud is pushed and driven forward by whichever wind in the heaven has the greatest power and influence. This power confirms in every point what was spoken by **Job** and cited before: <margin>Job 37:21.</margin> *Suddenly the air will be thickened into clouds, and the wind passing by will drive them away.* <note>original: "Subito aer densabitur in nubes & ventus transiens fugabit eas"</note>

It is easy to gather, then, that a cloud is framed from the air in this fashion: the air fills the entire vaulted heaven. Therefore, the world below the moon is violently forced to move before the breath of one wind. When it is encountered in its flight by a wind opposite to the first—even if it is of weaker force—that second wind resists the chased air in its motion. Through that resistance, air is joined to air and thickens by degrees. This is just as I told you regarding the steep mountain or rock: by denying passage to the air that fled from the pursuing wind, the mountain caused the air to condense.

When this is rightly considered, it is apparent that the Aristotelian claim <note>original: "Peripateticall assertion"</note> is unjust and erroneous. That theory asserts that a vapor raised out of the earth and water up to the middle region of the air is metamorphosed or changed into the form and substance of a cloud by the coldness of that place. As already proved, this is most improbable because the southerly winds—which are the primary parents of clouds and abundant rain—are hot due to the temperature of the places from which they are sent. Their warmth would likely neutralize <note>original: "qualifie"</note> the coldness of the region through which they march or pass. Therefore, they would either cancel the effect of that cold or so weaken its power that if it produced any clouds at all, they would be thinner and smaller than those produced by cold winds. The wind **Eurus** <note>the East Wind</note> would also have the same effect because of its great heat. Yet, we find all of this to be quite the opposite in our experience. The southerly winds actually thicken <note>original: "incrassate"</note> the air and produce clouds that are generally more moist and thick than any others. Indeed, the fourth wind so condenses the air by its presence that (as **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar</note> affirms) it makes objects appear...

Regarding the third and last doubt—which is whether the clouds are only moved superficially by external winds and the heat of the Sun (as *Aristotle's* imagination suggests), and not by any central agent that rules them as it pleases, and at whose command the winds themselves are obedient—truly, I answer that, contrary to the belief of the *Peripatetics* <term>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, known for walking while teaching.</term>, the clouds have an internal agent. This agent calls the winds to carry out his will, pushing and moving his cloudy vehicle or chariot whenever, wherever, and whichever way he pleases. For as this Agent is universal <note>original: "catholick"</note>, he is not absent from the spirit of the winds, even though he is centrally present in the cloud. Because he is present within the spirit of the winds, he operates centrally in the air through the angelic spirits of those winds. # Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5.

A cloud is the revealing and manifesting of the invisible mundane spirit <note>original: "mundan spirit," referring to the cosmic spirit or spirit of the world</note>, which is hidden in the treasury of God—namely, the heavens. This happens by the central operation of Divine Wisdom and its windy ministers <note>original: "windy ministers," meaning the winds acting as agents of God</note>, which are prompted by the will of God to form a vaporous heap or cloudy substance. The spirit of wisdom builds this as its secret place or vehicle to move in, in order to carry out His will in the heavens above as well as in the earth and waters below.

Or, expressed in this way:

A cloud is the turning of the invisible air into a visible, thick, and gloomy consistency. This is achieved by the will of God through the meeting of opposite or transverse winds <note>original: "transversall winds," winds blowing across one another</note> to accomplish His secret will and pleasure.

Or else, in this manner:

A cloud is a certain visible, condensed heap of air. The Spirit of Wisdom, being expanded everywhere, creates and composes this as if out of nothing—that is to say, out of an airy, invisible substance which it extracts from its mystical treasury to perform the will of God in both heaven and earth.

In these definitions, or rather descriptions, the material substance appears to be a coagulated mist or a condensed mass of air. The "formal cause" <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "formal cause" is the shape or nature of a thing</note> is displayed in the shape and form of the cloud. The "efficient cause" <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being</note>, or central agent, is the essential act of Divine Wisdom, who employs and rouses its windy ministers to work externally through compression. We also see the storehouse <note>original: "magazine"</note> or treasury from which the substance of the winds is produced: the heavens or the air, which is called "the treasury chest of God" <note>original: "Arca Dei thesauraria"</note>. To conclude, the "final cause" <note>The "final cause" is the ultimate purpose for which a thing exists</note> is revealed in this: that the cloud is ordained to bring about the effects of God’s mercy and kindness <note>original: "clemency and benignity"</note>, as well as His severity and anger.

<margin>Job 28:25</margin> To defend the first part of these descriptions, we find it written: "God by His wisdom apportions the weight of the air and weighs out the waters (or clouds) in measure; He assigns laws to the rain and makes a path for the lightnings of the thunder" <note>original: "Deus sapientia sua aptat pondus aeri & appendit aquas in mensura, facit pluvia statuta & viam fulgetro tonitruum, &c."</note>. That is to say, according to the will and command of the Divine Spirit, the air or substance of heaven is changed from a lighter or thinner state and weight to a heavier or thicker one. The degrees of this change <note>original: "mutation"</note> are expressed in the following words: first it was air, then clouds, then rain or common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> water. Also, the text seems to suggest that the lightning is the internal or formal light of the cloud, which is not revealed except by the breaking <note>original: "violation or ruption"</note> of the compound and the removal of darkness. Again, it is said by Job (as previously mentioned), "The air will be thickened into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away" <note>original: "Aer condensabitur in nubes, & ventus transiens fugabit eas"</note>. And regarding clouds of snow, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 43</margin> "The gathering of the spirit scatters the snow" <note>original: "Congregatio spiritus aspergit nivem"</note>; that is, the air being gathered together scatters snow upon the earth.

Regarding the efficient cause, it appears to be God, or Eternal Wisdom. Therefore, in the preceding text it is said, "God by His wisdom balances the waters or clouds in measure" <note>original: "Deus sapientia sua aptat pondus aeri, & appendit aquas vel nubes in mensura"</note>. <margin>Psalm 147:8</margin> And again, "God covers the heavens with thick clouds" <note>original: "Nubibus densis obtegit Deus cælos"</note>. But all this was sufficiently expressed before. As for the final cause set down in the aforementioned definitions, it is confirmed by the Scriptures in this way: <margin>Job 37:11</margin> "For the purpose of irrigation, God wears out the thick cloud and disperses the light of His cloud; whatever He commands them to do upon the earth—whether it be for a punishment <note>original: "flagellum" or "scourge"</note> or out of favor and <margin>Baruch 6:60</margin> kindness—He makes them ready to accomplish it" <note>original: "Pro irrigatione fatigat Deus densam nubem, & dispergit lucem nubis suæ, quodcunque præcipit illis faciendum in terra sive ad flagellum, sive ad faciendam beneficentiam efficiet ut prestò sit."</note>. And Baruch says, "When God commands the clouds to pass over the whole earth, they perform what is commanded of them." So we see that these creatures are drawn out of their secret dwellings to do the will of Him who created them.

## CHAP. VII.

### *How the reason for the composition of clouds is visibly demonstrated by our experimental instrument. Also, in this section, snow is defined both falsely and truly.*

Now I think it most appropriate to demonstrate to you how clouds are created by the opposing blasts of two winds of contrary natures: specifically, a Southerly wind in a position of power and dominance, and a Northerly spirit which also blows, but in a way that cannot be felt. 

I told you in the chapter where I demonstrated the cause of the Southerly winds that happen in winter using our experimental instrument <note>The author is likely referring to a "weather-glass," an early form of the thermometer used to show how air expands and contracts with heat and cold.</note>. Just as the air trapped in the weather-glass dilated itself by the mere touch of a warm hand—and in that expansion fled from the hand toward the cold region of the water (which was clearly proven because the water suddenly moved downward)—so it is in nature. The thick winter air in the southern hemisphere, at the approach of the sun toward the regions beyond the Equator <note>original: "the Line"</note>, dilated itself by the power of that ever-acting and refining spirit which God placed within the Sun. 

Consequently, the expanded southern air traveled quickly or flew away to seek a larger space. But upon entering the northern hemisphere (which, due to the Sun's absence, had become wintry <note>original: "brumall"</note>), it met the stable air of that region, which was then contracted by the northern cold. Because of the cold’s dominance, the North wind blows to some degree, even if it is not felt. When it meets the warm southerly spirit, it condenses that spirit along with the rest of the air into clouds. 

This is the reason why almost always (at least where no northern blasts are noticed) southerly winds bring an abundance of clouds and rain with them. The hot southerly power of the divine agent increasingly refines and thins the winter air it finds there until it has purified it through expansion <note>original: "rarefaction"</note> and returned it to the nature of true summer air. Thus, the extra parts of the air after expansion were chased away (as was said) into the northern region. There, it is condensed again, partly by the restrictive act of divine power and partly by the thickness <note>original: "spissitude"</note> of the northern air, which denies it free passage except in the form of clouds. For the cold, thick air of the northern hemisphere, stirred and brought to life by the northern blast or its properties, resists the hot, vaporous air, and so it condenses little by little.

To conclude, I could here set down the Aristotelian definitions of snow, frost, hail, ice, and other such weather phenomena <note>original: "meteors"</note>, and then strongly challenge and contradict them with other true descriptions proven by the testimony of Holy Scripture. For example, Aristotle seems to claim that snow is a cloud congealed by great cold, which is changed into a snowy substance before it can be perfectly dissolved into water. We should not believe him in this case because, as has already been proven, he is ignorant of how a cloud is actually constructed. Furthermore, he wanders away from the meaning of the Scriptures, according to which we have defined snow in this way:

Snow is a weather phenomenon which God draws out of his hidden treasury in the form of wool to carry out his will upon the earth, either as a punishment or an act of mercy.

->Or thus:<-

Snow is a creature produced out of the air, or the heavenly treasury of God, by the cold breath or blast of the divine spirit in the form of wool, to perform his will on the earth.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 43</margin>
In this view, the source of its original substance is identified as the air, or the matter of the heavens. Therefore, the text says, "The gathering together or condensation of the spirit engenders and sprinkles the snow upon the earth" <note>original Latin: *Congregatio spiritus aspergit nivem*</note>.
<margin>Job 38</margin>
And Job asks, "Have you entered into the treasuries of the snow?" <note>original Latin: *Pervenistine in thesauris nivis?*</note>
<margin>Psalm 143:16</margin>
Also, the form and the primary cause are expressed this way: "God by his word sends out the snow like wool; who is able to resist his cold?" <note>original Latin: *Deus verbo suo nives emittit sicut lanam, coram frigore ejus quis consistat?* Note: This is usually cited as Psalm 147:16 in modern Bibles.</note> So we see that God, through his Word—which operates in his restrictive property through cold—is the essential, efficient, and all-powerful actor in the production of snow.

I could, as I said, explain all of this at great length, but because I do not intend to dwell on...

on these particulars, forasmuch as in the description of the cloud, I have sufficiently pointed at the rest, I will proceed unto my inquiry touching *Aristotle's* opinion concerning the beginning of fountains, that we may perceive thereby whether he has erred as far in that mystery as he has done in the rest.

### CHAP. VIII.

#### What *Aristotle's* opinion is, touching the generation of Fountains and Rivers, and whether he in his opinion does agree with the verity of the true wisdom.

Since therefore it is apparent that *Aristotle's* doctrine is erroneous and deceitful touching the generation and essence of the winds and clouds, we purpose in the third place to bring his judgment and opinion, concerning the beginning and origin <note>original: "originall"</note> of fountains and rivers, unto the touchstone of truth, that thereby we may perceive whether it will endure the trial and not shrink (as the proverb is) in the wetting.

The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, as well Christians as Gentiles, are as much deceived in their meteorological grounds concerning the generation of fountains and rivers as in the rest of which we have spoken before; and therefore their Master *Aristotle* (all things being well weighed in the balance of justice) ought to be accounted by all true Christians as a seducer and deceiver of the world; and consequently his doctrine touching this point ought of right to be repudiated and rejected.

*Aristotle*, with his Peripatetic sect or faction, is of the opinion that because the belly or bowels of the earth are full of cavities and hollow passages, vapors—to avoid a vacuum <note>original: "vacuity"</note>—must necessarily ascend from the center or bottom of it. These vapors, clinging in their ascent to the sides of the hollow vaults and narrower passages or veins of the earth, resolve into water, which, distilling down by drops, engenders fountains and rivers.

In this opinion of theirs, they conclude that the matter of fountains is nothing else but a vapor arising from the bottom of the earth, which is resolved, liquefied, or condensed into water through cold and heat together within the earth; no differently than, according to their saying, the cloud, rain, snow, and hail arise and are generated in the air from a vapor, first condensed and afterwards liquefied.

But if we shall duly examine every part of this description, we shall perceive that they require both a double matter and a formal agent in this generation of fountains. For they feign that the remote matter is a vapor, and then the near and immediate matter they imagine to be drops of water, which are caused by the concretion or condensation of that vapor. Also, they make their two efficient causes cold and heat; for, they say, it is the office of cold to condense and congeal the trapped <note>original: "included"</note> vapor into water, and that it is the heat and cold together which make the water fluid <note>original: "fluxible"</note> and movable. Let it therefore be lawful for me (*judicious Reader*) to answer these Peripatetic philosophers with an overworked axiom of their own, and consequently to fight them with their own weapons. Their axiom is, *It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer* <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora."</note>. Now, if this original work in the producing of fountains may be performed most conveniently by one and the same subject of water, without altering it first into vapor by thinning it <note>original: "subtiliation"</note> and afterward by condensing that subtle vapor back into water; then I make no doubt but you will conclude with me that this Peripatetic definition is vain, imaginary, and sophistical by their own rules.

Sect. 1. Mosaic Philosophy.

We find, in the first place, that it is not an accidental and imaginary heat or cold that acts in the generation of this natural phenomenon <note>original: "Meteor." Consequently, we ought to regard it as the act of <margin>Wisdom 1</margin> God's Spirit which fills the earth (as *Solomon* says) and operates all the natural effects within it. ->**Definition of a Fountain**<-

For otherwise, the world would have to undergo an increase or a decrease in its substance—that is, sometimes it would be larger, and sometimes smaller. But, as *Solomon* asserted, even though all the rivers run into them, the seas are never the greater. So also, though fountains rise in one part of the world and sink in another, and although the air moves from the warm or summer hemisphere to the cold and winter hemisphere by thinning <note>original: "attenuation"</note> caused by the active spirit of the Lord, yet the world is no larger or smaller in its existence for all that. 

Therefore, whatever winter properly operates in one hemisphere of the world, the summer hemisphere must necessarily act in the same proportion in the opposite region. For if great rains are produced in their winter beyond the Equator <note>original: "the Line"</note>, we must necessarily have a great drought in the summer on this side of the Equator. When it is hottest with us, it will be coldest with them; if it proves temperate with us, it will be so with them; just as the Sun, being at the Equinox <note>original: "Æquinoctiall"</note>, makes days and nights equally long and the season temperate for both hemispheres. 

These things being maturely considered first, I proceed to my practical conclusion. My natural observation upon this is that the air included in the weather-glass <note>An early instrument, like a thermometer, used to show the expansion and contraction of air in response to temperature.</note> is made wintry <note>original: "Hybernall"</note>, or takes on the nature of winter, by the dominance of cold. That this is so is proven by the rising or drawing up of the water; for there is such a natural tie between the air and the water that if the air contracts itself into a narrower place, the water will immediately rise up with it and toward it, because it is joined <note>original: "contiguous"</note> to the air. 

By this, therefore, it is apparent that the contracting and attracting power of the northern spirit—or rather, the divine power <note>original: "puissance"</note> which is manifested in cold—first attracts, contracts, and condenses the expanded air. Then, the air so contracted by the northern spirit draws or attracts the water from beneath upwards, and that occurs without altering the water below into anything different from the water above; so that, in conclusion, it is but one and the self-same water. 

Look here, therefore: by this demonstration, it is proved feasible and possible that water may be sucked and drawn from the caverns of the earth (which is fostered and maintained by the sea) even to the tops of high mountains. This happens by a natural means or operation, without any necessity of changing the form of the water into vapor, as *Aristotle* vainly surmises. Indeed, his theory goes against his own axiom: *It is pointless to do with more what can be done with fewer* <note>original: "Frustra fit per plura quod fieri potest per pauciora"</note>. By its expansion, it will strike down or drive out the water that the air (previously contracted by cold) had sucked or drawn up. Again, the visible sinking of the water points to and proves the invisible expansion of the air.

### Section 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

...in the earth, which continues from the *northern* region to the *southern*, so that there might be a relationship or continuity between the northern and southern waters, just as there is between the northern and southern air of the heavens. Since the wide sea **D**, which stretches from north to south, is the head from which all springs and rivers originally arise, I see no reason why it should seem strange to anyone when I say that the northern fountains are related by a continuity of substance to the southern, and the southern to the northern. 

Therefore, I conclude that when the general <note>original: "catholick"</note> northern air of the hemisphere **EFG** is cold, it sucks or contracts into itself the air in the vein <term>vein: a channel or conduit through which water flows underground</term> of the earth **A**. This air, being contracted, lifts the water out of the wide sea **D**, as is clearly demonstrated by the *weather-glass* <note>an early form of thermometer (thermoscope) that measured temperature by the expansion and contraction of air</note>. For when the cold external air has contracted the air in the head and neck of the glass by cooling it <note>original: "congelation"</note>—and I compare this head and neck to the vein in the earth, because the vein of the earth is closed and has no outlet—then the water is drawn up by the contraction of the air out of the vast water in the pot or basin, which I compare to the sea. 

On the other side, in the summer or southern hemisphere **EHG**, where the Sun is present, the general air is thinned or rarefied. This dilating air around the fountain and in the cavity of the vein beats down and lowers <note>original: "abaseth"</note> the water in the southern mouth of the vein in the earth **B**, towards **C**. Thus, in the summer, the springs are often found either completely dried up or at the very least significantly lowered. 

Now, therefore, I say that because of the lowering of the waters in the summer-like south by the thinning of the air, and the drawing of them up in the winter-like north by the cold, the water is more easily raised in the cold north. Again, the rising of the waters in the north (which were lowered the summer before) is caused by the contraction of the empty air that occupied the place in the vein of the earth during the summer. As we see in the *weather-glass*, and by the expansion of the air in the south, the water is easily hidden there within the earth. So it appears that water is partly driven and pressed down in the south by heat, and consequently drawn up with greater ease at the north, being partly elevated in the north by the cold winter. It is as if a cord were put into a hole in a large piece of timber, going down at one end and ascending at the other, like this:

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram showing a U-shaped conduit or tunnel passing through a rectangular block of material (representing the piece of timber mentioned in the text). The left end of the conduit is labeled 'A' and the right end is labeled 'B'. A rope or cord is illustrated passing through the length of the conduit.</image-desc>

If the cord is strongly pulled up from the north **A**, and as strongly pushed or pressed down from the south **B**, it will sink more easily at the south **B** and rise in the north **A**.

The exact same thing will happen, but in reverse order, when the Sun (and consequently summer) is in the northern hemisphere **EFG**. For then the springs will be lowered there and raised in the southern parts. The seas, draining or soaking into the depths <note>original: "bowells"</note> of the earth **D**, act as the common medium <note>original: "commune medium"</note> or cistern for both extremes—receiving the water pressed down and distributing that excess upward to the surging, increasing, or winter springs.

Consider the conclusion: if the central heat were greater in the summer, then vapors would be more abundant in the summer, for the larger the fire, the more smoke there will be. And again, because of the great cold in the caverns...

All of our experience teaches us that this is erroneous; and, to conclude, **Aristotle’s** assertion in this must surely be false. 

But I know it will be objected that it is obvious to the eye that standing ponds and similar humid places are dried by the summer heat. How can that be, unless it is because the Sun attracts the moisture and consumes it by converting it into vapors? 

I answer: first, that the Sun does not "draw" but only rarefies <note>original: "rarify"; to make less dense</note>, and then the rarefied substance tends to move upward. But if the Sun were to use up all the moisture of lakes and ponds in that way—namely, by converting it into air—I will tell you what absurdity would follow. It would mean that the Sun, by reducing all the waters into vapors, would thicken the air. On the contrary, our **weather-glass** <note>an early instrument for measuring temperature through the expansion and contraction of air</note> teaches us, by that model of air contained within it, that heat thins and rarefies the air rather than thickening it. 

Furthermore, a greater error would fall squarely upon **Aristotle’s** doctrine concerning the generation of clouds if this were so. For since his opinion is that a cloud is generated from vapors extracted out of the earth and water by the attractive force of the Sun and stars, it would follow that in the summertime we should have more clouds and more rain than in the winter. But this is as false as the rest. 

Instead, I say that because the air is more rare and thin in the summer—due to the presence of the divine act in the Sun, which rarefies and thins the air by its continual action—we therefore have fewer clouds in the summer. For (as I proved before) clouds are made by the compression of air. The air is then renewed by a circular course, through the resolution of those meteors <term>meteors: in this period, any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or lightning</term> it produced back into their first invisible matter, which was simply air. 

I must confess that some part of the waters are thinned <note>original: "subtiliated"</note> and, by expansion, pushed into the winter hemisphere. However, the greatest part sinks down through the invisible pores of the dry and thirsty earth, which drinks it up and keeps it in her bowels until it is sucked out by the contraction of the air, which fills the earth's pores and cracks. This contraction happens because of the cold of the following winter. For we see that even a hogshead <note>a large barrel</note> full of water will last a long time before the hot Sun will exhale it by thinning it. 

Moreover, it is certain that what the Sun rarefies in the daytime (so that it rises in a vaporous form upon the earth) commonly falls again in the nighttime as foggy mists and dew. Thus, it is simply removed from a contracted place and expanded and sprinkled in mist and dew over the wide and spacious fields. Now, that this is so is made evident because we always observe that summer mists and dew are most frequent around lakes and rivers. 

As a conclusion to this book and this whole section, I will now examine our "princely" **Peripatetic's** <note>original: "Peripateticks"; a follower of Aristotle</note> opinion regarding lightning and thunder, so that we may also see the validity of his physical doctrine in that area.

Having thus made a general inquiry into the philosophy of **Aristotle** regarding the origin of the winds, the clouds, and fountains, I cannot now help but examine his thoughts concerning the wonderful beginning or primary causes and admirable effects of lightning and thunder. In truth, these are meteors of such great marvel that they require the profoundest speculation to consider them justly as they ought to be. Therefore, I do not doubt that if a due examination is made of **Aristotle’s** validity concerning the research and discovery of so great a mystery, it will be found even more faulty than all the rest. 

Let us then observe, in the first place, what his mind is regarding the essence of lightning. **Aristotle’s** opinion is that the material cause of lightning is a hot and dry exhalation, drawn out of the earth and elevated into the middle region of the air by the power of the stars. There, it ignites partly because of a strong collision or concussion of clouds, and partly because of that *antiperistasis* <term>antiperistasis: a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when compressed by surrounding cold</term> which is had be-

<margin>Book 2. *Meteorology*</margin>
Between the heat of the exhalation and the coldness of the region, that inflammable matter so compressed <note>original: "coarcted"</note> into the belly of the cloud is set on fire. Breaking out of its prison, it tends downward because of its terrestrial and compact nature; and he concludes that the violence of this eruption is that noise which men commonly call by the name of Thunder. This, I say, is the summary of **Aristotle's** mind regarding lightning. And truly, **Aristotle** seems in some sort to be excused if he errs in this inquiry, as it is a doubt not easily resolved. Therefore, not only he, but also almost all other philosophers have been inconsistent in their resolutions touching this point, forasmuch as they have staggered and varied in this research, and have groped as it were in the dark to find its true light. 

For **Empedocles** judged the lightning to be caused by the interception or stopping of the descent of the Sun's beams. But **Anaxagoras** would have it to be a portion of the ethereal or heavenly fire which descended from above into the concavity of the cloud, within which it was afterward enclosed; he says that this light, skipping and gliding out of the clouds, is called lightning, and the effect of its breaking forth is thunder. Others believe these flashes of fire proceed from dry winds which, being surrounded, compressed, or constricted within the clouds, set those clouds on fire; thereupon comes that noise which follows—that turmoil in the clouds. And again, many others have determined it otherwise. So we may rightly say regarding this point: *As many men, so many opinions* <note>original: "Quot homines, tot sententiæ"</note>. 

And now, concerning the opinion of **Aristotle**, it is in itself so contrary and contradictory to the authority of true Wisdom that some of his learned Christian disciples have, in the open field of the Peripatetic <note>the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle</note> combat against the Truth, turned tail (as the common phrase is) and become apostates, renegades, or relinquishers of the faith they had in their master's sincerity regarding this doctrine. For we find it written thus in the *Philosophical Pearl* <note>original: "Margarita Philosophia," a famous 16th-century encyclopedia by Gregor Reisch</note> (as was said before): <margin>*Philosophical Pearl* in the chapter on lightning.</margin> *Some of the philosophers, considering the wonderful operation of lightning, have assuredly held or thought it to be not a work of nature, but the immediate effect of the most high God* <note>original: "Quidam Philoſophorum conſiderantes mirabilem fulminis operationem, ipſum non opus Naturæ ſed ſummi Dei effectum immediatum arbitrati ſunt"</note>.

But to come to the particulars of his definition: He says that the material cause of lightning is taken from the Earth; the agent in its elevation is the astral power; the external, accidental, or incidental efficient cause is the collision, concussion, or knocking together of opposite clouds because of the <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>a philosophical theory that a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more intense when trapped by cold</note> that occurs between the heat of the exhalation and the cold of the air's middle region, by which the ignition <note>original: "accension"</note> or setting on fire of the exhalation is made. And lastly, he shows the reason that lightning moves downward—namely, because its substance or matter is terrestrial and of an earthy compaction. I will therefore confute every one of these points in order, first by philosophical or natural reasons, and lastly by the authority of the Holy Scripture.

As concerning the material substance of lightning, which he says is a hot and dry exhalation and a terrestrially compacted substance derived from the earth: First, it seems to be but a fiction, because it is proved that the stars have no attractive power or force, as was proved before. Then, because if the windy exhalation—which is light and more apt to rise and penetrate due to its subtlety—is denied passage into the middle region of the air, then much more must this kind of exhalation have its passage barred or hindered into that cold place, since it is (as he confesses) grosser, more terrestrial, and apter to be inflamed.

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book 5.

...would be ascribed with such boldness by the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles to God’s essential power, and be derived from his presence? Or would the Prophet testify that *he made his angels winds, and his ministers flaming fires*? How poorly might a true seeker into divine mysteries judge the beginning of the angels and spiritual lights if their material substance were merely an "accidental exhalation"? <note>Fludd is mocking the Aristotelian idea that lightning is just a random puff of gas from the earth.</note> Again, we are taught that the heaven or air is the treasure-house from whose depths the winds, clouds, snow, hail, lightnings, and the rainbow are extracted and shaped by the Spirit of God to do his will.

<margin>Job 28:25</margin>
And therefore, as stated before: *God by his wisdom proportions the weight of the air, and hangs the clouds or waters in measure; he makes laws for the rain, and a path for the lightning of the thunders.* <note>original Latin: "Deus sapientia sua aptat pondus aeri, & appendit nubes in mensura, facit pluvia statuta & viam fulgetro tonitruum"</note> Thus it is evident that the matter of all meteors <term>any atmospheric phenomenon</term>, whether watery or fiery, is carved by the word or wisdom of God out of the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> air. Consequently, they do not come out of the earth, nor is there any need for the "attraction of the stars" in this business. The pure matter of lightning is always within the divine power and reserved in his secret treasure-house, to be called or chosen at his will—he who created all things to work how and in whatever way he pleases. For would it not, I ask you, be a wondrous thing if such a great quantity of exhalations could be drawn out of the earth in an instant and raised by the stars to suddenly and unexpectedly rain down fire and brimstone on Sodom and Gomorrah? Our Aristotelians will say, according to their custom, that it was "miraculous." I answer that, despite that, the meteor was material, for it was fire and brimstone. Now I would dearly like to know from them: from what magazine or storehouse did it come? Did the stars draw it up from the earth, or did God not collect it immediately out of his own airy or invisible treasury? For Saint Paul says that all visible things were first made of things that were not seen.

Secondly, regarding the agent <term>the force causing the action</term>, Aristotle is even more deceived than he is regarding the matter. First, he claims the agent which draws up the exhalation is the attractive power of the stars; then he surmises that the efficient cause which ignites it must be partly the clashing together of two clouds, and partly the conflict between the heat of the exhalation and the coldness of the place, which together cause the exhalation to ignite. Good God, what a "Gallimaufry" <term>a confused jumble or medley</term> he would make! What a confusion of external actions or efficient causes he invents, when there is only one indeed—the most internal or essential one—which moves whichever way it desires and operates all in all. Are these superficial, accidental, and external agents really the primary movers and life-givers of the bright lightnings? And yet it is said that God animates and brings them to life with his presence. What can we Christians think of the Aristotelian doctrine, when it would pretend the immediate act of God in his prime angelic creatures is something as poor and mean as the accidental rising of fumes caused by stars, or the clashing of clouds happening by chance, or a conflict between heat and cold?

Truly, it was no marvel if, when his invention failed in the research of such a high mystery, Aristotle was forced to such weak shifts that are scarcely believable to wise men. For we behold the admirable effects of lightning: how it pierces the scabbard without hurting it and melts the sword; how it enters the purse and liquefies the money; how it even pierces the barrel or hogshead and consumes the wine without the vessel being altered. Yes, and what is more, it has understanding and reason to punish wicked mockers of this wondrous work of God, possessing an angelic reason to correct the presumptuous. We cannot but say of Aristotle that he is only imbued with the wisdom of this world, and not with that which is from God, seeing as he foolishly imagines that lightnings do not have an internal principle and a most essential agent which makes them work and move at will wherever they please—even as the wind is said to *blow where it wishes.* <note>original Latin: "spirare ubi vult"</note>

There was also a promising young scholar, a great follower of *Aristotle* and a debater in the schools—a man (as it would seem) more confident in *Aristotle's* doctrine than in the teachings of Holy Scripture. Sect. 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

In and upon the Cherubim, by the winds, He lifted water and rain out of the clouds and set them on fire by sending forth lightnings from His throne. In conclusion, though He uses many instruments <note>original: "Organs"</note>, the essential act that operates in and through them all comes from one simple and pure identity. This identity contains all things within itself, just as unity in arithmetic is surely considered the father of all numbers. 

Thus we see that the young man mentioned before was lost because he relied too much on the empty and deceptive <note>original: "prestigious," meaning illusory or misleading</note> doctrine of his Aristotelian <note>original: "Peripateticall"</note> master. For he taught his honest Christian companions the false doctrine of his pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> master during their greatest need—specifically, when the angry hand of the Almighty was in the heavens ready to threaten them if they did not call out for grace from Him. God spoke out of the clouds in time and wished them to cast away all fear, but the young man made them believe that the lightnings were random <note>original: "contingent"</note> things in nature, occurring as if by chance and not endowed with sense or reason, as they were shaped and directed by external and superficial principles. 

He and his companions should have remembered that saying, so often repeated by the Wise Man: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom* <note>original Latin: "Timor Domini est principium Sapientiæ"</note>. If he and the others had acknowledged that it was God who spoke in the thunder, surrounded by His powerful angels, they would not have been so careless. They would have prayed to Him heartily and utterly forgotten Aristotle’s concept of an independent acting nature, considering that God is the only Nature-creating Nature <note>original: "Naturating Nature of Natures," likely referring to the theological concept of *Natura Naturans*</note> of all things. 

I could tell you many other wonderful stories within my knowledge, but I will only insist upon these two. About five or six years ago, there was a daughter of a man named Piper from Colnbrook <note>original: "Colebrook"</note>. She was gleaning corn after the harvest was carried, accompanied by her mother and another young woman newly married to a glover in Colnbrook (who had been my servant). There was also another daughter of the same Goodwife Piper. 

A storm approached while they were in the field. The elder daughter—who, by their report, had been very disobedient to her parents and would often fearfully curse her mother—saw the lightning flashing around her and cried out, "A plague on <note>original: "Fy upon"</note> these lightnings, I cannot endure them; I will go home!" When the company urged her to call on God, she would not. Instead, they hurried to a high oak tree standing near a park fence <note>original: "Park-pale"</note>. She leaned her back against the trunk and said, laughing, that she was not afraid now. "For," she said, "I am as safe as in my mother’s parlor." 

The newly married woman, who had been my maid, sat down and leaned her elbow on her knee. The sister sat a little closer to the fence, the mother stood under another tree nearby, and in a dry ditch under the oak, another girl took shelter. But despite all their imaginary safety, they could not escape the wrath of God. The lightning fell on the very top of that oak, and the bolt plowed a furrow all the way down the tree without stopping. It struck the eldest daughter—who thought she was so safe—and killed her instantly. It also temporarily paralyzed the arm of the newly married woman who was leaning on the knee of the girl who was killed. The girl in the ditch was stunned as if she were dead. The sister sitting nearer the fence saw a globe of fire descend the tree and felt as hot as if she were in a furnace, but suffered no other harm. The mother under the next tree, having her foot stretched out toward the tree where her daughter sat, was struck lame in that foot. 

The newly married woman was struck in such a way that, in a state of distraction, she ran up the lane crying out, "Lord, open your holy heavens! Lord, open your holy heavens!" At last, they were all carried with the dead girl in a cart from the village to the town of Colnbrook, where the others recovered within a few days. 

I saw the place immediately after this and spoke to the newly married woman, my former servant. These things were confirmed to me at her own house, where her husband also told me of a wondrous thing that happened to him in the meantime. Being very concerned for his new wife, he saw the storm and put on his new cloak, took his old one under his arm, and went out into the tempest to meet her. As he went through a field, great flakes of fire passed by him, whose fronts were blunt and whose backs were shaped like fire-dragons <note>original: "fire-drakes," a term for fireballs or meteors</note>. Suddenly, as if by a great gust of wind, they blew his hat off his head. When he followed it and stooped to pick it up, he found a piece of the new cloak he was wearing had been so skillfully <note>original: "artificially"</note> cut out in such a neat triangular form that he marveled at it.
