The second story is this. During the time of the Great Plague <note>original: "great sickness time"</note>, I returned from *Wales* and stayed for a while with my noble friend, the Lord Bishop of *Worcester* at *Hartlebury Castle*. There, I was informed of a strange misfortune caused by lightning and thunder about five weeks before my arrival, some three or four miles from the castle. I felt compelled to go see the place, and in the company of my worthy friends Mr. *Finch* and Sir *Thomas Thornborow*, I viewed the site. It was under a tall and wide-spreading elm tree upon a little hill. The local inhabitants who lived nearby related that two sons of wealthy farmers <note>original: "yeomens sons"</note> were passing by with a load of hay drawn by four oxen and two horses, driven by a servant of one of their fathers. As the thunderstorm overtook them, the driver went up the hill and placed the load and the animals under the elm. He crouched under the load of hay, while the two youths sat upon a bench or turf seat built around the tree. At last, there came a fearful stroke of thunder, at which the laborer stooping under the cart said, "Good Lord, what a crack that was!" At these words, the boys laughed out loud and, mocking him, repeated, "A crack!" But immediately a noise was heard in the upper branches of the tree, and a solid matter all on fire came down directly between the boys. It struck the hair of one of them into the tree and set the other so intensely on fire that the man under the cart and others were forced to run down the hill to fetch water to quench it. When the fire was out, his skin was as hard as roasted pork. Thus they paid dearly for their mockery and contempt of God's judgments, when they truly ought to have prayed to God to preserve them from the agents <note>original: "ministers"</note> of His wrath. It is a dangerous thing to sport with and laugh at the Saints <note>In this context, Fludd likely means holy things, divine power, or God's messengers</note>. There is the Thunderer from above who has messengers able to avenge His cause in the twinkling of an eye, if He but nods to them.

I know that some Aristotelian philosopher <note>original: "Peripatetick"</note> will reply that it is only meant metaphorically when the Scriptures say that God speaks in thunder, and it is not to be understood literally. If that were true, then the plainest phrases in Scripture—such as those regarding clouds, snow, hail, and so on—must also be understood that way. Therefore, it was either a real speech or not real; and if it were not real, it would lead me toward error rather than truth. But Scripture is full of this kind of language, and therefore the whole harmony of Holy Writ interprets it as being real. Again, others acknowledge the speech is real, but they say that when God speaks in thunder, that act is miraculous and not natural. To this I answer with the words of the patient *Job*, saying:

<margin>Job 37:11</margin>

> *For the purpose of watering the earth, God burdens the thick clouds, and He scatters the light of His clouds.* <note>original: "Pro irrigatione fatigat Deus densam nubem, & dispergit lucem nubis suæ"</note>

By this, it appears that God ordinarily gathers the clouds together and makes them His mechanical instruments to utter His voice to mortal men, for the flourishing of the annual fruits upon the earth. And therefore He says this in another place:

<margin>Job 36:28–31</margin>

> *If a man should consider the spreading out of the thick clouds and the thunderous crashes in His tabernacle, He spreads His light over it; by these things He shall judge the people and give food in abundance.* <note>original: "Si consideraret homo extensiones densarum nubium, fragores in tugurio illius extendit super illud lucem suam, cum his judicaturus est populum & daturus cibum abunde."</note>

<margin>Ecclus. 43:11–17</margin>

Regarding the last clause of his definition, wherein he seems to assert that lightning moves downward because its substance is of a terrestrial, compacted nature: I answer that this reason is far too weak, considering the "giant" author <note>The author is being sarcastic about Aristotle's reputation</note> who alleged it. ### CHAPTER XII.

->*How lightning and thunder ought rightly to be described by the true Philosopher, and that seriously, according to the tenor of Holy Writ.*<-

Since, therefore, it has been made manifest in the preceding chapter that *Aristotle* has utterly erred in his conceit <note>term: notion or theory</note> regarding the material, essential, and formal causes of lightning, let me gather—as near as my weak capacity will allow—what should be the true nature and original essential cause of lightning, according to the harmonious consent of the Holy Scriptures.

> Lightning is a certain fiery air or spirit, animated by the brightness of JEHOVAH, and extracted out of his treasury (which is the heavens, or the universal air) to do and execute his will, for the good or the harm of his creatures.

Or else in this manner:
> Lightning is a shining brightness proceeding out of the clouds (being the pavilion of JEHOVAH) and is sent from the throne of God even down to the earth, covering the surface of the seas.

But if we would describe lightning with all its attributes, and consequently express the whole essence of thunder (which is of a mixed nature), we may do it thus, based on the testimony of the Holy Bible:
> Lightning is a fire burning from the face or presence of JEHOVAH, at the sight or contact of whose brightness the clouds pass away; and the Almighty thunders and utters his voice from heaven, and sends forth his arrows for the destruction of the wicked.

Or thus:
> Lightning is a fire proceeding from JEHOVAH, being sent out of his dark tabernacle from above; at the sight of which the waters or clouds, as if terrified, and the abyss, as if troubled, hasten away. In this turmoil, the voice of his thunder moves circularly, and the fiery or kindled coals are sent forth like arrows from a well-bent bow, to effect his will, both for blessing and for vengeance, in heaven and on earth.

Or in this way:
> Lightning or flashing <note>original: coruscation</note> is a clear and pure light in the clouds above, which the wind that passes by purifies, etc.

By the first of these descriptions, the manifest material cause of lightning is expressed to be a fiery air; the place out of which it is drawn is the storehouse of God, or the heavens. Also, the formal cause is expressed in that it is described as a fiery spirit or air. The efficient cause, I said (according to the testimony of truth), is the will or word of God, on which depends that spirit of wisdom by which God operates all things. Lastly, the final cause <note>term: the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing</note> is also noted, because it is said that it was created to do the will of him who ordained it, either for the pain or pleasure of mortal men. All of this is evidently confirmed by the passages of Scripture mentioned before.

<margin>Revelation 4</margin>
The second definition is confirmed by the Book of Revelation, which says, *Lightnings* <note>original: Fulgura</note>

> Thunder is a noise made in the cloudy tent or pavilion of JEHOVAH, over which he extends the beams of his Light, covering the surface of the Sea and illuminating the earth, so that he may judge the people and give them food abundantly.

Therefore, it is manifest by this that God appears in Thunder as much for the effecting of things that are natural and necessary—both for the punishment and nourishment of his creatures—as he does for miraculous purposes.

To conclude, it is most apparent by what has already been said that the opinion of the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who sought to explain natural phenomena through physical causes rather than divine ones.</note>—both Christian and <term>pagan</term> <note>original: "Ethnick"</note>—is very thoughtless and erroneous. They claim that lightnings are "hot and dry exhalations" drawn out of the earth and lifted high into the middle region of the air by the sun's attraction. They believe that these exhalations, being trapped in a cloud and ignited—partly by clouds knocking together and partly by the coldness of the atmosphere—cause thunder by the eruption of their flames. I would have every wise Christian observe carefully whether the mystery of a tempest and whirlwind consists of such a small and insignificant thing as Aristotle would make us believe; or, if it instead arises from a far more profound and unsearchable abyss. For Truth itself reports that lightnings are the fiery lights of God that proceed from his throne, and thunders are justly termed the voice, word, and eloquence of Jehovah. 

For this reason, Jehovah—reproving the boldness of these worldly philosophers who presume to judge his unsearchable actions or dive into the depth of his mysteries regarding the essential causes of these <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and lightning, not just space rocks.</note> without the warrant and assistance of God's Spirit—seems to speak these words to them. He rebukes those who falsely make the world believe that his hidden and secret acts are the result of their vain imaginations (which vanish in the end and come to nothing, because they are grounded on nothing but foolish and self-centered fantasies):

<margin>Job 38</margin>
*Listen with your ears and consider the marvelous works of the strong God. Do you know when God disposes of them, when the light of his cloud shines forth? Do you understand the wonders of God, who is perfect in knowledge, regarding the balancing and weighing of the thick clouds? Which is the way the lightnings flash out, being divided into parts? From whose womb does the ice come, or who has fathered the frost of heaven? Which is the way that leads to the home of light, and where is the place of darkness?* <note>original Latin: "Auribus percipite, & considerate mirabilia Dei fortis. ### CHAP. XIII.

->*A conclusion of this work, including an admonition to all good Christians to beware of pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy and to stick and cleave fast to that which is taught to us by the Scriptures, for the reasons set down here.*<-

Let it now be permitted for me, in concluding this section—O you Europeans, who seem to spend your days so seriously and zealously in the Christian religion—to turn the sharp edge of my pen and the rougher file of my speech toward you. You, being far too seduced by the false doctrine of Aristotle, think and imagine the meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, thunder, and lightning.</note>—but especially lightning and thunder—to be a common natural thing of little or no value at all, as being produced only by nature due to a hot imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note> of the air. 

I would request you, as a true Christian ought to do for his brethren, to observe well and attend with diligence this admonition which I will give you as a farewell. I besee the you not to scorn or reject my previous assertion, which has told and sufficiently proved to you that lightnings and thunders—and indeed all other meteors—are the immediate works of God's hand. By this endeavor of mine, you may not only bring comfort and consolation to your souls when you hear the terrible voice of the Lord—making you remember your past sins and iniquities and heartily pray for his pardon, rather than having him hold your offenses against you in his anger—but <margin>Job 37.</margin> also give the honor and glory to him who, thundering from above, works marvelously.

I would have you know, therefore, that the worldly-wise men of this Christian world of ours—who are, as it were, pages or followers of the pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers—have hitherto blindly, or like lunatic persons, erred in their imaginations. Because they are instructed in the blind wisdom of this world by their pagan tutors and doctors, they will not be brought to believe that God works all things in heaven and earth immediately <note>meaning "directly," without an intermediate physical cause</note> only by his word. Instead, they believe he works mediately—namely, through other necessary natural or supernatural means as essential efficient causes—even though the Holy Text instructs us in plain terms that it is one and the same essence which acts and operates all in all by his word, using each creature only as his organ or instrument in which and by which he moves and works his will. 

Is not this tenet or assertion of theirs (I ask you) completely opposite and contradictory to the divine authority, which says <margin>1 Cor. 8. 5.</margin>, "*Though there be those who are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth (as there be many gods and many lords), yet for us there is but one God, that Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. But every man has not that knowledge*," etc.? From these words, we may gather that although we worldlings attribute this or that work to angels, or stars, or winds, or a created nature according to the doctrine of pagan wisdom, yet such true...

# Sect. 1. Mosaical Philosophy.

In their mouths and writings, the lying and false spirit of *Aristotle* has taken too deep a root or possession, claiming for itself the primary and superior place. Therefore, although my warning may seem wild, ridiculous, and of little or no value to those who are wedded to their own will and blinded <note>original: "hood-winked"</note> by *Aristotle’s* subtle teachings, I would have them know that it is a matter of great importance and high consequence, as it concerns and touches the honor of God. 

For through this knowledge, true Christians may fundamentally know and understand the real and essential causes of storms <note>original: "tempests"</note> and other natural events and operations. They will thereby perceive that these things do not happen by chance <note>original: "case fortuit"</note>, nor do they operate by any power of their own, as the imaginative pagans <note>original: "phantastick Ethnicks"</note> have invented or imagined in their writings. Instead, these events are brought forth <note>original: "traduced"</note> out of the holy treasuries by Divine Providence. They are sent down here below by the operation of the Word and the execution of his angelic ministers, either to afflict and punish <note>original: "scourge"</note> the wicked for their offenses, or to remind them of their sins so that, through the fear of these events, they may be driven to repent. 

So it is that when they, to their terror, hear the voice of the Lord in thunder from above and behold the fiery flashes of his wrath and indignation, or see the dreadful floods <note>original: "inundations"</note> caused by an abundance of snow or rain, they might be moved to repentance. They may be humbled and incited to call upon their Creator for aid, praying to him heartily to turn away all dangers from them, to calm his storms, and to pacify the fury of his fiery or watery ministers. They should ask him to grant them milder and more favorable weather, with gentle and fertile rains, and to bless and save the crops of their lands, as well as to preserve their cattle which feed upon them, their houses, and other such necessary belongings <note>original: "additaments"</note> from the violence of his tempestuous angels or spiritual instruments. 

Conversely, whoever neglects this doctrine—which is founded on true wisdom—and wallows like a sow in the mire, choosing instead the rules of that worldly wisdom which is mere foolishness before God, will consequently imagine all these meteorological <note>original: "Meteorologicall"</note> marvels to proceed by chance and accident, without the action of any internal spiritual principle. For that reason, they will neglect them, esteeming them only as "natural" things. Therefore, they will neither dread them, as they indeed ought to do, nor yet acknowledge him who is their true author and the immediate actor within them. Such a person is justly numbered among those men at whom the Wise Man aims in this speech: <margin>*Wisdom 13.*</margin> *“All men,” says Solomon, “are vain by nature who are ignorant of God, and who cannot understand him through the things that are made, nor recognize the workman by considering his works.”*

## The Epilogue to this Section.

Thus, wise and Christian reader, you have understood the main difference between the wisdom of this world—which the Apostle affirms is but mere foolishness before God—and that which descends from above and issues from the Father of Light, which is the essential and true Spirit of Wisdom <note>original: "Sapience"</note> or Instruction <note>original: "Discipline"</note>. 

Consequently, you may easily discern how pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy, which is grounded upon worldly wisdom, is but a vain fallacy or a deceptive invention <note>original: "prestigious Figment"</note>. This is because it relies only on the traditions of men and the basic elements of this world. Therefore, only the philosophy of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles is truly <note>original: "mely," likely a printer's error for "truly" or "purely"</note> real and essential, for it is founded upon the Universal <note>original: "Catholick"</note> Christ, or the Eternal Spirit of God, in whom the fullness <note>original: "plenitude"</note> of Divinity resides. And therefore I may boldly conclude, and speak to you, as I would to other Christians, in the language of Moses, saying:

<margin>Deuteronomy 30:19</margin>

> I call Heaven and Earth to witness this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, good and evil, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live <note>original Latin: "Contestor hodie contra vos Cœlum & Terram, me vitam & mortem, bonum & malum, benedictionem & maledictionem, præposuisse tibi. Quare elige vitam, ut tu cum semine tuo vivas."</note>, and increase in the knowledge and understanding of God. For in true Wisdom consists all true philosophy, certain science, and complete instruction.

# TREATISE.

## The First Book.

### The Argument of the First Book.

<margin><insert>S e 45</insert></margin>
After the Author had understood through diligent inquiry that all **Sympathy** <note>natural attraction or affinity</note> and **Antipathy** <note>natural repulsion or discord</note> sprang immediately from certain different passions of the Soul, or the life-giving spirit—one being **Concupiscible** <note>desiring or seeking toward</note> and the other **Irascible** <note>rejecting or prone to anger</note>—and yet perceived these effects to exist in vegetable and mineral creatures as well as in animals, he was seized by a special desire to find their radical cause or beginning. 

When he had well pondered and considered that eternal **Unity** (which is the head and root of all things) in its simple and absolute nature, he could discern no such diversity in its essence, seeing that it exists forever as only one and the same Identity. For, according to Holy Writ, *As his darkness is, so is his light* <note>original Latin: Sicut tenebræ ejus, ita & lux ejus</note>. <margin>Psalm 139:12 <note>The original text cites Psalm 138:11 following an older numbering system.</note></margin> 

Therefore, he gathered that a dual effect or principle, completely opposite to one another in condition and disposition, must necessarily spring and arise from these two distinct properties within that one entire essence: namely, **Nolunty** <note>the act of "not-willing" or divine withdrawal</note> and **Volunty** <note>the act of willing or divine expression</note>. The first was expressed by darkness, and the other by light. 

For when this mental Eternity and infinite Light—in whom in truth there is no darkness—wills not, it reserves itself within itself; that is, it reflects <insert><note>The following phrase is underlined in ink</note>its beams into itself</insert>, and so gives form to nothing by its presence. Instead, it leaves the universal **Abyss** or **Chaos** (which is said in this state to dwell and exist in the divine power) dark, deformed, quite void, and destitute of its life-giving act or resplendent brightness. This negative action is the perfect character of his **Nolunty**, the general effects of which are darkness and privation. 

But when this hidden unity sends out the kind and healing brightness of its essence (which is the expression of his **Volunty** or will) into the deformed **Chaos**, then deformity, darkness, and privation are forced to give way to their opposite rivals: Conformity, Light, and Position <note>actual existence or presence</note>, which are the affirmative acts of life and essential existence. 

By this object of his contemplation, he gathered that the act of **Volunty** and that of **Nolunty** were within one essential Unity, which was all goodness. Consequently, **Nolunty** in it is nothing else but its **Volunty**; for since the Unity is one and all, so also is its **Volunty** but one Identity within it, and yet all and over all with it. By this, it acts or works its pleasure, both privatively <note>by taking away</note> and positively, as much in the heavenly virtues as in the inhabitants of the earth. <margin>Daniel 4:35</margin> And therefore darkness and light are all one in this **Archetypal Unity** <note>the original divine model of the universe</note>, because all...

<summary>The author argues that the opposing forces of sympathy and antipathy in nature originate from a single divine source, which manifests through the dual acts of "willing" (light/creation) and "not-willing" (darkness/privation).</summary>
<keywords>metaphysics, divine will, Volunty, Nolunty, Chaos, light and darkness, Archetypal Unity, Sympathy, Antipathy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument that while God is a singular unity, the created world manifests through two opposing principles: light (Volunty) and darkness (Nolunty).</meta>

...everything in it is good, because it is truly and absolutely good in itself. As for the contrary effects—namely, the deformed and privative <note>original: privative; meaning characterized by the absence or lack of something</note> darkness of the crude chaos, or unorganized abyss, and the informing <note>the act of giving form to matter</note> act or positive emanation of light—they indeed appear as such to creatures. They seem to produce an infinity of contraries in this world, which mortals judge to be either good or evil, according to the effects they experience. 

However, it seems most apparent to the Author that these two contrary outflows or extensions, which effectively proceed from one eternal essence, were the principles of all things. The dark Chaos produced the waters from her womb <margin>2 Peter 3</margin>, which was the only matter from which the world, and consequently the heavens and earth, were made. And the life-giving emanation or radiance of the eternal light bestowed form, shape, virtue, and motion upon it. 

When the Author had discovered all of this and seriously pondered it, his reason clearly informed him that the world was compacted and framed of contrary stuff. For how is it possible that opposite and discordant parents should bring forth children who do not disagree in condition from their kind? And yet, such was the will of the Creator that these two dissonant accords should, in the beginning and shaping of an Image like Himself, be united into one Unison or unity by the inviolable tie of His never-dying Spirit of love and concord. This was done so that the matter (which is the substance of the dark waters) might serve as a female to the formal and masculine radiance, or illuminating spirit, which issued from Him. Thus, He made from that duality—or confusion of unities—a typical <note>symbolic or representative of a type</note> Trinity in Unity, modeled after the similitude of the Archetype. This Archetype, being purely spiritual, was the eternal life and formal being of the world (remaining itself without any beginning). For that cause, the world being its image must also have a universal <note>original: catholick</note> life or soul by which it may act and live, according to the pattern from which the form of its essence and the matter of its existence flowed. 

For that reason, it must be endowed with the opposite properties of willing and nilling—or **Volunty** and **Nolunty**—and, by consequence, of lovable attraction or hateful expulsion. Therefore, the Author observed that both the internal and external type, or typical world, must necessarily be subject to contrary passions and alterations proceeding from similar properties. Sometimes it is apt to incline toward the disposition of darkness, following by a natural instinct the condition and inclination of matter or water, which was the offspring of the dark Abyss or Chaos over which the divine power has dominion. In this condition, it takes on the character of the Unity's **Nolunty**. At other times, it affects and imitates the action and property of light, which flows from the eternal and all-acting fountain of unity. This is the virtuous effect of the sacred **Volunty**. 

It seemed to the Author that because the whole world was composed of these two contrary properties—namely, formal light and the moist dark matter—it must follow that the universal soul (or general life-giving spirit) and every particular essence (which is derived from that universal soul just as beams come from the Sun) must be subject to opposite passions and alterations. 

From this, therefore, springs that original love or hatred known to exist between the good Angels and the evil Spirits. From this issue all those constant mutations and alterations that happen in the ethereal and sublunary <note>the region below the moon; the earthly realm</note> heavens—namely, by reason of the cross-variety of the starry influence. From this proceed those oppositions and contrary effects that are breathed forth from the winds. From this are derived the discord and concord of the Elements, along with the diversity of natures in meteorological impressions. From this flow the multiplicity of affections, the opposition of dispositions, the passion of spirits, and, in a word, the **sympathy** and **antipathy** observed between all creatures, whether simple or compound, be they animal, vegetable, or mineral.

Sect. 2. Mosaic Philosophy. 131

The Author therefore concludes upon these grounds that it is only just and reasonable to agree with the opinions of the two notable and famous Philosophers, Heraclitus and Empedocles, regarding this point. The first, Heraclitus, presented it as an infallible maxim: *That all things are made and composed of strife and friendship* <note>original: "Quod omnia fiant per litem & amicitiam"</note>—that is to say, of hatred and love. The second, Empedocles, pronounced it as an oracle of truth: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 42:25.</margin> <margin>But Evil is a defect or deprivation of Good, just as darkness is the absence of Light.</margin> *That the soul is composed of four elements, and of peace or concord, and contention or discord* <note>original: "Quod ex quatuor elementis, & ex amicitia & lite composita sit anima"</note>. By this, he meant that contrary disposition which exists between the watery spirit and the bright mental beam in regard to their origin. 

By using the word *strife* <note>original: "litem"</note>, he argues for both spiritual and physical contention. This refers to the opposing power and ability found between formal light and dark matter. It applies both to the body during the act of decay (when the soul seeks to part from it) and to the "irascible passion" <note>The "irascible" part of the soul was thought to be responsible for anger, courage, and the drive to overcome obstacles</note> of the soul, in which the spirit labors and suffers unnaturally. In these opinions, the aforementioned philosophers do not seem to differ from the Son of Sirach <note>The author of the biblical book of Ecclesiasticus</note>, who says:

> All things are double, one against another, and he has made nothing imperfect <note>original: "Gemina sunt omnia, quorum alterum est contrarium alteri, nec quicquam factum est quod mancum sit"</note>.

### CHAP. I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' containing a landscape with a path winding through foliage and a prominent tree in the background.</image-desc>No man, no matter how highly advanced in the sphere of mathematical perfection or how deeply he has dived into the mystical depths of complex arithmetic, can—with the sharp vision of his most mature understanding—discern anything that can justly claim for itself a place or rank before Unity (the number one). For this reason, the wisest philosophers candidly confess that Unity is the only principle or root of all number and multitude. 

Likewise, every person of judgment ought to acknowledge that this fundamental Oneness <note>original: "radical Identity"</note>, when considered in its pure and absolute nature, cannot be limited by any size or measurement. It cannot be contained by any part, divided into distinct portions, nor defined by any substantial <term>quiddity</term> <note>the inherent nature or "whatness" of a thing</note> or entity. 

Based on this, wise men have judiciously concluded that Unity is the most ancient and fundamental principle of all others. It encompasses within itself all substances, quantities, and qualities. This is much like how the geometric point, when considered in its naked simplicity, is observed to be indivisible and scarcely perceptible—indeed, it is almost impossible to define. And yet, the point is clearly known to be the certain beginning not only of every geometric line but also of all other continuous mathematical dimensions. It encompasses all magnitudes and is not encompassed by any.

Since these two principles of all dimensions precede and excel all others in order, rank, and antiquity, expert mathematicians used them as a symbolic imitation or image of the most internal, central, and hidden point of Divinity—that most divine and brightest Unity. This Unity remained in that very state in which it stood before the creation of the world: specifically, when it kept itself within itself and remained hidden from all potential creatures. Afterward, God was pleased to enact and make these creatures manifest by revealing Himself, or by the sending out of His life-giving light, so that He might dwell in His simple and absolute nature of Unity, without regard for the things He would create. In this manner of the Unity's being and existence, it could...

# Mosaical Philosophy. Book I.

...should not be regarded as God, because up to that point He had not produced any creature by which He might be adored or acknowledged as God. Neither could He rightly be styled or termed a Father, for He did not appear to have conceived of any Son or offspring—whether archetypal <note>The original blueprint or idea</note> and ideal, or typical and worldly. Nor could He be considered the *highest good* <note>original: "Summum bonum"</note>, since the deformed matter, or dark Chaos—or rather *Hyle* <note>A Greek philosophical term for primordial matter</note>—had not yet tasted His bright and all-activating blessing. This blessing was concealed and hidden in its potential darkness and obscurity, and was therefore devoid of all form. Neither could He be called beautiful, since He had not yet shared His beauty for the decoration or activation of any creature. 

Nor could He rightly be said to be eternity. In this state of being hidden within Himself, He seemed to human understanding not to exist at all, and consequently to have no connection or interaction with eternity, everlastingness <note>original: "æviality"</note>, or time. Moreover, He could not claim the name of "principle" <note>In the sense of a beginning or source</note>, because He had no relation yet to anything that sprang or issued from a beginning. 

To conclude: the nature of this simple, unified <note>original: "Monadicall"</note> existence before everything was created was so hidden and obscure to mortal apprehension, and so unknown in its order and antiquity—indeed, so inscrutable and incomprehensible in its essence—that it could not be defined as substance, quantity, or quality. It was rather conceived to be a certain transcendent entity or existence, reserved only within itself and consisting of itself. He had no foundational root or beginning to spring from, but existed only from and by Himself. In His divine power <note>original: "Puissance"</note>—as in a place without end or limits—all things that are now clearly visible were then enfolded <note>original: "complictly"</note>, although to our limited understanding they were regarded as nothing. 

For this reason, those learned in the laws of true wisdom have recorded in their everlasting registers that this mystical infinity—when it was thus wrapped in the gloomy tangle or profound abyss of darkness, remaining as if vacant or resting within itself without any action (or, as they say, having no regard for anything)—was termed in Hebrew **אין** <note>Ayin: literally "nothing" or "naught"</note>. This means 
<margin>Reuchlin, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*, Book 3.</margin> 
"Nothing," "Without End," or "Non-Being" <note>original: "Nihil, Non finis, Non Ens"</note>; in plain English, it is "nothing at all" to our imagination. This is because the weakness and poverty of man’s capacity and intellect <note>original: "ingeny"</note> regarding divine things is such that we are accustomed to judge that something does not exist at all if it does not appear clearly to our sight. 

For this reason, the wisest practitioners of the abstruse and hidden Kabbalah <note>original: "Caball"</note> have termed this original Unity, in His secret state, the *dark Aleph* <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"</note>. The Hebrew letter Aleph is recognized among the Jews and Kabbalistic Rabbis as the symbol for the number one; consequently, it is taken hieroglyphically to represent God. He is understood to be that absolute Monad or Unity which was only in itself and remained resting in itself, without any act of emanation <note>The flowing out of divine light into the world</note>—which He afterward used when He was pleased to work through Creation. Therefore, the wise philosopher Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many mystical texts were attributed</note> (not disagreeing with Holy Scripture) says: "The One, before the beginning of the world, shone for itself and not for others" <note>original: "Monas ante mundi exordium sibi ipsi & non aliis reluxit"</note>. Unity 
<margin>*Pymander*, Book 12 and Book 3.</margin> 
or Identity shone only to itself and in itself, and not to anything else. And in another place: "There was an infinite shadow in the abyss, and moreover water and a thin intellectual spirit were within the Chaos through divine power" <note>original: "Erat umbra infinita in abysso, aqua insuper, & Spiritus tenuis intellectualis per divinam potentiam in Chaos inerant"</note>. There was an infinite shadow upon the face of the abyss, and furthermore, water and a delicate intellectual spirit were in the Chaos through divine power. 

And Moses confirms the saying of that wise philosopher: "Darkness was upon the face of the abyss" <note>original: "Tenebrae erant super faciem abyssi"</note>. By this, wise men may discern 
<margin>John 1.</margin> 
and contemplate, though from afar, what the divine power <note>original: "Potentia"</note> was before any creature explicitly appeared out of the darkness. They may also easily understand the true principle and foundation of darkness: namely, the enclosing or retaining of the actual beams or light of immortal life and being within this bright, fundamental unity, in which there is no darkness. Thus, original darkness can be considered nothing else but the absence of the fundamental Unity’s bright emanation, which is the fountain of all action. Neither can that divine, life-giving 
<margin>Genesis 1.</margin> 
and creating Light be present when the will of that simple and absolute Essence in Unity is not minded to send forth the treasure of its shaping <note>original: "informing"</note> beams into the void <note>original: "deformity"</note>. 

It follows of necessity that darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and that the earth was void and without form, before the Divine Essence shone forth. Darkness was made the tabernacle of rest and repose because, where the divine act or sacred emanation is absent, all things are only potential. Consequently, they exist without actual truth, being, as it were, completely dead.

# Section 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

...dead, and without life or motion; and the property of coldness and dullness <note>original: "stupidity," here meaning a lack of sensation, motion, or life</note> had dominion during that state of privation. This is because heat is produced by motion alone, and motion has its beginning from Light, and all brightness flows from this Unity, which is termed the Father and Fountain of all Light. 

Therefore, it follows that if this Divine Essence keeps itself within itself, then the dark Chaos reserved only in the Divine Power <note>original: "Potentia Divina"</note> must be deprived of motion. It is inclined to thickening <note>original: "inspissation"</note> and condensation because of its congealing and cold property, which thickens and makes things gross through contraction. It is the fountain of all privation and an enemy to the life and being of creatures, because it is contrary to action, motion, and heat, which are the servants of the Divine emanation. Consequently, it is the fountain of death, deformity, and non-existence. 

In conclusion, just as Light is the source of life, status, action, motion, and—in a word—of the Will <note>original: "Volunty"</note> of God in His revealed Nature, so too is this primordial darkness the source and well-spring of death, privation, rest, or vacancy. In brief, it is the source of the Divine essence’s Unwillingness <note>original: "Nolunty," referring to God's act of withdrawing or withholding His light</note>. 

On this point, the Scriptures justify that when God sends forth His health-giving beams and manifests the light of His countenance to His creatures, <margin>Psalm 104:29.</margin> *they are refreshed with goodness and life; when He partially hides His face and withdraws His lively and life-giving beams from them, they grow sick and their spirits are troubled; but if He totally withdraws His aspect of life from them, they immediately expire and breathe their last.* 

Regarding this, Moses also says: <margin>Deuteronomy 31:17.</margin> *"God forsakes the wicked and hides His face from them, so that many evils may come upon them"* <note>original: "Deus malos relinquit, & abscondit faciem suam ab iis ut obveniant iis mala multa"</note>. <margin>Psalm 13:1.</margin> And David says: *"How long will You hide Your face from me? Gladden me with Your countenance; Your visitation preserves my spirit," etc.* <note>original: "Quousque abscondis vultum tuum a me? Exhilara me vultu tuo: visitatio tua conservat Spiritum meum"</note>. 

By this, it appears that this Divine Essence observes both the action of His Unwillingness <note>original: "Nolunty"</note> and His Will <note>original: "Volunty"</note>, both after His creation of the world and before it. In the first case, He withdraws or withholds that virtue of life from the creature, which is the act of privation; in the latter, He gives life and preservation to it. For by this expanding property, He created the world and all things within it.

<margin>45</margin> Thus I have expressed and made manifest, according to the small strength of my understanding, the state and being of this radical and eternal Unity before anything was created by it. I have shown the effects it produced in the potential and deformed Mass, or the material subject of all things. This matter was contained and understood in a hidden or implicit way <note>original: "complicitly"</note> within that Omnipotent and incomprehensible point of Divine perfection. In that state, it remained as "Nothing" as far as we are concerned <note>original: "quoad nos"</note>, because it was without form, which alone gives a thing its name and essence. Therefore, in the state of its non-actual being, wise men have termed it the Divine Power <note>original: "Potentia Divina"</note>.

For it is an easy matter to consider that every inferior thing issues from a superior; every physical thing from a spiritual one; every visible thing from an invisible one; every temporary thing (namely, that which has both a beginning and an end) from an everlasting <term>original: aevial; referring to things like souls or angels that have a beginning but continue forever</term> thing; and every everlasting thing from an eternal thing (that which has neither beginning nor end). Therefore, that eternal point or brightest Unity, which has no beginning and consequently no end, is the fountain from which all everlasting and temporary things essentially proceed, just as *all numbers flow from Unity* and are contained within Unity. For however far a number extends itself, it always has a unity to begin it and a unity to conclude it; and in truth, it has nothing besides unity to create and compose it from within. 

But for your better instruction, you may observe by a diligent insight into algebraic <term>original: cossical; from "cosa," an early term for the "unknown" in algebra</term> numbers how the Divine and centrally formal Unity contains all creatures within itself, both before they were made and since their creation. For we must note that there is nothing in the world that is not either a root, or a square, or a cube, or some other similar figure framed and composed of these. The root represents the beginning of all algebraic proportions or magnitudes. The square deciphers the simple and spiritual originated figure created by the multiplication of that root. The cube is composed through the increasing of that square or originated shape by its root. So we may discern that the entire cubic body, and consequently the square, is contained in the root, and in conclusion, is nothing else but the root multiplied into itself or from itself. 

But so that my demonstrations may approach a little nearer to our purpose, let us, I pray you, diligently consider the nature and property of this Divine Monad <term>original: Monady; the number one as a metaphysical principle</term> or Unity as it is in its simple and pure existence. We shall find it—without any departure from its own precise or central depth—to contain "complicitly" <note>meaning "enfolded" or "implicitly"</note> within itself the three previously mentioned algebraic dimensions, and consequently all other things which it has now made evident through creation in this representative <term>original: typical; an image or type of the divine</term> world. This is easily proved by this arithmetical demonstration: if we multiply unity as a root by itself, it will produce only itself (namely, unity for a square); which, being multiplied again by itself, will bring forth a cube, which is identical to the root or square—that is, a simple unity. By this it is evident that although we have three various branches here which seem to differ in their formal progression—I mean a root, a square, and a cube—yet in essential truth and reality, there is only this one Unity or Identity, in which all things remain potentially and in a most hidden manner.

...the framing of any typical <term>A "type" is a symbol or physical representation of a spiritual reality.</term> one. Because of this, it is evident that nothing is really formed in this world that was not ideally fashioned in the archetype or eternal one. But lest some hypercritical person should object to these scriptural passages and other sources I have cited regarding this point, and claim (as some of them have already done) that my opinions are completely at odds with the ancient Fathers and Schoolmen, I will briefly express some of their views on this subject. St. Augustine's <note>original: "Austin"</note> opinion is that <margin>Book 85, 45.</margin> *the ideas are eternal and unchangeable forms in the divine mind.* <note>original: "Quod idea sunt formæ æternæ & incommutabiles in mente divina"</note> And Duns Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308) was a highly influential Franciscan priest and philosopher-theologian.</note> maintains they are <margin>Book 1, Distinction 3.</margin> *objective things known by the divine intellect.* <note>original: "Res objectiva, cognita ab intellectu divino"</note> But there is nothing in God except that which *is* God, because the Godhead is one and the same Spirit. Therefore, it follows that the ideas in God—though they are many (for man was made after one fashion, and a horse after another, etc.)—are all one in God, as St. Augustine seems to prove and confirm elsewhere in these words: <margin>On the Trinity, Book 6, last chapter.</margin> *The supreme and highest intellect is a certain art of the omnipotent and wise God, full of all the unchangeable living reasons; and all things are one in it, just as it is one of the One with whom it is one.* <note>original: "Primus & summus intellectus est ars quædam omnipotentis atque sapientis Dei, plena omnium rationum viventium incommutabilium; & omnes unum in ea, sicut ipsa unum de uno cum quo unum."</note> And in another place he says: <margin>Soliloquies, Chapter 31.</margin> *You are my God, and the Lord of all that you have created; with you the causes of all stable things remain, and the unchangeable origins of all mutable things abide with you, and the reasons of all rational, irrational, and temporal things live forever.* <note>original: "Tu es Deus meus, & Dominus omnium quæ creasti; & apud te omnium stabilium sunt causæ, & omnium mutabilium, apud te, immutabiles manent origines, & omnium rationabilium & irrationabilium atque temporalium semper vivunt rationes."</note> And Boethius <note>Boethius (c. 477–524 AD) was a Roman senator and philosopher whose work bridged classical Greek thought and medieval Christianity.</note> puts it this way: <margin>Book 3, On the Consolation of Philosophy, Meter 9.</margin>

-> *yourself most beautiful, bearing the fair* <-

The Word was made manifest out of the dark and deformed Chaos, from which also the humid nature—or the Abyss of waters—did spring or proceed into action by the creating emanation. This humid mass was nourished and animated by the Word and framed into the Elements, as was said before. But I will go a little further and confirm all this more rationally and demonstratively by the authority of Holy Scripture. *Job* says: <note>original: "Revelat Deus fundamenta è tenebris, & educit in lucem umbram lethalem"</note> *God reveals the foundations of the world out of darkness, and he discovers or brings forth into light the deadly shadow, etc.* (Job 12:22). Here, by "the foundations," he understands the waters, which were secretly contained in the dark and misshapen abyss; from these waters, the heavens, the earth, and consequently the whole world were afterward framed by the Word, according to the archetypal pattern. 

So we perceive here that two principles of a completely contrary nature proceed from and out of one and the same Identity or Unity in Essence: namely, a deadly darkness (which is like the shadow of death) and an admirable, life-giving light. One was the <term>matrix</term> <gloss>receptacle or womb</gloss> of form, and the deformed depths of the other contained that matter without form from which the world was afterward framed. Therefore, the wise man says:

<margin>Wisdom 11:17. Job 26:7.</margin>
<note>original: "Manus omnipotentis mundum ex informi materia effecit"</note> *The hand of the Almighty has made the world out of matter without form.* (Wisdom 11:17). According to this tenet, *Job* also says in another place: <note>original: "Aquilonem extendit Deus super inane & vacuum, & suspendit terram super nihilum"</note> *God stretches forth or spreads the North upon emptiness and inanity; that is to say, on a thing that was void and destitute of shape, and hanged the earth upon nothing.* (Job 26:7). 

In this speech, by "emptiness," "void," and "nothing," he means the misshapen darkness and deadly shadow he spoke of in the previously mentioned place—the matter without form mentioned by *Solomon*. While this was <term>in Potentia Divina</term> <gloss>in the Divine Power</gloss>, it was merely nothing to man's weak capacity, because it was not yet actually created or given form; for it is form alone that gives a thing its name and essence, as all Philosophers confess.

<margin>Job 12.</margin>
By this, therefore, we may discern how all things are essentially comprehended in this eternal and radical Unity. Because He is one, He is infinite; and being infinite in His dimension, essence, and power, He must of necessity comprehend in Himself all finite things whatsoever. He is in all and fills all, and yet He is beyond all; as the one who surpasses and encompasses everything, He exists only in Himself, yet He is never absent from the creatures He has framed by His Word, according to His Will. For first, from His <term>Volunty</term> <gloss>Will</gloss> proceeded His Word, *Fiat* <note>Latin: "Let it be done"</note>, and it was done. 

Now that we have identified the <term>privative principle</term> <gloss>the principle of absence or lack</gloss>—namely, deadly darkness and deformity drawn from the infinite center of all things (whose circumference is nowhere to be found)—we will dive into the nature of that formal and lively Light. This light also issued from the same original Root and most ancient beginning of all things, so that we may, with the best colors of our understanding, paint and describe that excellent formal Essence. This Essence redeemed the humid matter (or watery substance) out of the captivity of the deadly and misshapen darkness or shadow of death (to use *Job's* language), and by it, all things have their being and beautiful existence.

### Section 2. Mosaic Philosophy

They stubbornly maintain that there were two coeternal principles; of these, they made one to be God, whom they termed the Prince of Light and the beginner and Author of life, health, and all goodness. The other they attributed to the Devil, whom they entitled the Prince of Darkness and the origin and principle of opposition, death, sickness, and all evil. They believed the Devil, or Prince of Darkness, was coeternal in being with God because there can be no goodness that does not have a relationship with its contrary, namely badness. For this reason, they insist that the god of evil and naughtiness must have a coeternal existence with the God of goodness. By this means, they would not only exclude the Devil from the category of created beings but also banish Unity from the bounds of nature and force <term>Duality</term> <gloss>a state of being two; the opposite of unity</gloss> (which in truth is nothing else but a confusion of Unities) into its place. 

Indeed, this point seemed so delicate and difficult to examine and resolve that some of the wiser sort of "Poetical Philosophers" inclined toward their side, as appears by the mystical and allegorical expressions they enigmatically rolled up or wrapped in their fabulous stories. Among the rest, we find that the poet *Pronapis* in his *Proto-cosmus* <note>original: "Proto-cosmus," meaning "The First World"</note> asserts that *Demogorgon* (by which is meant the greatest of the Gods) was guarded or encircled by Eternity and *Chaos*. He writes that at one time, while *Demogorgon* was in his majesty, he perceived a great tumult and troublesome motion stirred up in the bowels of *Chaos*. To help her in her <term>labors</term> <gloss>the pains of childbirth</gloss> and ease her of her trouble, he put forth his hand and, performing the office of a midwife, suddenly delivered her of the foul and deformed monster *Litigium* <note>original: "Litigium," meaning "Strife" or "Dispute"</note>. After this monster had stirred up great storms and troubles and had ambitiously attempted to soar or fly upward, it was immediately cast down into the deep by *Demogorgon*. 

But when he perceived *Chaos* still in labor and miserably oppressed with fervent sighs and dropping sweats, *Demogorgon* would not remove his hand from her in these agonies until she was delivered of *Pan*, along with his three sisters who were called the *Parcae* <note>original: "Parcae," the three Fates of Roman mythology who spun the thread of life</note> or Destinies. When *Demogorgon* was greatly moved and taken with the beauty and excellent form of *Pan*, he made him the ruler of all his familiar affairs in the world and commanded his three sisters, as his handmaids and ministers, to obey his commands and will. It follows that *Chaos*, having been overburdened and oppressed with the weight of so great a heap or mass as she labored with, and now being delivered and freed from it, placed her son *Pan* upon her throne at the persuasion of *Demogorgon*. 

This is the parabolic fable of *Demogorgon* and *Chaos*, commonly told by the poets. Their allegory implies that the generation and procreation of all things sprang from the highest God or Creator, whom they signify by the name of *Demogorgon*. Eternity is joined to him by an unbreakable link in one essential society because only he is truly to be called Eternal, who is and ever was the beginning or primary cause of all things. They also imagine that *Chaos* was a third member in that endless society; for she is, according to *Ovid's* account, the common mixed and confused matter or "stuff" of all things in the world. Therefore, the ancients affirmed her to be coeternal with God, being a raw mass or dark abyss out of which *Demogorgon*, as a universal Father and Master-worker, did according to his will procreate and fashion all things. Therefore, they esteem this <term>universal substance</term> <note>original: "catholick Substance"</note> or matter of all things to be the general Mother, on which and out of which the universal Father begat and framed every thing. For this reason, they concluded that there were two general parents of things from endless antiquity: a Father and a Mother. 

However, they agreed that God was their chief cause, and they intended for *Chaos* to serve only as his passive companion to conceive upon. And although it may appear that the wise and divine *Plato* seems in some way to verify that *Chaos* was God's companion from all antiquity, he—as well as many others of similar depth—intimates to us that though she is termed a companion with God in the Creation, she actually issued from him by a certain eternal generation or production, and that God afterward framed all things out of *Chaos*. For this reason, they conclude that it sprang from God and is never divided from him; it also serves God as a female companion for procreation and generation, no differently than *Eve*, being framed out of *Adam*, was called a companion to *Adam*. This is the opinion of both the heathen philosophers and mystical Cabalists. But to proceed in the explanation of this allegory: the hand of *Demogorgon* represents the Divine Power. # Mosaic Philosophy. Book 1.

...foul shape signifies the true Prince of Darkness, the Author of opposition, and the Father of discord. Therefore, for his presumptuous attempt against the Prince of Light and the Lord of Life, he was cast down into the abyss. By the second birth of Chaos, namely *Pan*, the poets point to the universal nature of the world and the peacefulness and harmony of contrary elements. They argue that after that great discord which occurred in the first opening of the womb of Chaos, harmony followed in the second place. This harmony was as beautiful and acceptable to God in the latter birth as deformed discord was foul and hateful in His sight in the first.

Thus you see how, in the very beginning of the world, all the elements were at strife in the bowels of the Chaos. The three *Fates* <note>original: Parcæ</note> or Sisters of Destiny—*Clotho, Lachesis,* and *Atropos*—who were born with *Pan*, signify the three orders of time: namely, time present, time past, and time to come. *Clotho* has the care of the present time, and her office is to twist the thread of life. *Lachesis* is the superintendent of the time to come; she looks after the flax or hemp which is not yet spun or twisted. And *Atropos* signifies the time past, which is irrevocable; therefore, she finishes and cuts off the thread now spun. 

I infer from this parabolic relation that though the Chaos or dark abyss existed with God before the world's creation, yet the infinite and sole eternal Unity—the radical Essence—created it and produced it out of itself. For that Eternal Unity says:

<margin>Isaiah 45:7</margin>
"I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming the light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil <note>original: Ego Dominus & non est alter, formans lucem, & creans tenebras, faciens pacem, & creans malum</note>." 

It is as if He had said: "I am the Father of Light, or of the bright Spirit of Wisdom, and I created the dark Chaos out of which I framed the world. Out of that Chaos, I produced both the harmony and discord of the elements in the world—that is to say, *Strife* <note>original: Litigium</note> and *Pan*." So we may still discern that there is but one Eternal Unity which in itself is both male and female and everything that can be imagined. He produces all things from Himself and in Himself, just as Adam contained within himself Eve, who was the Mother of the "little world" (or mankind) after Adam. Therefore, Hermes says:

<margin>Pimander</margin>
"God, the Mind, being most full of the fertility of both sexes, and being life and light, brought forth another Divine Mind by His Word <note>original: Mens autem Deus utriusque sexûs fœcunditate plenissimus, vita & lux cum verbo sic alteram mentem peperit</note>." 

And the Scriptures seem to suggest as much in this sense: "Shall I, who give the power of generation to others, be myself barren? <note>original: Qui ceteris generationem tribuo, an sterilis ero?</note>"

It is evident, therefore, that from one and the same radical Unity—existing before all antiquity—both the matter and form of all things proceed. Regarding their birth or existence, they appear <term>evial</term> <gloss>having a beginning but no end</gloss>, though in their essential Root they are eternal in God, the abstruse <term>Monad</term> <gloss>original: Monady; the number one or a single unit</gloss> of all things. 

The dark Chaos and the bright informing Spirit are two principles opposite and contrary to one another in nature and property. From the dark principle proceed discord, evil, cold, congealing, rest, death, privation, and negation (or <term>Nolunty</term> <gloss>the "un-willing" or negative aspect of the divine will</gloss>). From the other—which is the type of beauty and grace, namely the bright beginning—light, harmony, goodness, heat, resolution, motion, life, and position (or <term>Volunty</term> <gloss>the "willing" or positive aspect of the divine will</gloss>) are poured out into the nature of the world to cause it to exist and live. Yet, both of these are merely main branches arising from one and the same essential Unity. 

Because they cannot pass or exceed the limits of their infinite fountain, they are in Him both light and darkness, differing in no way in essence from their Root, which is all in all. As the Psalmist says:

<margin>Psalm 139:12</margin>
"Darkness is to Him as the light itself <note>original: Tenebræ sunt ei, sicut ipsa lux</note>." 

For all is one in Him, who is only one and the same in Himself: 

<margin>Romans 11:36</margin>
"In whom, by whom, and therefore from whom are all things." 

His *Volunty* and *Nolunty* are but one and the same in Him, for He is a single Identity. What is His *Volunty* is equally His affirmation and His negation, which are both but one "good" in Him who is all goodness. And yet, regarding the creature, when His negation has the supremacy, He hides the light of His loving countenance, and all is dark; then He operates in a state of privation. Where He hides His face, all is deformed and, as it were, void of essence and goodness. Look, here is His negative or privative *Volunty*, which may rightly be termed His *Nolunty*. If His affirmation has dominion, He emits the beauty of His kindness, and the creature’s waiting spirit is enlightened by His presence and consequently filled with goodness. Look, here is also His affirmative or positive *Volunty*, called *Volunty* in the proper sense. 

Lest any man should think this strange, let him observe the mental beam which is assigned by God to man to fill him with reason and adorn...

And yet this Unity in essence, which is the Image of God, operates by two contrary properties. One is inclined to affirm, give, and grant a petition through a friendly outpouring (behold, here is the act of "position" <term>position: here used in the sense of "placing" or affirming a state of being</term> outlined in man’s spiritual Unity). The other is to deny, take away, or oppose the request of the one who asks, through a "privative ablation" <term>privative ablation: the act of taking something away or withholding a benefit</term> of the desired rewards. (Behold, here is the effect of negation described; for the mental beam does not shine out toward the petitioner, but is reserved or pulled back into itself.)

In these two actions, we can observe only one effect that is praiseworthy in this simple and absolute unity toward the petitioner. For even if I grant a request through the friendly and compassionate outpouring or emission of my mental beam, so that it matches the petitioner’s wish; or even if I deny his demand against his desire, so that it appears to be a great evil or misfortune to him; yet to my own mind, both the affirmation and the negation appear good and are founded upon good reason. Therefore, they are indeed only one thing, though they seem different to the person asking. 

In the same way, in the eternal and archetypal mental Unity—of which our own understanding is a reflection—the act of both "Volunty" and "Nolunty" <term>Volunty and Nolunty: archaic terms for "willing" and "not-willing" (nilling)</term> is all one, and that is goodness. For He who is all goodness has no internal conflict, even though in the creature, who is subject to the effects of either His withholding or positive will, His withholding or dark action is judged as evil. Conversely, His positive and light outpouring, which is full of love and kindness, is received as good and therefore embraced with joy. For

# Mosaic Philosophy. Book 1.

...can be ignorant that either of these opposite properties, so familiar within one pure <note>original: "sincere"</note> essence, is absolutely good, in that it is completely excellent in goodness in itself—even though nothing is more terrible, fearful, abominable, and wicked to a creature than its own death and corruption. 

If we Christians deny this property within the Ideal Unity—namely, that God can deprive a creature of its life by withdrawing the act of life from it back into Himself—we might rightly consider ourselves inferior in judgment to the pagan <note>original: "Infidell"</note> poets and philosophers. They verify the axiom of the wise man: <margin>Ecclesiastes 11:14</margin> *Good and evil, life and death, riches and poverty, are all from God.* <note>original Latin: "Bonum & malum, vita & mors, honestas & paupertas, à Deo sunt"</note> By this, he suggests that this one essential divinity operates in opposite ways in the created world through a two-fold differing property. 

Their allegorical story is this: Proclus, following the ancient theology of Orpheus, Hesiod, Euripides, and Aeschylus (who hid divine secrets in their fables and stories that they had learned from divine persons and those deeply learned in the mysteries of God), describes the properties of the supreme and archetypal Son <note>The "archetypal Son" refers to the divine Logos or Word</note> through the symbol <note>original: "shadow"</note> of the visible and typical Sun. He expresses that one and the same eternal essence operates in all things, both negatively <note>original: "privatively"</note> and positively. 

These poets call it by the name of **Apollo** during the day, because they claim that in his position and kind nature (manifested by the life-giving property of the Sun), he composes the creature out of seven parts. The Pythagoreans used the number four <note>the quaternary</note> to signify matter, which is framed of the Elements; for it is the square of 2 (an imperfect number) <margin><insert>2+2=4</insert></margin> and therefore represents matter. By the number three <note>the ternary</note>, <margin><insert>3</insert></margin> which is the number of perfection, they express the "form" <note>the organizing spirit or soul</note> of things. So, these two numbers combined <margin><insert>4+3=7</insert></margin> make up the number seven, which includes the perfect completion of the creature. 

Furthermore, they name it **Dionysus** during the night—namely, in his dark and negative disposition. They say that under this name, he tears and divides into seven pieces that same creature which he had composed under the title of Apollo (his positive property or solar and divine nature). 

<margin><image-desc>A hand-drawn sketch of a flower with two large leaves and a three-petaled bloom on a single stem.</image-desc></margin> 

Thus, they seem to argue that the very same unity in essence is the author of destruction and corruption as much as the generation and life of the creature. They call it by different names only according to the variety of its property—no differently than the Kabbalist calls God "Dark Aleph" <note>original: "Aleph tenebrosum"</note> in his hidden and negative property (when He keeps His beams of life within Himself or withdraws His face from the creature), and "Light Aleph" <note>original: "Aleph lucidum"</note> when He shines forth and extends His beams of life upon it. 

By this, we Christians may see that even the Pagans acknowledged what the Scriptures testify, though they did so through allegory: they concluded that it is only in the power of one and the same radical unity to save or destroy, to give life or take it away, to will or to refuse, and, in conclusion, to operate all and in all according to its pleasure. 

Thus we have confirmed that these two opposite conditions spring from one eternal root and operate in this world through contrary effects. Consequently, the mass of waters (from which, as St. Peter testifies in <margin>2 Peter 3</margin>, the heavens and the earth were made of old) came out of the dark chaos and was, as it were, its second birth. The poets call this **Pan**, or universal nature. The wise philosopher can easily see that this passive portion of the world is naturally inclined toward darkness and all its negative conditions. 

If it were not for the "formal" <note>The "form" or organizing spirit</note> portion of the world, which proceeded from that bright spirit of wisdom—which Solomon calls <margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:24-26</margin> "the breath of the power of God, and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty; the brightness of the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the goodness of God"—all things would be the same. It is this Spirit <margin>Job 26:7; Job 28:25</margin> that divided the waters into distinct orbs or spheres, gave a proportional weight to the air, hung up the waters in the thick clouds by measure, gave orders to the rain, and made a path for the lightning and thunder. If it were not for the act of this Spirit, all things would be indistinguishable. It is this Spirit that said: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 24</margin> "I came out of the mouth of the Most High, and covered the earth as a cloud; I alone compassed the circuit of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep." <note>original Latin: "Ab ore altissimi prodij & rotunditatem coelorum circumivi solus in profundo abyssi ambulavi"</note> 

This was the bright Wisdom which **JEHOVAH** possessed <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> in the beginning of His ways, before His works, before all time, and before the world was made—when there was no abyss, no fountains, before the mountains were raised, or the earth created.

### Section 2: Mosaic Philosophy.

<margin>John 1.</margin>
*When he made the heavens, it was there; when he fortified the superior waters, it was there; when the limits of the sea were framed, lest the waters should pass their bounds. When he gave the earth her foundation, it was there with him, as a helper to compose all things. To conclude, by it all was formally made, and without it was nothing made and preserved.* <note>The author is likely paraphrasing Proverbs 8:27-30 regarding Divine Wisdom, though the marginal note refers to the Logos in John 1.</note> So, if it were not for the continuous action of this formal spirit <note>The "formal spirit" refers to the formative, essential power of God that gives shape and "form" to matter.</note>, the watery matter of the world would return to the deformed state of her mother, Chaos. For while it is in this world, matter is inclined toward the disposition of her mother, being passive, feminine, and serving as the mother of all things. In another respect, the vivifying and bright emanation of the eternal Unity has become the masculine actor or father of all things; it gives life to everything in this world, as the Apostle teaches us and as the aforementioned poets seem to suggest under the name of Apollo, or the father of light.

Once this is well observed, we may—by revealing these two abstruse and mystical principles of Light and Darkness—reach the radical knowledge and origin of true sympathy and antipathy. It is evident that sympathy proceeds from that concording and vivifying love arising from the benign emanation of the Creator, who desires to be joined with his like and seeks to preserve his like by union. Conversely, antipathy issues from that discording, privative <note>original: "privative"; meaning a quality defined by the absence or taking away of something.</note>, and hateful affection which darkness and deformity bring to the children of light and life, and to all their beautiful offspring.

By this it appears that before the divine Word separated these different properties (namely, light from darkness), all things were one and the same, without distinction or difference. That Unity was not to be numbered among created things; light was darkness, and darkness was light, and neither was discernible. Nothing was truly distinguished; all were one in the first matter of all things, which was within the eternal Unity. At that time, there was neither light nor darkness, day nor night, heaven nor earth, spirit nor body, good nor evil, pure nor impure, things that can be created nor things that can decay <note>original: "generable nor corruptible"</note>, nor "this" or "that." And yet, nevertheless, all these things—both spiritual and corporal—proceeded from that potential subject which remained enfolded <note>original: "complicitely"</note> in that infinite Unity, which was, is, and ever shall be, all in all, and over or beyond all. 

Oh, the admirable wisdom of God in all his works! All things proceeded from one matter, which nevertheless was none of the specific things that were made. All things were deeply hidden and secret, but, according to our Savior’s words, nothing was so hidden or obscure that it would not be revealed and made to appear by the penetrating operation of the admirable word *Fiat* <note>Latin: "Let there be."</note>. By its divine spagyric <note>original: "spagericall"; Spagyric refers to the alchemical process of separating and then recombining elements to purify them.</note> action or virtue, that one thing was divided into two contraries, and names fitting their natures were given to them. One, as I have told you, was called Light, and the other Darkness; the first was also called Day, and the last Night. Thus was the pure separated from the impure. 

From this, it follows that the whole world was originally divided into two contrary kingdoms that correspond to these two radical branches of one Unity. By this relationship, it is easy to express what, in truth, is light and darkness, day and night, goodness and badness, heaven and hell, truth and falsehood, humility and pride, justice and injustice, gladness and sorrow, sweet and bitter, action and passion, life and death, generation and corruption, pure and impure, wholesome and pernicious, medicine and poison. To conclude, it explains what is amiable and what is odious, what is concord and what is discord, and, consequently, what is sympathy and what is antipathy among the infinite creatures in this world.

We find it justified both by sacred authority and the testimony of pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophy that the whole world, and every creature in it, is composed of these two contrarieties or opposite natures. The son of Sirach says, in the passage mentioned before: <margin>Ecclesiasticus 42:24</margin> *All things are double, one against another, and he has made nothing imperfect.* <note>original Latin: "Gemina sunt omnia quorum alterum contrarium est alteri, nec quicquam factum est quod mancum est"</note> Based on this, the philosopher Heraclitus concluded that all things in the world are made by strife and concord. Empedocles also held that the soul is composed of the elements, and of friendship and enmity. Finally, lest some scrupulous reader

...should condemn me for making such a long discourse on these two contrary principles, which proceed from one root, I thought it most appropriate to assure every judicious person that the true knowledge of them is of special importance. This is because the two aforementioned principles are observed to be the real and only foundation of both universal Philosophy and Theology. For the root and basis of them both consists of the true understanding of these two contraries. Therefore, if they are not first well explained and conceived, how is it possible afterward that they should be rightly handled in true Philosophy or understood in those places of Holy Scripture where they are so often mentioned? Regarding the explanation of this most profound Sphinx-like riddle <note>original: "Sphyng-an Riddle"; a reference to the complex and difficult nature of the riddle posed by the Sphinx in Greek mythology</note> or abstruse question—namely, why God, in his secret sense or mental intent, did raise up and ordain out of the unformed matter (or that which was ideally outlined within himself) these two contraries to cause all things in the world to be put into a mutual dissonance, or fight and conflict with one another, so that nothing is found which participates in goodness that does not also have its contrary (that is to say, which does not communicate with badness, insomuch that God himself is not without an adversary)—truly, it is too hidden a Kabbalah <note>original: "Caball"; referring to the Jewish mystical tradition and hidden lore</note> to be explained by mortal capacity. Indeed, it may well be esteemed the profoundest secret of all the divine mysteries. Therefore, a mental perspective is required that is well-cleansed and purified <note>original: "mundified"</note> from every misty cloud of ignorance and error to search into the depths of this question. Consequently, it is impossible to be revealed to anyone except those to whom God immediately bestows his grace and Holy Spirit, which is the searcher of all mysteries. This Spirit is in us, and it breathes and blows when and where it pleases. It is called in the Scriptures the Spirit of Truth, the Spirit of Sanctification, the Spirit of Illumination, and the Spirit of Revelation, which is the best interpreter of the Divine Secrets mentioned in Holy Writ. Truly, it does not become us of our own accord to inquire why God made this or that, or why he did it in this fashion. Instead, it behooves the zealous to refer all of this to the time when these secrets shall be discovered, which will come to pass when the seventh Seal shall be opened <note>A reference to the Book of Revelation 8:1, symbolizing the final unveiling of divine secrets at the end of time</note>. For then that high mystery—which is the final cause of why and for what end God's Providence will reveal itself through these two opposites and completely extinguish all enmity out of the world—shall be discovered. Nevertheless, regarding the end of this dissonance, the Apostle says that it will be when the Son has delivered the Kingdom to God the Father, and when he has abolished <note>original: "evacuated"</note> every dominion, authority, and power. He must reign until he has made his enemies his footstool, and the last enemy that shall be destroyed is Death. So, just as two contrarieties or discords proceeded from one Unity or unison—namely, Light and Darkness from one Divine Essence—so also these two dissonant branches or confusion of Unities will at last be reduced or return again into one harmonious Unity, in which no dissonance will be found. This will happen when these words of the Revelation are accomplished: <margin>Rev. 21.</margin> *Behold, I make all things new: for the old things have passed away <note>original: "Ecce omnia nova facio: vetera enim transierunt"</note>.* But leaving this side-discussion <note>original: "allaterall discourse"</note>, we will proceed directly in our inquiry into sympathy and antipathy. In order that we may penetrate these with greater speed and ease, and dive deeper into the research of their actions, it is fitting that we should first describe the manner in which the world lives through the participation of these two—namely, Light and Darkness. I will express to you in few words what the Ancient Philosophers have determined about the soul of the world, and lastly, I will show that their opinions do not err or vary much from the testimony of the sacred Bible.
