# Section 2.

...some self-conceited and little-skilled persons in so profound a mystery, which is so highly prized and esteemed by others who have, with the Lyncean <note>Referring to Lynceus, an Argonaut famed for his supernatural sharpness of sight; here meaning extremely piercing or keen-sighted</note> eyesight of their understanding, dived and penetrated into the secret bowels of Nature and with due reverence contemplated her central and eternal Agent. Afterward, my meaning is to set down the concordance <note>agreement or harmony</note> which is observed between them and Holy Scripture. 

The Kabbalist’s tenet is that the great Angel whom they term *Metatron* <note>original: "Mitattron"</note> (which by interpretation is the **Gift of God** <note>original: "Donum Dei"</note>) is that very same universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> Spirit which animates the whole world. Based on this, Rabbi Moses <note>Likely referring to Moses Maimonides, the influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher</note> does aver it to be the **Active Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus agens"</note>, or the general intellectual agent from which all particular forms flow. <margin>*Reuchlin, On the Art of the Kabbalah, book 3.*</margin> And they say that from this universal angelic Spirit, all singular virtues—as well animal as vital and natural—do proceed, which they also call Angels, of which there are an infinite number in respect to our capacity. 

The philosophers Democritus and Orpheus, along with various Pythagoreans, do not much differ from the opinion of these Rabbis, except in the variety of the name only. For they imagine that all things are full of gods; therefore, they offered divine honors, prayers, and sacrifices unto them in the creatures, and did worship each of them with a different fashion of ceremony. But they had evermore that regard unto JEHOVAH, the eternal Unity and Father of all things, that they referred all these gods unto one *Jupiter*. This point, nevertheless, being ill-understood by the ignorant, was an especial cause of idolatry, because the simple people fell into the worshipping of the creature instead of the Divinity which was in the creature. And for this reason, Solomon says: <margin>*Wisdom 13.*</margin> **All men are naturally vain who lack the knowledge of God, and who could not understand Him who truly exists from those good things that are seen, nor acknowledge the Workman by considering his works.** <note>original Latin: "Vani sunt homines omnes naturâ in quibus est ignorantia Dei, & qui ex iis quæ spectantur bonis, eum qui est, intelligere non potuerunt, neque ex operibus consideratis, ipsum opificem agnoverunt"</note> 

In like manner, the Platonists called the general virtue, which engendered and preserved all things, the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "Animam mundi"</note>. To this opinion, the Arabic Astrologians seem to adhere, forasmuch as they maintained that every particular thing in the world has its distinct and peculiar soul from this vivifying Spirit. To this opinion also Mercurius Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed</note>, Theophrastus, Avicenna, Algazel, and all the Stoics and Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> seem wholly to consent or agree. 

Again, Zoroaster and Heraclitus the Ephesian conclude that the soul of the world is that universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> invisible fire, from which and by the action of which all things are generated and brought forth from potentiality into act. Virgil, that excellent Latin poet, calls it that mental Spirit which is infused through every joint and member of the world, whereby the whole mass of it—namely the heaven and the earth, or spirit and body—are in a hidden <note>original: "abstruse"</note> manner agitated and moved. His words are these:

<margin>*Aeneid, book 6.*</margin>
> ->**A Spirit within nourishes, and a Mind,**<-
> ->**infused through the limbs, moves the entire mass...**<-
> <note>original Latin: "Spiritus intus alit totamque infusa per artus / Mens agitat molem, &c."</note>

<margin>*Psalm 19*</margin>
A Spirit (he says) does nourish within, and being infused over all the joints or members of the world, it does move the whole substance of the same. Marcus Manilius, as also Boethius and Augurel <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, an Italian humanist and alchemist</note>, being later poets, are of Virgil’s opinion. For Manilius says:

<margin>*In Astronomica, addressed to Augustus.*</margin>

*Some say that whatever fills the Heaven, the Air, the Earth, and the wide Seas is stirred up by a soul, through the virtue of which all things in the world live; and also that the world itself exists by it. But because there is no bodily substance that is void of a soul, and because the world and every part of it consists of a body, there is an intermediate spirit between this soul and body. They call this neither a soul nor a body, but a middle substance, participating in both, to bring both extremes together into one.* <margin>The Art of Chemistry, chapter 4 <note>original: "Arte chym. c. 4."</note></margin> The wiser sort of Alchemists make the Soul a certain infinite nature or power in all things, which procreates like things from their like: for this nature engenders all things—yes, and it multiplies, nourishes, or sustains them. They also style it *the Ligament*, or bond of the elements, since by it they are fastened together with the symphonic accords of peaceful harmony, even though by themselves—that is, in regard to their matter—they are discordant. Also, it is termed the true virtue that mingles and proportions everything in this sublunary <note>the world below the moon; the earthly realm</note> world, allotting to each specific creature a convenient and well-agreeing form so that one thing might be distinguished and varied from another. In conclusion, the mystical Rabbis <note>referring to Jewish scholars of the Kabbalah</note> assert that this occult <note>hidden or secret</note> fire is that Spirit of the Lord, or fiery love, which when it moved upon the waters, imparted to them a certain harmonious and hidden fiery virtue, without whose lovely assistance and favorable heat nothing could be generated from them or multiplied within them.

Thus you may discern the manifold opinions of both Christian and Heathen philosophers concerning this *Anima mundi*, or soul of the world. These will appear to vary little or nothing at all from the tenet <note>original: "tenent"</note> of Holy Scripture in meaning, but in words only. Neither are these opinions as heinous or abominable as some Christians of our age—who are more superstitiously zealous than truly understanding—will make them out to be, if they will scan the matter wisely and with moderation. For then they shall really perceive that it concurs with the Bible of Truth. To confirm what I now say, my purpose is, in the first place, to express to each learned and well-minded reader the harmony of the Scriptures regarding this point. Then I will compare every one of the aforementioned opinions with the meaning and grounds of that harmony, so that every wise man may better conjecture and guess at the truth of the business before he rashly enters into censoring that deep and profound mystery which concerns Divine action in natural effects.

I told you in my preceding discourse that the Eternal Unity, which is the God of gods and Beginning of beginnings, caused two diverse principles to issue out of himself by a double property in one essence. One of these was potential and in no way yet enacted <note>original: "inacted"; meaning activated or put into motion</note> by the brightness of his emanation; in that respect, it is termed Darkness, privation, and "Nolunty" <note>original: "Nolunty"; from the Latin *noluntas*, meaning "unwillingness" or the negative aspect of the Divine Will</note>, opposite to Light and a friend to death and rest. The other was actual and nothing else but a pure universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> form and brightness, which is termed Light, Position, and "Volunty" <note>from the Latin *voluntas*, meaning "will" or "desire"</note>, and in nature is opposite to Darkness and a friend to life and action or motion. 

Then I signaled to you that by the bright appearance of Eternity, or the Eternal Spirit of Wisdom (which I termed, using the language of the Scriptures, the radiant emanation or flowing-out from the Almighty, which is all one with him in essence), the deformed waters were enacted and made manifest out of this dark Principle or Chaos. That is, they were reduced from *Divine Puissance* <note>original: "Potentia Divina"; Divine Power or Potential</note>—the formless state in which they remained—into the *Divine Act* <note>original: "Actum Divinum"</note>. <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> And because all the humid and passive universal nature, of which both the heavens and the earth were framed, issued from this mass of watery matter—which the Poets call *Pan* <note>original: "Pana"; referring to the Greek god Pan as a symbol of universal nature</note> or the second birth of Chaos—we must imagine it to be that spiritual matter of the world which was made fertile and capable of multiplication by reason of that hidden active and formal Light or invisible fire. By this, it is evidently proved that this thin spiritual water, or humid nature, is in itself no more than a human spirit without the life-giving act of life. For just as in the soul of every living creature two things are primarily required—namely, an Agent and a Patient <term>the active force and the passive receiver</term>—so where one of these is missing, there can be no created soul. If the world's life were only the essential breath of God, without the vehicle of the created humid spirit (which is the matter of heaven), then 그 life would be simple identity <note>an undifferentiated state</note> and would have one and the same property. Consequently, there would be no variety of action, nor any contraction or expansion <term>systole and diastole</term> in things, and therefore no action or passion in the soul. For without a passive nature there can be no action, and without an active nature there can be no passion <note>experience of being acted upon</note>. Now, the matter that proceeds from water is the subject of all passion—just as here, mother Chaos was the female or passive element to the action of Demogorgon <note>a name for the primordial creator-god</note>, or God. Also, action or form, which proceeds from light, is the subject of all action, just as its father, Eternity—the bright emanation of the spirit of wisdom from the fountain of light—was the male or agent. From this, therefore, it is easy to gather first what the soul of the world is, and of what parts it consists. We must consider that as every creature has an interior and exterior, so we must diligently search for an internal and an external in the soul, since it is a creature. By this, the great question—so often turned over by the Peripatetic <term>followers of Aristotle</term> philosophers and so poorly resolved by them—may be fully determined and clarified <note>original: "enucleated"</note>, if it pleases the wise and impartial reader to consider things as they truly are. Consequently, it creates the earthly body and the heavenly spirit from nothing, or from non-actual existence. The **spirit** is that inward created spirit of the world—the subtle substance of the waters or the moist nature—considered simply in itself, which is animated and illuminated by that Archetypal emanation. The **soul**, or *anima*, is the union made between this moist created spirit and the uncreated formal emanation that performs the act of informing or creating. 

Through this, we may discern, first, what the *active forming power* <note>original Latin: "forma informans"</note> or *creative nature* <note>original Latin: "natura naturans"</note> is; and then what the *formed shape* <note>original Latin: "forma informata"</note> or *created nature* <note>original Latin: "natura naturata"</note> is. 
*   The **active forming power**, or **creative nature**, is God, or the divine emanation which created all things. 
*   The **formed shape**, or **created nature**, is the created light, or the spirit shaped and illuminated by the presence of the bright uncreated Spirit. 

The uncreated Spirit, when clothed with or inhabiting that created spirit, is said to be *clothed or covered with light as with a garment* <note>original Latin: "vestitus, or amictus lumine quasi vestimento"</note>,

### Sect. 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

According to the assertions of those Gentile and ethnic <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> philosophers whom I have cited before—which I will prove in no way disagree or vary from the testimony of the Holy Text—I will compare them in order to make this clearer. First, I will begin my account with the Kabbalists' <note>original: "Cabaliſts"</note> great angel, whom they call *Metatron* <note>original: "Mitattron"</note>. By interpretation, this name means *Gift of God* <note>original: "Donum Dei"</note>, which they say is the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> intellectual Agent from which all specific forms descend. <margin>1 Tim. 6. 13.</margin> The Apostle says that the Lord gives life to all things. <margin>Prov. 3.</margin> And Solomon says that the Spirit of Wisdom is the tree of life and the fountain, or beginning, of life. If this Spirit is the fountain of life, then the Son of Sirach <note>original: "Syrach"</note> says: *God poured it out upon all his works, and upon all flesh according to his gift* <note>original: "effudit Deus illam supra omnia opera sua, & supra omnem carnem secundum datum suum"</note>. <margin>Gen. 1.</margin> And this was that universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> angelic Spirit which God sent out as a spiritual messenger from himself and out of himself, in the form of an emanation, to move upon the waters and to inform and give life to them. It gives life and being not only to the great world <note>the macrocosm or universe</note> but <margin>Joh. 1. Ephes. 4. Colos. 3.</margin> also to every particular part of it. This emanation was the Word of God, by whom all things were made and given life, since life was in it. I mean that Christ who fills all things, who is all in all, as the Apostle says, and who in the <margin>Heb. 1.</margin> beginning made the earth; the heavens were the work of his hands. After his creation of all things, he does (as Saint Paul tells us) *bear up, support, and sustain all things by the life-giving power of his Word* <note>original: "portare omnia verbo virtutis suae"</note>. This <margin>Psal. 33. 6.</margin> David also confirms: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established and settled, and by the breath of his mouth, all the virtues thereof* <note>original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt coeli, & Spiritu ab ore ejus omnis virtus eorum"</note>—namely, their life, preservation, and being. The Apostle therefore seems to conclude this: *God, needing the assistance of no one, <margin>Acts 17.</margin> gives life and breath and all things to every creature* <note>original: "Deus non aliquo indigens dat vitam & inspirationem & omnia"</note>. 

Every philosopher cannot but <margin>1 Cor. 12.</margin> acknowledge that the *Soul* <note>original: "Anima"</note> is nothing other than that which animates or gives life to a body or spirit. Why then should not the universal divine Spirit—which fills all, and operates all, and in all—be termed the fountain of the world's life? And shall it not operate and produce the life-giving and multiplying effect of its nature, but instead be idle and vacant in the creature? 

Did God send forth his operative Spirit to be still and not to act? Indeed, the Father operates in it by his Will, and it carries out the Will of his Father in the creature's spirit, which it possesses, animates, and guides in whatever way he pleases. And for this reason, <margin>Judith 16.</margin> Judith says: *Let every creature serve God, because you spoke and they were made; you sent your spirit and they were created* <note>original: "Deo serviat omnis creatura, quia dixisti, & facta sunt; miſisti spiritum tuum, & creata sunt"</note>. # Mosaical Philosophy. Book 1.

The Platonic "Heptachord" <note>A seven-stringed musical scale used here as a mathematical model of the universe</note>—which Plato invented and adapted to demonstrate the soul of the world—consists of seven strings or proportions, partly even and partly odd: namely 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, and 27. Although Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD)</note> and Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD)</note> drew these proportions out in a single line, it seems to me that Adrastus and Calcidius <note>Early commentators on Plato's *Timaeus*</note> more fitly expressed and adapted them to the sides of a pyramid or triangle in this manner:

| | 1 | |

At the summit or top, where both lines meet in one point, the number 1 is expressed as Unity. These most vividly express the general kinds of all creatures, along with their harmony.

## Section 2. Mosaical Philosophy.

...harmony. In the first place, it describes the symphonical degrees of the Soul of the World, as shall be explained hereafter. First, following the example of the **Archetype** <note>The original model or divine pattern from which all things are made</note>, from the number 1 issued the number 2. This is termed by the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe</note> as the "confusion of unities." Therefore, it is the radical or beginning imperfect number. 

In its confusion and imperfection, the number 2 stands in the same relation to the Unity from which it sprung as the bright eternal Unity stands toward the dark Chaos. This Chaos is a **rude, disorganized, and undigested mass** <note>original: "rudis indigestaque moles"</note>. It is rightly termed "imperfect" because the eternal emanation, which is all perfection, had not yet made it perfect. For this reason, the watery matter that issued out of it is inherently imperfect, just as the number 2 is considered imperfect in comparison to the number 3. 

All perfection consists of three terms: a beginning, a middle, and an end. 
* If you take one of the unities of 2 for the beginning and the other for the middle, then there is no end. 
* If you put one unity for the beginning and another for the end, then you have two extremes but no "mean" or middle; therefore, it is also imperfect this way. 
* Or, if you place one unity for a middle and the other for an end, you still have imperfection because there is no beginning. 

In the same way, if Unity had not sent out its actual emanation as a bright Unity of life, the number 2 (or the deformed matter of Chaos) would have remained in its dual, confused, or imperfect state. That is, it would exist without the form or shape of any perfect thing. It would be a plain **Nothing** <note>original: "Nihil"</note> or **something in potentiality but not in actuality** <note>original: "Aliquid in potentia & non actu"</note>. 

So, I say that matter, before it was shaped by the Unity of Light (which makes the third Unity), was **empty and void** <note>original: "Vacuum & inane"</note>. It was void because it lacked the presence of the informing Unity, or the actual emanation, to give it the title of "goodness." After the bright emanation was made, then emptiness was changed into fullness; potentiality into action; darkness into light; and deformed matter into well-formed and living waters. In a word, imperfection became perfection. 

Thereupon it was said that "God saw that it was good"—meaning it was filled with His virtuous essence, who was all good and the only goodness. By this logic—namely, by adding the formal Unity to the state of confusion and imperfection (the material duality which symbolizes Chaos, the mother of matter)—perfection is brought into the world. By animating the purest and subtler waters, it unites the mental light with the heavenly spirit in an **angelic essence**, which afterwards animates and gives form to all things. 

This formal union is symbolically expressed by the figure 3. For this reason, 3 is termed the first number of perfection, the number of the Soul, and the radical number of "form" in the course of nature. From this point forward, the Platonists and Pythagoreans express matter (which is imperfect in itself) by even or "imperfect" numbers. 

In the **Archetypal world** <note>The divine world of ideas and patterns</note>, designated by 1, 2, and 3 in the form of the sacred Trinity, there appear to be three ideal dimensions in one divine nature or eternal essence. In their progression, these present a Root, a Square, and a Cube, which signify a supreme soul, a spirit, and a body of the world, ideally depicted in the Archetype. These three seem to be raised out of the number 1 or Unity. Multiplying 1 by the root 1 produces 1 and itself, which makes 2 (a simple ideal square); multiplying it again by 1 results in 2 and 1, which makes 3 (a Cube). This demonstrates the perfection of the Ideal world which was in God. 

If we take the two radical compounded numbers for roots, we shall produce the created or **exemplar world** <note>The physical world modeled after the Archetype</note> according to this pattern. Namely, we shall find three dimensions—longitude, latitude, and depth of matter—by searching out the Root, Square, and Cube of matter. 

The root of matter was 2. For although the supreme Unity had expanded itself into 2, representing its first-born issue, all was dark **as far as we are concerned** <note>original: "quoad nos"</note> because the holy Spirit of Illumination had not yet shone forth. We must imagine that the multiplication of matter in the world is nothing but the varying levels of penetration of formal light into the watery abyss or material multitude. The thicker matter is, the nearer it appears to its root, 2 (the dark Chaos). Conversely, the thinner and more transparent it is made by the rich presence of the formal emanation’s light, the nearer it appears to the root of formal Unity. 

If this mystery is rightly understood, all science—even in the **most abstruse philosophy** <note>The most difficult or hidden parts of philosophy</note>—may easily be deciphered. The root of matter, which is 2, represents the dark Chaos. The root of form, which is 3, signifies that the root 2 (the dark waters) is animated by the formal or bright emanation...

You may observe that where this harmonious proportion between form and matter is absent, there must necessarily be both spiritual and corporal dissension, or discord, and consequently antipathy. We see also that the root of life is fixed in the angelic composition, which is made of simple, light, and pure spiritual matter. Thus, the eternal wisdom (sapience), or essential soul, is the "act" or driving force of the Angels; the eternal angelic spirit is the act or essential life of the stars, or heavenly influence; and the starry influence is the soul and life of the winds. These creatures draw from the divine fountain of them all, being one spirit in essence, but multiform in regard to the variety of "organs" (physical forms) by which it works variously in the world.

The Empyrean heaven animates the stars, or ethereal region, which we refer to the "square." And the starry heaven is, as it were, the male—the multiplier and vivifier of the elementary region and its creatures—which we compare to the "cube." 

Truly, not only the obscure Kabbalists but also the most profound philosophers have created an everlasting memory of this perfect and formal root, or "ternary" number (3), with its triple dimension. 2. The formal, which is extracted from the vocal for the celestial world.

The first part was uncovered and exposed to the wind, rain, hail, snow, and all other weather effects produced in the <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The region below the moon; the physical earth subject to constant change</note> with its perpetual alterations. Therefore, this region, representing the "cube of matter," is rightly compared to the elementary world, which is composed of the denser waters as a fluid and unstable substance. For this reason, it is properly called the "world of darkness"; thus, the Evangelist in one place calls the Devil the "Prince of Darkness," and in another, the "Prince of this world." This region also relates to the physical body of man.

<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>

For this reason, the heaven is called by the Hebrews אשמים (*Shamayim*), from אש (*esh*), meaning fire, and מים (*mayim*), meaning water; in Greek, it is called *Aether*, meaning "as it were, fiery air" <note>original: "quasi igneus aer"</note>.

As for its activity and motion, it receives these from that eternal emanation which *Solomon* said is "the most movable of all things." In truth, it is the first universal mover, the President of the <term>primum mobile</term> <note>The "first moved" sphere that carries all others</note>. By its action, all the inferior intelligences move their rolling and twinkling fires, just as many external wheels move and receive life from the motion of a central wheel. 

Thus, we see why this region of the world is called "Heaven" or the "sphere of equality"—because it is a mixture of form and matter in equal proportions. We also see why it is called the "sphere of the soul of the world," because it is composed of the pure spirit of the waters (which is female and passive) and the bright fire or act of eternity. For the divine Mind acts through this humid nature—which serves as its vehicle—to show forth its life-giving and emanating property through this spiritual organ. Therefore, all life consists of "essential heat" <note>original: "ex calido essentiali"</note> as the masculine or active element, and "radical moisture" <note>original: "humido radicali"</note> as the female or passive element. This region, therefore, refers to the vital soul in man and relates to the geometric "square" of both form and matter, which sits in the middle between the "cube" and the "root."

### Mosaical Philosophy. Book 1.

...substance is almost light and fire, and it is thought to be the seat of the angels, who are the ministers of their great Prince, the Lord of Light. This is proven by the presence of the two Cherubim—or fiery angels—which shadow the <term>mercy seat</term> <note>original: "propitiatory"; the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant</note> with their wings. This heaven relates to the intellect in man, which the Hebrews call *Nessaniah* <note>Likely a variation of *Neshamah*, the highest level of the soul in Jewish mysticism</note>, the Greeks call *Nous*, and the Latins call *Mens* (or the "mental beam"), which has dominion over the human soul. 

So we may discern that in the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>original: "great world"</note>, the angelic heaven—being the most formal and fiery—is, as it were, the soul of the <term>ethereal heaven</term> <note>The region of the stars and planets</note>. Through it and from it, this region receives its life, motion, and being. By the same proportion, the celestial or ethereal heaven is the soul or "agent" of the elementary region. For by means of the Sun, Moon, and Stars, which dart down their beams and influences upon the earth like arrows against a target, the earth, the water, and all things within them act, live, generate, and multiply. 

Because of this, all philosophers consider the heavens to be the Male and the earth and other elements to be the Females. Between these two, all generations are made in and upon the earth and in the sea; for the earthly body cannot operate without a heavenly touch. Indeed, even man himself requires the heavenly act and aid for his generation. Therefore, **Aristotle** concludes that *"the sun and man beget man"* <note>original Latin: "sol & homo generat hominem"</note>. Again, all philosophers generally agree on this: namely, that *"superior bodies act upon inferior ones, in the manner of a male upon a female"* <note>original Latin: "superiora agunt in inferiora, more maris in fœminam"</note>. 

The maxim of all such <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Mystics who study the Kabbalah</note> who are well-versed in mystical <margin>Reuchlin, Book 3. *On the Art of the Kabbalah*</margin> theology asserts that *"all inferior things represent the superiors; and as it is below, so it is acted above"* <note>original Latin: "omnes res inferiores sunt representativæ superiorum; & sicut fit inferius, sic agitur superius"</note>. In truth, a notable person well-versed in this obscure learning asserts that the <term>evial</term> <note>original: "æviall"; relating to eternity or the realm of angels</note> or angelic heaven is framed after the pattern of the eternal and ideal world. The temporal, elementary heaven or region is the image of the celestial or ethereal one. Thus, the images and actions of the darker world have their ideal shapes in and from the lighter, starry world. The starry world's shapes and actions were first delineated in the intellectual or angelic world, and those, in turn, proceed originally from the radical pattern without beginning in the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original divine blueprint in the mind of God</note>.

I conclude, therefore, that both theology and mystical philosophy agree that God is well pleased with the holy **ternary** <note>The number three</note>, which is the first odd number in arithmetic progression. We Christians honor a Trinity of Persons in one Deity, and **Aristotle** says that we are instructed by a natural kind of instinct or habit to honor God by the number three. He speaks with reason here, since in the ideal world there were three properties extracted out of one unity, after whose example the real world was afterward made. Thus, the Trinity in Divinity was the root of the formal composition of all worlds. 

By the root 3, the intellectual or angelic world was defined; by the square 9 ($3 \times 3$), the celestial world; and by the cube 27 ($3 \times 3 \times 3$), the elementary world—as we may gather from Platonic learning. But as for the Kabbalistic Rabbis, they consider the quantitative proportions of this ternary in another way. Just as the cube of three consists of three 9s, they take these three 9s and order them in this ternary position: **999** (nine hundred ninety-nine). 

Following the rules of <term>arithmetic</term> <note>original: "Algorism"</note>:
1.  The first **9** (on the right) is a simple digit. Because of its simplicity and essential nature, they attribute it to the nine orders of angels belonging to the intelligible world. 
2.  The middle **9** (representing tens) seems to partake partly of "form" (simplicity) and partly of "matter." Therefore, they allot it to the nine orbs or spheres of the starry heaven. 
3.  The third **9** (representing hundreds) implies a deeper and more material composition belonging to the elementary world. 

All of these eventually terminate in Man, who is like a passage (following the figure of unity) from them toward celestial things, and from there toward the intellectual. 

To conclude: **Unity**—in whom the philosopher **Leucippus** placed the sovereign good and happiness—when added to these three sets of nine, makes a complete **1,000**. This is the cube of ten and the end of all numbers according to Hebrew calculation. Beyond the number 10, as Aristotle asserts, no one has ever found any new number. After this aforesaid type or image, the ancient Law divided the fruits and goods coming from the earth, ordaining the "centenary" number <note>The number 100</note> as being more material and gross...

### Section 2. Mosaic Philosophy.

This is rightly termed the idea or image of a unison. Just as the unison, like one essence in divinity, includes three persons—representing the three accords in the archetypal harmony—so also the **octave** <note>original: *Diapason*</note> includes the two other accords within itself: namely, the **perfect fifth** <note>original: *Diapente*</note> and the **perfect fourth** <note>original: *Diatessaron*</note>. Now, I can prove that this most perfect consonant of the octave is planted in the middle of a unison and begets within itself two perfect chords or octaves. Take a lute or a bandora <note>a stringed instrument popular in the 16th and 17th centuries</note> and strike any string open. Then, stop that same string exactly in its middle; each half will sound an octave above that open unison. Thus, the unison made by striking the whole open string will be divided into two octaves, which are the most perfect consonants relative to the whole.

This is clear evidence that the perfection of the octave is seated in the Sun. Consequently, the formal and lively accord of the whole world is in that central or middle place, just as the heart—the seat of life—is in a human being. Yet, through the Sun's beams, this life of the world is made universal <note>original: *catholick*</note> and fills everything, just as the vital blood spreads itself everywhere in the **microcosm** <note>term: the "little world," a traditional philosophical term for the human body as a reflection of the universe</note> through the channels of the arteries. 

But I fear I have followed this point too far in order to prove and maintain the existence of the soul of this world. Therefore, I will leave it and come directly to the point. In my *Mosaic Philosophy*, specifically in the fourth book, I have fully proved and maintained that St. Jerome’s translation is correct: namely, **"He set his tabernacle in the sun"** <note>original: *Posuit tabernaculum suum in sole*</note>. I will proceed now to the second opinion of the philosophers.

The ancient philosophers Democritus and Orpheus, along with the Pythagoreans, judge that "all things are full of gods." They refer all these gods back to one **Jupiter**. By "gods," they intend the divine virtues infused into things, which Zoroaster called **"divine attractions"** <note>original: *divinos illices*</note> and Bishop Synesius called **"symbolic charms"** <note>original: *Symbolicas illecebras*</note>. Others term them "lines," and others "forts," upon which the virtue of things depends. They do not err much in this saying, except in appearing to divide the Godhead into many different gods. However, they seem to excuse themselves of that error by saying all those gods had a "relation" to one Jupiter; by using that word "relation," they preserve the continuity and indivisibility of the Soul. 

They agree, therefore, with the Scriptures in their meaning that this divine essence is in all things. As the Scriptures acknowledge, the universal Spirit of Wisdom is one simple Spirit; yet it is termed by Solomon as **"manifold"** <note>original: *multiplex*</note>
<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
regarding its many actions or properties in the creatures it animates. It is said to
<margin>Wisdom 1.</margin>
fill the universe, and the incorruptible Spirit of God is said to be in all things,
<margin>Wisdom 12.</margin>
giving life and motion to all. For it is **"more movable and full of life than any-**
<margin>Wisdom 7.</margin>
**thing else; being only one thing, it is able to do all things while remaining permanent within itself; therefore, it animates all, being in everything and everywhere."** 

For this reason, the poets say: **"All things are full of Jupiter"** <note>original: *Omnia Jovis plena*</note>. That is to say, the essential beams of this eternal Jupiter—or **JEHOVAH**—are in every particular place of the world, making things live and exist through different properties. For this reason, they conclude that **"all things are full of gods"** <note>original: *omnia diis plena*</note>, as was said before. I come now to the third point.

The Platonists, and all those philosophers who agree with them, differ in nothing from Orpheus, Democritus, and the rest, except that they call that the **Soul of the World** which the others term Jupiter. The gods who possess all things, they call "peculiar souls" or "mental beams," which depend on and have a 
<margin>Wisdom 12:1.</margin>
continuous relation to the **Soul of the World** <note>original: *Anima mundi*</note>. Just as the **incorruptible Spirit of the Lord, which fills each particular thing, is not separated from that moist fountain that fills the universe.**

It is evident, therefore, by what has already been said, that all the following opinions of the philosophers regarding the Soul of the World can be fully confirmed and maintained by these same reasons. Therefore, I will say no more regarding this point at this time.

I conclude, then, that since the Soul of the World has for its internal action the bright emanation of the eternal Unity, and uses the subtle universal created Spirit as its moist vehicle <note>term: a medium or "organ" through which a higher force acts</note> or material organ—which is its external part, in which and by which it operates in all and over all—we must acknowledge that there is a kind of contrariety in the universal Soul itself. Otherwise, action and passion would not exist in the created Soul. This soul is called "created" because it is made of "alterity" (that is, of two things): namely, of a created passive part, which is an offspring of the dark Chaos...

And therefore <margin>Hermes</margin> *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic Corpus</note> did not speak wrongly when he said that the world was the image of God, and man the image of the world. This being the first thing to be considered, I proceed as follows:

The variety of species upon the earth fundamentally proceeded from the very act of creation, when the word *Fiat* <note>original: *Fiat* (Latin); "Let it be done"</note> was spoken, and immediately the will of the speaker was accomplished by his Son, who was sent into the world by way of emanation to do the will of his Father. And there are some who do not hesitate to say that all the species or kinds of creatures were expressed in and by the <margin><unclear>Exodus chapters 1 and 2</unclear></margin> 22 Hebrew letters—not the external ones which are commonly painted with ink or art (which are but shadows), but the fiery, formal, and bright spiritual letters which were engraved on the face or surface of the dark *hyle* <note>term: *hyle* is a Greek word for "matter" or "substance"</note> by the fiery word of the eternal Speaker in the beginning. Therefore, they are originally termed *Elementa quasi Hylementa* <note>original: *Elementa quasi Hylementa* (Latin); "Elements as if Matter-elements"</note>, or Elements, as they were engraved in the forehead of the <margin>Maimonides, Book 8, Chapter 1</margin> dark abyss or *hyle*. Because of the essence of that divine Word—which received the mystery of the typical creation, traced it out after the archetypal pattern, and outlined it in characters of formal fire—the language framed from it was called *Lingua Sancta* <note>original: *Lingua Sancta* (Latin); "Holy Language," referring to Hebrew</note>. This language is much spoken of by the learned Rabbis of our age but little known or understood by them, yet it is of infinite importance for the true explanation <note>original: "enucleation"</note> of sacred mysteries as well as all true Kabbalistic <note>original: "Cabalisticall"</note> complexities. 

But to proceed: according to the tenor of the divine Word and his formal characters—the effects of which passed unalterably into the world—each species or kind was framed. Furthermore, every individual of each kind was made diverse and distinct from others, in shape and proportion as well as in condition and property.

Now, as I said, this Spirit of the Lord carried out the will of his Father in creating everything so differently, despite being in itself one and the same essence. So also did it, and still does, continue and maintain every one of these species or kinds through multiplication or generation in their successive states. It preserves every individual during its lifespan through both an elementary and an ethereal kind of nourishment <note>original: "nutriment"</note>, which descends from heaven according to its spiritual nature to nourish the spirits of each individual according to its kind. For you must understand that just as the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> soul of the world is common to all, so is the air made the chest or closet of its golden treasury or spiritual food. While it swims hidden <note>original: "occultly"</note> like a golden vapor showered down from heaven in the air, filling and replenishing everything, it is just as capable of sustaining and multiplying the life of a serpent, a sheep, a fish, or a bird, an oak, a herb, or such as it is of a man. 

For as soon as the magnetic power or virtue of the creature (which causes a refreshment <note>original: "refection"</note> from this heavenly nectar every minute) has drawn in a portion of this universal spirit or nature, it leaves its universal or general nature and works specifically. That is to say: if it is in a dog, it converts itself into his nature; in a whale, into his nature; in a man, into his; in an oak or myrtle, into his; in wheat, into the proper nature of wheat, and so in all other kinds. Consequently, it is the cause of every creature's spirit being nourished and sustained within itself. For this was the Creator's ordinance: that by whichever spirit the creature was first created in its kind, by that same spirit it should be maintained, preserved, and multiplied. Therefore, the philosopher bursts forth into this speech: "There is in the air a hidden food of life" <note>original: *Est in aere occultus vitæ cibus* (Latin)</note>. <margin>In *The New Chemical Light* <note>A famous alchemical text by Michael Sendivogius</note></margin> By this, he means that quintessential food which we receive from the general Spirit of life in the world, which by the appointment of God hangs ready in every part of the air to provide the spiritual food of life for every elementary creature. The main virtue of this consists in the eternal, life-giving Word and Spirit of all things. Therefore the Text says: <margin>Acts 17:25, John 10:12, Psalm 30:6</margin> "God gives life and breath and all things" <note>original: *Deus dat vitam & inspirationem & omnia* (Latin)</note>. And again, "Your visitation preserves my spirit" <note>original: *Visitatio tua conservat spiritum meum* (Latin)</note>.

We are also taught by Christ in our "Our Father" <note>original: Pater-noster</note> to pray for our daily bread, and it is called there *supersubstantial bread* <note>original: Panem super-substantialem</note>, as Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> interpreted it. And our Savior, speaking of this spiritual bread, says: *Our Father gives us true bread from heaven; for it is the true bread which descends from heaven and gives life to the world* <note>original: Pater noster dat nobis de coelo panem verum, panis enim verus est, qui de coelo descendit, & dat vitam mundo</note>. 

But I know it will be alleged against me that the bread mentioned here refers to spiritual bread, and not that which nourishes the body. I grant that, in a true sense, they do not speak wrongly, for this bread or food is spiritual; therefore, it is stored in the heart and arteries of the creature and is nothing in itself but pure life. Does not our Savior say, *Man lives not*

*only by bread, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God* <note>original: Non solo pane vivit homo, sed omni verbo quod procedit ab ore Dei</note>? These words were understood by Moses to refer to that <term>Manna</term> <note>The miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert</note> by which the Israelites were nourished in the wilderness. And the Apostle calls the food with which they were nourished the *spiritual Rock*, which was Christ. Therefore, that spiritual Rock said, *I am the bread of life* <note>original: Ego sum panis vitæ</note> *which descended from heaven, etc.* In this Word, therefore, is life alone, and in no other food; and it is this element in the nourishment which provides sustenance, and not the physical creature alone, for life was in the Word only. For this reason, it was said, *And he saw that all things which he created were good* <note>original: Et vidit quod omnia quæ creavit essent bona</note>; that is to say, they were not void or empty, but full of God’s essential being, which is God alone. For it was He who, by his presence, made the creature good by participation <note>The idea that created things are "good" only because they share in God's perfect goodness</note>. 

I will tell you what some of the <term>Ethnic Philosophers</term> <note>Ancient Greek or Pagan philosophers who were not Christian</note> say regarding this point. In truth—and it is a great pity—they had a deeper insight into the divine mysteries of God in nature than some in our own age who call themselves Christians. Yet these people are actually barren in the true foundations of Christianity, being quicker to judge and condemn the old philosophers as <term>reprobates</term> <note>Those rejected by God and destined for damnation</note> reserved for damnation solely for not bearing the name of a Christian, rather than observing the beam in their own eye. This blindness causes them to judge their brothers rashly, when judgment on that point belongs to God alone. They forget the Apostle’s saying, which asserts *that all men are of God's generation* <note>original: Act. 17; Acts 17:28–29</note>. 

*But to the purpose:* This is why the philosopher Zeno called the vital soul in a man *natural fire* <note>original: Ignem naturalem</note>, and Prometheus terms it *the celestial fire that enriches man with life* <note>original: Ignem coelestem homines vitâ ditantem</note>. Because Prometheus obtained full possession of it, the poets imagine that he was punished by Jupiter’s command for stealing this celestial fire. Hermes calls it *the fire of the Word*, which clings to the <term>humid nature</term> <note>The moist or watery fundamental substance</note> of the world. Zoroaster and Heraclitus say that it is that invisible fire from which all generation and multiplication is made. 

Since, therefore, this never-dying fire of life is in every living creature, it is necessary for its preservation and multiplication that it be nourished by something like itself in the air every moment—or by the <term>vehicle</term> <note>A substance that carries or transmits another; here, the air carries the spirit</note> of the air—lest it should vanish and the creature perish. This is what the philosopher Parmenides seems to suggest when he says, *Nature rejoices in its own nature* <note>original: Natura suâ natura laetatur</note>. For this very reason, the fiery power of life, located in the center of the creature's heart, does with comfort and delight draw and suck into itself—by a certain <term>magnetic faculty</term>—its like out of the air through breathing; for, as I told you, this hidden food or nourishment of life is in the air. This is the reason, therefore, that a certain author, who was deeply learned in the mysteries of nature, broke out into this speech: *O heavenly Nature of truth, which multiplies the natures of God!* <note>original: O Natura coelestis veritatis, naturas Dei multiplicans!</note> And again: *O strong nature, nature conquering and overcoming, and making two natures rejoice!* <note>original: O natura fortis, natura vincens & superans, duasque naturas gaudere faciens</note>

For by the power of this, not only life but also the fruits of reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note> are produced infinitely. We infer by what has already been said that the elementary air is full of the influences of life, growth <note>original: "vegetation"</note>, and the formal seeds of multiplication, because it is a storehouse that abounds with divine beams and heavenly gifts. 

Nor does our assertion only apply to the animal kingdom of composition, but also to that of the vegetables. For by this spirit they grow; by this they multiply infinitely; and, in conclusion, by this they exist and have their being. For by my own eyewitness experience I am a witness—and, if necessary, I can quickly demonstrate—that in the vegetable is a pure volatile salt, which is nothing but the essential air of the specific substance, which is wheat or bread. This volatile salt is an unctuous liquor, as white and clear as crystal; yet inwardly it is full of vegetating fire, by which the species is multiplied *infinitely* <note>original: "in infinitum" </note>. For it is a magnetic power by which it draws and sucks its life abundantly from the air and sunbeams, which is the principal storehouse of life, because in it the eternal emanation of life planted his Tabernacle (as I have plainly demonstrated in the fourth book of my *Mosaical Philosophy*). 

I have seen this volatile saltpeter <note>In 17th-century science, "saltpeter" (nitre) was often considered a vital, life-giving substance found in the air, not just an ingredient for gunpowder</note> of this vegetable, once freed from its elementary bonds and being in its oily nature in the form of a liquor. I perceived it to be so desirous of the beams of life that lurked in the air and were darted from the sun, that in the space of three hours, it changed from a white crystalline color into a bloody ruby. By this I was easily taught the reason for formal multiplication in both animals and vegetables; for by this reasoning, a grain of wheat is multiplied into a million. 

Again, no true philosopher can be ignorant that the saltpeter of every thing—which is only air—by virtue of that mystical spirit which dwells in it, attracts air as well as the celestial form to itself, since the form cannot be inspired except by means of its airy vehicle. By this very means also, the quantity of the airy substance, as well as the formal quality, is augmented, which causes both growth and multiplication. By the strong magnetic attraction of the celestial tincture <note>An alchemical term for a fundamental essence or spiritual quality</note> which hovers in the air, or the volatile salt which is of the substance and nature of blood in animals, it is easy to know how blood in the animal's body is transformed from a white, milky substance <note>original: "chylous substance"</note> into a deep and ruddy blood. 

By reasoning from its growth and multiplication in substance, it is an easy matter to guess the manner of growth and vegetation, and also of the quantitative multiplication by way of reproduction in the animal. For truly, I have observed such a worthy experiment in this vegetative salt in wheat—of which the blood of man is full by eating bread—that we need not doubt that it is the only substance of growth in both the animal and the vegetable. For one day, when I had cast away the dregs <note>original: "fæces"</note> or superfluous part of the substance out of which I drew the salt liquor into a large <term>pipkin</term> <note>a small earthenware cooking pot</note> and covered it with a thin plate of iron, within three weeks or a month's space, I found it to have struck up out of the pot right through the plate of iron. It made above a thousand blades, like iron-colored saffron, grow up out of its surface, which argues the admirable vegetative property that it has within it. 

But letting this suffice to express the hidden power of this secret fire of God in nature, in all vegetables, minerals, and other animals, I will now turn the focus of my speech only toward that wondrous act and operation which this admirable Spirit effects in the "little world," or man.

The spirit of life was so inspired into man by God that he was made a living creature, no differently than when the *Spirit of God* <note>original: "Elohim Ruach"</note> was breathed on the waters, and they were animated and brought to life, becoming a great world—which the Platonists for that reason called a *Great living creature* <note>original: "Magnum animal"</note>. But as the world was made after the image of God before man was made, and afterwards man was framed by the Word through that same Spirit in the world, after the pattern of 그 spirit of life and the substance of the waters which were in the great world. Therefore, we must conceive that man has the vivifying means of his sustenance, preservation, and multiplication by generation from the soul of the world and its elements.

The soul or life is in the air, the mental spirit is in the soul, the Word is in the mental spirit; and the Word is the Father of them all. And he concludes in that place: *That the Word is the Image of God, the mental beam the image of the Word, the vital soul the image of the mental beam, the air of the vital soul, and the body of the air* <note>original: "Quod Verbum sit imago Dei, mens verbi, anima mentis, aer anima, & corpus aëris"</note>. By this we may discern the wonderful connection that every portion of each rank <note>original: "dignity"</note> in the Great World <term>the Macrocosm or universe</term> has to the others in the composition of the Little World <term>the Microcosm or human being</term>. Therefore, it is made evident that the purest portion of elementary matter is air; the purest height of the air is the vital form, in which is the mental beam; and in it is the Word, which is God. We must observe that by *mind* <note>original: "mentem"</note>, or the mental spirit, is meant the life-giving Spirit of Wisdom which fills all things, whose fountain, as *Ecclesiasticus* teaches us, is the Word of God. 

It is as if I, along with *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed</note>, should say: the bright and eternal Spirit of life in the quintessential spirit <term>the "fifth essence," the purest substance beyond the four elements</term> makes the soul; the soul in the air is conducted into the body, where it performs the effects of giving life and the internal reproduction <note>original: "multiplication"</note> of the species. Therefore, he says in another place: *The soul of man is carried into his body in this manner: The mental beam is the rational spirit, the rational spirit is in the soul or ethereal spirit, the soul or ethereal spirit is in the airy spirit, and the airy spirit is in the body. This spirit is spread through the veins, arteries, and the blood, and it stirs and moves the living creature on every side* <note>original: "Anima hominis in hunc vehitur modum: Mens in ratione, ratio in anima, anima in Spiritu, & spiritus in corpore: Spiritus per venas arteriasque sanguinemque diffusus, animal undique ciet"</note>. 

We must therefore imagine that the air which is drawn into our heart by breathing <note>original: "inspiration"</note> is full of that divine treasure of life. Residing in the heart of man, it sucks and draws his life into it by a magnetic force and power; for nature desires and rejoices at the presence of its own kind, as has been said. And again, that the heart is the precious storehouse of the active treasure of life, we may gather from this speech of *Solomon*: *Guard and keep your heart with the greatest diligence, seeing that from it proceed all the actions of life* <note>original: "Cor tuum custodi supra omnem observationem, quia ab eo procedunt actiones vitæ"</note>. The nature and instruments by which the spirit magnetically attracts—and expels after attraction—that part of the moist vehicle of air which is useless and superfluous, are these:

Since no creature (among which we consider Man to be the chief) can live for even a moment without the sparks of life and reproduction <note>original: "generation"</note> that swim in the air, it is most necessary that they should be drawn and sucked in by the creature every minute. Without this necessary act and its healthy effect, the animal will immediately be suffocated or strangled. For by the deprivation of air, the soul will soon cease its life-giving operation; for the soul is nothing else but a portion of eternal light in the soul of the world <term>Anima Mundi</term>, which is composed (as I proved before) of the divine emanating power and the subtle, moist nature of the world. The first provides the *innate heat* <note>original: "Calidum innatum"</note> or natural heat of life, and the last provides the *radical moisture* <note>original: "humidum radicale"</note> for the creature's existence. Therefore, by the breathing of air, this double power is renewed and refreshed in the creature every moment. 

This Spirit, therefore, the animal (and consequently man) breathes or sucks into the left chamber, ventricle, or region of the heart through the contraction of the straight fibers of the heart, while the transverse and diagonal <note>original: "oblique"</note> fibers are relaxed, whereby the heart is dilated or opened. This action is called by physicians the *Diastole*. In the time or interval of this motion, the heart draws into its left vessel—by way of the pulmonary vein <note>original: "Arteria venosa"</note> out of the lungs, where it was first conveyed by breathing through the windpipe <note>original: "aspera arteria" or "weesell-pipe"</note>—a portion of the airy storehouse of nature. This contains the vital treasure ordained by God for life-giving and spiritual/reproductive <note>original: "seminal"</note> purposes; that is to say, for the nourishment of the vital and internal reproductive spirits. This is no different from how the liver is used to suck and draw the milky juice <note>original: "chylous juice"</note> of coarse nutrition to create and foster the natural spirits, which are intended for growth <note>original: "vegetation"</note> or the increasing of the bodily parts. 

Again, after nature has received and drawn this airy spirit (with its hidden or secret treasure) into her well-adorned and subtly adapted laboratory—I mean the heart—she begins in it to analyze <note>original: "anatomize"</note> and search the depths of this attracted air. [The heart] reserves only the purest [part of the air], which is nothing but a subtle volatile salt <note>original: "volatile salt"; in early chemistry, this refers to a chemically active, vaporous substance believed to carry the life force</note>, adapted to serve as a vehicle for the divine fire of life, or the true life-giving Spirit, in its ethereal and quintessential nature. As for the selected Spirits of life, the heart encloses them in its large arterial storehouse called the *Aorta* or *Arteria magna* (the *great Artery*), immediately sending the more sooty <note>original: "fuligions"; referring to the smoky or waste-like byproducts of the "fire" of life</note> and useless parts of the air back the way they came through exhaling. This expelling action is performed by the contraction of the transverse fibres of the heart and the relaxation of the straight ones; by this means, the heart is contracted or compressed. This movement is called *Systole* by physicians. We must understand that for the better preservation of this golden treasure of life within His arterial treasure-house, God has so ordered nature that there is a triple valve or gate, like three half-moons <term>semilunar valves</term>, to close it in and keep it secure for the body's needs. This prevents the spirit from flying away through the passage it entered. Therefore, this three-leaved gate is fashioned in such a way that it opens inward and is closed from the outside, so that what enters the great Artery cannot return. Similarly, at the mouth of the pulmonary vein <note>original: "venal artery"; in the 17th century, the pulmonary vein was often called the "venal artery" because it carries oxygenated "arterial" blood but has the structure of a vein</note>, there is a double gate made of two valves that open outward and shut within. Thus, fresh air may easily enter, but the included treasure—after the expulsion of the sooty vehicle or superfluous air—may be retained.

Now I will briefly express to you the action of this heavenly Spirit. After it is enclosed in the arterial trunk, it is certain that it spreads itself through the branches or divided channels of the heart over the entire body. Through those branches called the *Carotids* <note>original: "Charotides"</note>, a refined portion of it ascends to the brain through those small conduits. I say that the super-celestial part of this chemical extraction (being the most excellent fountain of life) claims the noblest and highest region of this microcosmic <term>human</term> palace as its seat and possession, serving as its Imperial heaven. Here the mental beam soars in its rational vehicle, choosing this place for its chief tabernacle or *heaven of heavens* <note>original: "cœlum cœlorum"</note>; yet the beams of its power are reflected into every branch of its divided arterial cabinet. For this reason, all physicians—both Pagan <note>original: "Ethnick"</note> and Christian—have concluded that voluntary human action has its seat in the brain, being the region of the "animal" (soulish) virtue or faculty. Meanwhile, the other two actions of man—namely the vital action in the heart and the natural action in the liver—seem to be subject to the brain, because they are *involuntary actions*. This is why the brain is the seat of reason and understanding. 

Then, in the second rank, that portion of the introduced Spirit which is refined in the forge of man’s nature and found fit for the action of life is conveyed into those branches of the great Artery called the *Cervical*, *Humeral* <note>original: "Cervicales, Humerariæ"</note>, and those which assign life to the region of the chest or breast. There it takes on the impression of spiritual vivacity belonging to those parts. Similarly, the *Coronary* arteries assume the internal or ideal shape of spirits belonging to the heart, and so on through the other arterial branches and the heavenly treasure they contain. Thus, this invisible spirit—lurking and, as it were, swimming in the thin substance of the airy spirit—not only expands and dilates itself to give life to every member of the body, but also by a contraction of itself into a "spermatic cloud" (which happens during the act of intercourse through a certain magnetic virtue animated by divine love), this spirit is miraculously conveyed into two preparing arterial spermatic vessels from every member, but especially from the three principal organs. There, this celestial Spirit, full of divine fire, acts according to the image of the radical Archetype <term>the original divine blueprint</term> in whom all things were first spiritually and ideally designed before they existed in the material world. (Even the Prophet David gloried in having received the complete image of the Temple described by the hand of God, which was later built). This spirit contains the invisible form of that human body which was shortly to be enacted and brought forth into man’s sight. That is to say, it ideally possessed the shape of the inward or spiritual man; likewise, the image of the external or physical man, being composed of the four Elements, proceeds from the visible sperm which issued from the two venous spermatic vessels.

Did you not pour me out like milk, and did you not curdle me like a cheese? You endowed <note>original: "indue"</note> me with skin and flesh, and compacted or joined me together with bones and sinews. You exercised your kindness towards me in giving me life, and your visitation <note>original: "visitation"; meaning God's active oversight or presence</note> has preserved my spirit. In all this, this difficult point appears to be fully explained and opened, both regarding the act of generation <term>reproduction</term> and the aforementioned mystery of the preservation and continuation of the child's life, both in the mother's womb and after birth. For in this passage, "Did you not pour me out like milk," he seems to argue that the spermatic mass <note>the material seed</note> was well-ordered and composed by the spirit of life, from which a man was afterward explicitly outlined and framed. Then he goes forward to the second stage of reproduction, "And did you not curdle me like cheese," by which it appears that the divine Spirit thickened the seed into a more solid substance like cheese, according to that other saying of *Job*, "Remember, I pray you, that you made me like clay" <note>original: "Memento quæso quod sicut argillam fecisti me"</note>,

etc. Remember that you made me as clay, etc. Then he proceeds thus: "You clothed me with skin and flesh, and joined me together with bones and sinews," etc. And now in this stage he comes—after the thickening <note>original: "coagulation"</note> of the spermatic mass—to the completion of the specific human parts or members from which the external man is made in the womb, just as the spiritual image of the son was in the arterial seed of the father before it was cast into the womb. By all this, it appears that the divine Spirit operated all this outward man in his own person. Then, for the giving of life <note>original: "vivification"</note> to that external man so shaped out of the physical seed, he proceeds thus: "You have shown me favor with life"; showing by this that once the physical work was finished and made fit to house so noble and imperial a guest as the divine mental beam <note>the human soul, seen as a ray of God’s intellect</note>—namely, that of its builder, riding in a worldly vehicle <term>the body</term>—the lordly guest immediately possesses it and makes it live, move, and feel, according to

Neither was that breath of life devoid of understanding—that is to say, without the real beam of eternity—for it is said elsewhere: "There is a spirit in man, but the inspiration of the Almighty gives him understanding" <note>original: "In homine est spiritus, sed inspiratio Omnipotentis facit eum intelligere"</note>.

### The Argument of this Second Book.

<margin>129</margin>The author, having through diligent inquiry found the essential root of **sympathy** and **antipathy** (as already expressed in the first book), proved it to be one universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> simplicity in essence, though having a two-fold property. These properties are quite opposite to one another in nature and condition, no differently than "willingness" is to "unwillingness" <note>original: "Volunty" and "Nolunty," terms for the divine will to act and the divine will to refrain from acting</note>. He thought it was not enough to gather from circumstances and conclude "that it is so" <note>original Greek: ὅτι (*hoti*)</note>. Therefore, in this present book, he attempts with the most intense efforts <note>original: "tightest and highest stretched nerves"</note> of his understanding to search out "why and wherefore" <note>original Greek: διότι (*dioti*)</note>, and by what means this double act is scattered throughout the universe. 

Indeed, he finds this last branch so difficult to discover by mortal capacities that he considers it a great masterpiece in this research. For this reason, he is content to be guided into this difficult path of profound speculation by the light or "pole-star" of such sublime and purified theological and Kabbalistic <note>original: "Cabalisticall"</note> spirits who have received the explanation <note>original: "enucleation," literally "un-shelling"</note> of such a great mystery from that highest spiritual emanation. He is the only revealer of deep and hidden mysteries (as the Prophet Daniel and the wise Solomon assure us) who, because he is the essential actor in both **sympathy** and **antipathy**, is most able to describe and set forth this mystery—which men so earnestly hunt after—in its liveliest colors. 

By observing the rules and axioms of the Holy Scriptures, as well as the learned Hebrew and Egyptian Rabbis, the author has gathered that the eternal, divine, and archetypal world (which has neither beginning nor end) radically springs from one simple and universal fountain of light. It pours out a ten-fold emanation <note>A reference to the ten Sephiroth, or divine attributes, in Kabbalah</note>, endowed with a ten-fold property, into the aerial or angelic world (which has its beginning from the eternal one, but no end). The aerial world, in like manner, pours those divine outflows or emanations of light—by way of angelic vehicles—into the temporal world (which has both a beginning and an end). So it is that the ethereal or celestial region of the temporal world is made the storehouse or treasury of divine influences. From there, they are distilled down into the elementary...

# CHAPTER 1.

->*That Sympathy is the offspring of Light, just as Antipathy has its beginning from*<-
->*Darkness: The etymology or true meaning of both words;*<-
->*as well as the nature of both, are described here.*<-

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'S' featuring intricate scrolling foliage and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

Since the fundamental <note>original: "radical"</note> and essential Unity—along with its two opposite branches or properties, which are the characteristics of God’s <term>Nolunty and Volunty</term> <note>These terms refer to the "unwillingness" and "willingness" of God, representing the negative and positive aspects of divine power</note>—has been clearly described to you in general terms, along with their two universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> effects, namely love and hatred, and all those spiritual and physical passions derived from them (whether they are good or bad for the creature experiencing them), I think it is now most appropriate to enter into our main discourse. We shall dissect the inner workings of that sympathy and antipathy which are made manifest by their effects, not only in natural creatures but also in supernatural ones. 

No learned person, being instructed by daily experience (which is the mother even of fools), can be so ignorant and blind as not to discern the hidden miracles of both heavenly and earthly things. These shine forth daily in sympathy and antipathy—that is, in concords and discords—which are caused by a secret league or friendship that exists between things even from the moment of their first composition <note>original: "mixtion"</note> during creation. But before we presume to enter into this profound discovery, it is necessary to reveal the meaning or etymology of both words, so that we may better understand their distinct natures and essences.

*Sympathia* <note>original: "Sympathia"</note> is a Greek word—συμπαθεια (*sympatheia*)—and is derived from συν (*syn*), meaning "together with" <note>original: "una cum"</note>, and παθος (*pathos*), meaning "passion" or "suffering" <note>original: "passio"</note>, which comes from the verb πασχω (*pascho*), meaning "I suffer" <note>original: "patior"</note>. Likewise, *Antipathia* <note>original: "Antipathia"</note> is composed of αντι (*anti*), meaning "against" <note>original: "contra"</note>, and παθος (*pathos*). Therefore, the first term implies a passion born of unity, concord, and love, more properly called "compassion." The other implies a hateful passion moved by two resisting and fighting natures of opposing strength. 

I may therefore rightly define sympathy to be a consent, union, or concord between two spirits, shining forth or having their fundamental flow <note>original: "radical emanation"</note> from the very same or a similar divine property. As an example: All creatures that participate in those kind emanations or beams sent out from God through his angelic organs into the sphere of *Jupiter* are then emitted down to the earth. They are bestowed upon a multitude of creatures created under this property. For that reason, these creatures shine and emit their beams toward one another lovingly and joyfully because they all proceed from one root which descends through *Jupiter*. Also, those planets that are friends to *Jupiter*, or like him in condition (such as *Venus*, etc.), send down influences into creatures that are welcoming to those who, from their births, are sustained by and receive their constitutional qualities <note>original: "complexionary faculties"</note> from *Jupiter*. Therefore, they send forth beams of friendship or kindness toward one another. 

But on the contrary, where influences that are adverse in property—or from an opposing divine emanation—are sent down to the planet *Mars* (which is an enemy to *Jupiter*) and are poured out on creatures below, there will be ill and unwelcome encounters between the secret emissions of those creatures' beams. Thus, by a natural instinct, one seeks to fly and escape the encounters of the other, or to resist and fight against it, as shall be more largely and plainly expressed to you hereafter. 

Because the general cause of all sympathy and antipathy is a hidden and secret flow <note>original: "emanation"</note> or shining forth by the emission of beams from one creature to another, it is most necessary for us to unpack the bundle <note>original: "unloose the fardle"</note> of this profound business. In this way, we may more clearly behold and contemplate the fountain and root of all beams and radiations <note>original: "eradiations"</note> in general. Thus, we shall unfold and reveal the mystical reason for their differences and follow their extensions from the root to the trunk, from the trunk to the boughs and branches, and from those branches down to the individual twigs which nourish and foster an infinity of leaves and bring forth fruit in abundance.

# CHAPTER II.
## How and by what attributes or properties the Hebrew Rabbis and most profound Cabalists prove that the contrariety of natures proceeds from one eternal Essence, as if from the root of all things.

<margin>Reuchlin, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*, book 3.</margin>
**I**t is absolutely certain that just as there are an infinite number of creatures of different natures in the universal machine <note>original: "machin," referring to the structured universe</note>, every one of them was first created, and then generated and maintained after its birth—even until the day of its corruption <note>original: "corruption," meaning decay or death</note>—by various celestial influences or many thousands of different beams descending from above. For this reason, the wisest among the Kabbalistic Rabbis affirm: "There is not any plant or herb here below which does not have a star in the firmament that strikes it with its influence and, as it were, says to it, 'Increase or multiply'" <note>original: *Quod non sit ulla planta aut herba inferiùs, cui non sit stella in firmamento, quæ percutiat eam & dicat ei, Cresce*</note>. Nor do the Scriptures seem to contradict their opinion, as will be clearly explained later in the proper place. 

But because the fundamental <note>original: "radicall"</note> explanation of this matter requires deeper contemplation, it is necessary for the reader's education and instruction to perform a diligent investigation into the depths of this mystery. Specifically, we must first discover how all creation was brought about by the sending forth of the beams of God’s eternal Light, and whether that emanation is of one type or many and varied in its properties. I previously stated and clearly proved that all things were created in the beginning by one eternal Spirit of Wisdom. This Spirit was sent forth from the infinite Fountain of Light in the form of an emanation, radiation, or flowing forth to give form and life explicitly to all things which were previously contained implicitly within the divine power of that everlasting Unity—which is itself all in all. 

I proved this using these specific passages in Scripture: <margin>Wisdom 7</margin> Solomon calls this holy Spirit of discipline "the vapor of God’s power, the pure emanation and flowing forth of His brightness, the splendor or beams of His Divine Light, and the spotless mirror of His goodness" <note>original: *Sap. 7* refers to the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon</note>. <margin>John 1:8, John 1</margin> And Saint John says that in the Word is the life of all things, and that this Spirit was Light in which there was no darkness, and that by it all things were made, and without it nothing was made. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 1:24, Proverbs 8</margin> And the son of Sirach says that it came out of the mouth of the Most High. And Solomon says that it was with JEHOVAH in the beginning of all His ways during creation, and was that holy Spirit by which He composed or made all things in the Creation. 

Therefore, it is clear that it was through the emanation or sending forth of the universal <note>original: "catholick"</note> beam of divine Light that all specific things were differently framed, shaped, and animated. This was done through many streaming particular beams of light, multiplying from the root to the trunk or body—namely, from the Unity, fountain, or head, to the general emanation. This emanation can be rightly compared to the trunk of a tree, since all boughs, twigs, leaves, and fruit spring from it. Just as in a tree the trunk grows immediately from the root and yet remains connected to the root, which is the beginning <margin>Reuchlin, book 3, *On the Art of the Kabbalah*</margin>, so the divine emanation proceeds directly from *Ensoph* <note>In Kabbalah, *Ein Sof* represents the infinite God prior to self-manifestation</note>—the fountain or root of infinity—by way of an emanation that is not divided or separated from its eternal origin. Because of this, the Spirit is said to be the first thing created before all others, just as the trunk exists before the boughs, twigs, leaves, or fruit. 

Thus, regarding its essential existence, the Spirit is eternal; but regarding its emanation into the world, it is said to be "aevial" <note>original: "æviall," meaning eternal in the sense of having a beginning but no end</note>. This means it has a beginning but no end, and therefore becomes the head and prince of all the aevial world—by which I mean the angelic creatures. We continue, therefore, in the progression and multiplication of this universal emanation: from the trunk of the tree come the general, special, and individual branches. The strongest parts (after the trunk) are the main limbs of the body, then the boughs, then the twigs, and finally the leaves. We compare this to the various ranks of the angels in our angelic or aevial world. These ranks are assigned to them according to their dignity and the richness of the divine influences they receive from the root or fountain of Light, through the mediation of their "body," Jesus Christ. <margin>Colossians 1:13</margin> For this reason, it is said that "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creatures; for in him all things were made, both in heaven and earth, visible and invisible, whether they are Thrones, or Dominations, or Powers; all were made by him and in him, and he is before..."
